adeptus-ineptus-oder-entdeckung-der-fals: Adeptus ineptus, 1744. The inept adept. This book preserves that exposure. Scholars prize such firsthand sources. The paper lived through the years. It awaits future readers. The historical record keeps it. The archive guards it with care.
an-epitome-of-phrenology-1844: An 1844 epitome distilled phrenology to its essentials. The compact summary guided beginners. The phrenological primer. Those who study the era will use it. The archive keeps the paper open to all who seek it. Its pages add to the record of the past for readers.
artemidorus-oneirocritica-english-1644:
Artemidorus of Daldis wrote the Oneirocritica, antiquity's only complete surviving dream book. Robert Wood's English translation appeared in London in 1644, the first in the language. Artemidorus had traveled widely collecting dreams and their outcomes.

Across five books he catalogues what dream images signify for dreamers. Flying, losing teeth, snakes, and weddings all receive careful readings. He insists each dream be read against the dreamer's own station and life. Professional interpreters used manuals like his across the Roman world. The 1644 translation preserves early modern English in its rendering. Long before Freud, dream interpretation had this systematic ancient handbook.
arxiv-2511-20344:
Lee, Song, Yoon, Park, and Kang dissect how language models reason by analogy. Their 2025 paper probes proportional and story analogies inside LLMs. Analogy sits near the core of human thought. Models answer many analogy questions correctly already. Whether they truly encode relations was unclear.

Correct answers show relational signals in mid-upper layers. Both attribute and relation details flow there together. Failures often trace to missing relational content upstream. A second failure mode appears at application time. The relation exists but never reaches the new entity. Patching hidden states at key tokens can rescue transfer. That fix works to a useful extent in tests. Story analogies reveal an alignment signature as well. Success tracks strong structural mapping between stories. Failures show degraded or distractor-led alignment instead. Models thus abstract relations better than they apply them. Human-like analogy remains partial and brittle. Code for the analysis is public.
arxiv-2511-20544:
Ozguroglu and colleagues take AI out to smell New York City. Their 2025 paper releases New York Smells, a dataset pairing images with odor signals. Smell is central to animal perception yet nearly invisible to machines. Training data for machine olfaction barely exists anywhere. Lab-collected sets are small and disconnected from vision.

The team recorded scents in the wild across the city. An electronic nose captured signals from 3,500 distinct objects. Seven thousand smell-image pairs cover indoor and outdoor scenes. That is roughly seventy times more objects than prior datasets. Three benchmark tasks come with the release. Models retrieve images from smell and recognize scenes from smell alone. A fine-grained task separates different grass species by scent. Visual supervision enabled cross-modal representation learning here. Learned smell features beat hand-crafted ones widely used before. Real-world olfaction research gets its first large paired dataset.
arxiv-2511-20844:
David Szczecina offers in 2025 a simple defence against a common training problem: datasets whose labels contain errors. Deep networks memorise wrong labels, wrecking their accuracy on clean data, and most existing fixes assume a small clean subset exists to learn from. Szczecina's recipe needs none. First, a feature extractor learns from the images alone through self-supervised learning, which invents its own training signals; then supervised training runs on the noisy labels.

He tested two self-supervised methods, SimCLR and Barlow Twins, on the CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 image datasets. Noise came in two forms: synthetic, and the real-world noise of the CIFAR-N variants. Across every noise rate, pre-training improved classification accuracy and made label errors easier to detect afterwards. The advantage grew as noise increased. At low noise the approach merely matched models pre-trained on ImageNet, but at high noise it substantially outperformed them.
arxiv-2511-20944:
Yaw Osei Adjei and Fredrick Ayivor compare in 2025 two ways to catch business email compromise, the fraud behind over 2.9 billion dollars in annual losses reported by the FBI. The stakes are lopsided: a missed fraud costs about 137,000 dollars on average, a false alarm about 25 dollars of review time, a ratio near 5,480 to 1. One detector, a CatBoost model, reads psycholinguistic cues such as urgency and authority. The other, DistilBERT, reads the message's full semantics.

On a hybrid set of 7,990 emails mixing genuine mail with AI-written fraud, DistilBERT hit an F1 of 0.998 on synthetic threats, at 7.4 milliseconds per message on a Tesla T4 card. CatBoost reached an F1 of 0.949 while answering in 0.8 milliseconds, 8.4 times faster and on negligible hardware. Both showed theoretical returns above 99.9 percent under cost-sensitive tuning. The verdict: deep learning for GPU-equipped shops, the forensic stream for the edge.
arxiv-2511-21444:
Zhe Jiang and seven coauthors build an AI agent that diagnoses extreme weather like a seasoned forecaster, in 2025. Understanding why a heatwave or flood happened still depends on experts laboriously assembling charts and arguments by hand, a bottleneck as events intensify. Their Extreme Weather Expert, EWE, is the first agent framework built for this diagnostic reasoning rather than for prediction.

Jiang and his coauthors give EWE three parts: knowledge-guided planning, self-evolving closed-loop reasoning, and a meteorological toolkit that produces and reads maps and charts from raw data. To grade such agents, they release the field's first benchmark, 103 high-impact events with a step-wise scoring metric that credits partial progress. In experiments, EWE's components each proved necessary in ablation tests, and the Claude-4-Sonnet model performed best at key stages. The authors pitch EWE as expertise that poorer, storm-exposed nations can also use.
arxiv-2512-00144:
String theory needs extra dimensions curled into shapes called Calabi-Yau manifolds, whose geometry affects physical predictions. Mudit Jain and co-authors develop Bayesian tools for exploring those geometries in a 2025 study. They sample from a natural probability measure on the space of allowed shapes.

Sampling uses Markov chain Monte Carlo and normalizing flows on spaces with dimensions up to thirty. The authors report results on the spectrum of the manifold's volume and on divisor properties under physical restrictions. The work connects experimental data to string theory's axiverse, the large family of predicted axion-like particles. Axions are candidate dark matter particles, so the geometry has stakes beyond pure mathematics.
arxiv-2512-00744:
Zhengxin Chen, Xiaohai He, Tingrong Zhang, Shuhua Xiong, and Chao Ren work on learned image compression in a 2025 paper. Compression shrinks image files so they cost less to store and send. Learned methods, which train a network to do the shrinking, have lately beaten even the strong traditional codec called VVC.

Their strength comes from powerful nonlinear transforms that reshape image data before coding. The authors combine a multi-scale gated transformer with a prior-guided convolutional network. Transformers track broad patterns, while convolutional layers handle local detail. Joining the two could push file sizes down further while keeping pictures looking sharp.
arxiv-2512-00844:
Giles Winchester, George Parisis, and Luc Berthouze present FC-ADL in a 2025 paper on keeping microservice systems healthy. Modern software often splits into many small services that call each other. That design is flexible, but when something breaks, finding the fault fast is hard.

Most past detection methods watch each service's metrics without tracking how services depend on each other over time. FC-ADL uses functional connectivity, a measure of linked behavior between services, to spot anomalies and locate their source. Watching the links, not just the nodes, could help operators fix failures before users notice them.
arxiv-2512-01244:
C Monica Capra, Charles Holt, and Po-Hsuan Lin run experiments on timing and choices in a 2025 economics paper. In sequential play, one player moves first and another follows. When those moves are unobservable to each other, classic theory might suggest timing should not matter, since no information changes hands.

The authors test that idea, called virtual observability. Knowing who moves first can still shape expectations and choices, even when nothing is revealed. Their experimental evidence examines how strongly this timing effect changes behavior. The result matters for auctions, negotiations, and market design, where move order is a lever designers control.
arxiv-2512-01544:
Jianing Li, Weiyao Ke, and Jin Hu build a way to compute viscosity in dense nucleon matter. Such matter sits in neutron star cores. Its flow traits set how star quakes and mergers play out. Cold, dense matter acts as a Fermi liquid of quasiparticles.

The team starts from a linearized Boltzmann equation made for those quasiparticles. Their speeds shift with the medium they move in. The frame yields transport traits at mean-field level. Those traits feed models of merger waves and star cooling that scopes can test. Mean-field limits are stated up front, so users know which dense regimes the frame covers and which need fuller kinetic treatment.
arxiv-2512-02544:
Zhou Ziheng and four co-authors ask how society should reason about possible AI consciousness. As AI systems grow more capable, the question has moved from fringe talk to mainstream academic debate. The authors find fault with much of the current ethical discussion on the topic.

Many frameworks quietly assume contested functionalist views, they argue. Some also put speculative AI welfare ahead of concrete human interests, on shaky theoretical ground. Their human centric framework tries to keep ethics grounded under deep uncertainty. It aims to protect people first while the science of machine minds stays unsettled. The frame stays open on one point: what proof would be strong enough to change the call?
arxiv-2512-02744:
Rutger-Jan Lange, Bram van Os, and Dick van Dijk let model parameters drift over time in a new filtering scheme. Many economic and physical series change character slowly, so fixed parameters mislead. Score driven updates move parameters toward whatever improves fit to the latest observation.

Their implicit update maximizes the log observation density while penalizing jumps from the predicted value. The penalty uses a weighted norm, keeping moves smooth and stable. The result is an implicit stochastic gradient step. Filters of this kind serve forecasting in finance, energy, and climate, where regimes shift quietly. Smooth drift, not wild jumps, is what keeps a filter from chase its own tail when news comes in fast.
arxiv-2512-02944:
Patrizio Frosini and five co-authors introduce a new distance for comparing functions that take values in the plane. Multiparameter persistence studies data through several filters at once, summarizing shape in diagrams. A good metric between such summaries is the base of the whole method.

Their convex matching distance takes the largest bottleneck distance over all convex blends of the two components. Like the classic matching distance, it aggregates information from both real valued components. A well behaved metric lets analysts compare surfaces and fields, from medical images to material samples, with stable guarantees. Two part fields are the norm in scans and maps of stress. A sound way to rank them has work to do in more than one lab.
arxiv-2512-03244:
Step-by-step feedback can teach reasoning models better than final scores. Salman Rahman and co-authors propose Spark for that purpose in this 2025 work. Process reward models give dense feedback per step, but they need costly labels or ground truth.

Spark has three stages and needs no reference answers. First a generator makes diverse solutions, then a verifier judges them. The verifier uses self-consistency across parallel tries and critique across sequential steps. Cheaper step feedback could make reinforcement learning for reasoning more practical at scale. Reference-free rewards could cut the human labeling bill that limits process supervision today.
arxiv-2512-03944:
Quantum field theory on curved spacetime needs the response of operators built from differential equations on that background. Andrei O. Barvinsky, Alexey E. Kalugin, and Władysław Wachowski study integral kernels for such operator functions in a 2025 preprint. Their starting point is the heat kernel and its classic DeWitt expansion.

The authors show the kernel for a general operator function can be expanded by integrating the heat kernel series term by term. The expansion neatly separates geometry, carried by the standard coefficients, from the choice of function, carried by new scalar kernels they define. For important function shapes, those kernels are computed as multiple Mellin-Barnes integrals. The paper also handles delicate points: when term-by-term integration is legitimate, how to regularise divergent integrals, and what the expansion means physically.
arxiv-2512-04044:
Watermarking a language model's output is easy while the model stays behind an API, and much harder once its weights are public for anyone to run. Yizhou Zhao, Zhiwei Steven Wu, and Adam Block address the open-weight case with MarkTune in a 2025 machine learning preprint. Earlier weight-based watermarks, such as GaussMark, embed a detectable signal by nudging weights, but strong detection costs visible text quality.

MarkTune fine-tunes the model on its own outputs. The watermark signal acts as a reward, while quality loss is penalised. Updates are steered inside the model's representation space, finer-grained than blanket weight perturbations. Experiments show MarkTune improving the quality-detectability trade-off over GaussMark, approaching the frontier of inference-time watermarking. The watermark survived paraphrasing and fine-tuning attacks, and a model tuned on one dataset kept much of its detection power on unseen data.
arxiv-2512-04144:
Editing a fact out of a language model, or unlearning a whole topic, rarely stays contained: related knowledge degrades too, a side effect called the ripple effect. Roy Rinberg and colleagues build a way to measure those ripples in a 2025 artificial intelligence preprint. Their pipeline pulls semantic neighbours of any concept from a knowledge repository and writes multiple-choice questions at graded distances from the target.

Built on Wikipedia through an open retrieval system, their benchmark covers hundreds of biology seed topics with hundreds of thousands of questions. Eight unlearning methods tested on a Llama model showed the same signature. Accuracy drops are biggest near the erased target and decay with semantic distance. The pattern repeated across four base models, suggesting ripples belong to the method rather than the model. A crowdsourced human study validated the pipeline stages.
arxiv-2512-04244:
Thrust measures how pencil-like a spray of particles from a collision is, and its smallest possible value depends on how many particles share the energy. Matteo Cacciari tackles that minimum in a 2025 particle physics preprint. For some configurations the floor of thrust was unknown even for five particles.

For five particles in three dimensions, he finds an exact result, the first of its kind. For larger numbers he turns to numerical optimisation. Where optimisation cannot pin a definite value down reliably, he analyses the results with extreme value theory, using both a maximum likelihood estimate and a Bayesian approach. Results are given for three dimensions and for two, plus selected cases in higher dimensions.
arxiv-2512-04344:
Zitong Zhou and seven co-authors tackle a blind spot in testing compilers, the tools that turn code into fast programs. Compilers apply long chains of optimization passes, and testers usually fuzz the whole chain at once. That habit misses how passes interact, and many passes never fire at all. Their 2025 arXiv paper reports that a leading LLVM fuzzer touched only a small share of the optimization code in hours of runs.

Their tool, TargetFuzz, instead aims at one optimization at a time. The key trick uses composition styles: the structural patterns in code, such as nesting, adjacency, and repetition, that a given pass looks for. TargetFuzz mines real code for these patterns and mutates programs to stress each pass. Early study results show the targeted approach reaches deep optimization logic that chain-level fuzzing leaves untested.
arxiv-2512-04444:
Shuvrarghya Ghosh, Arkaprava Roy, and Anindya Roy ask how the Great Recession rewired the links between key measures of the United States economy. The crisis ran from late 2007 to mid 2009 and left long marks on output, jobs, and prices. Rather than track each measure alone, their 2025 arXiv paper compares the web of ties before and after the shock. Shifts in that web mark true structural change.

The team builds a shared-parameter model, spOUTAR, on a latent time series frame called OUT. The model fits two related multivariate series at once. It estimates the stationary link graphs for both spans in a joint Bayesian way. That joint fit shows which conditional ties between variables changed, vanished, or formed after the crisis. The approach gives economists a principled way to measure how a crash reshapes the economy's wiring, beyond one series at a time.
arxiv-2512-04644:
Wenzhang Du introduces contract-governed training for Earth observation models, a way to guarantee that satellite image tools serve every region they claim to serve. Such models usually train under unspoken sampling rules that chase global accuracy. No one checks which regions, classes, or rare strata get neglected along the way. His 2025 arXiv paper makes the promise explicit by grouping training samples into service contracts.

Each contract is a meaningful unit, such as a dataset paired with a region or a rare-crop flag, and carries a target share of training attention. A light governance layer, drawn as an Observed Service Agreement Graph, watches real coverage as training runs. Sampling weights, normalized per contract, push coverage toward the targets. Two knobs expose the trade between raw accuracy and fair service. The frame suits missions where a neglected region can mean a missed flood or failed harvest.
arxiv-2512-04744:
Siju Zhang, Guido Garay, Fengwei Xu, and co-authors report ALMA views of a newborn massive star's glowing bubble caught breaking out. Hypercompact H II regions are tiny clouds of ionized gas around young heavy stars, and their early motion is tangled in the dense cores that bore them. The ALMA QUARKS survey imaged one such region at record sharpness, inside a hub where filaments feed a hot molecular core.

The bubble is minuscule and dense, and its recombination lines show a global redshift past twenty kilometers per second against the parent core. Millimeter maps reveal a short arc plus a tail set across it. The team reads this as a dynamic champagne flow: slow expansion into a ready filament carves the arc and drives gentle shocks, while a faster breakout streams the other way. Birth, for massive stars, is a breakout a few thousand years young.
arxiv-2512-04944:
Fred Ciesla, Eric Van Clepper, and Jennifer Bergner test whether sunlight-driven chemistry in the disk that formed the planets can explain the oxygen isotope patterns found in Solar System solids. Those patterns, long blamed on photochemistry in the solar nebula, vary richly between meteorites and planets. The processing happens high in the disk, in a thin photon-dominated layer. Their 2025 arXiv paper models the chemistry while fine dust grows into planet building blocks.

The model follows oxygen isotopes through that growth. Its verdict is negative: the observed evolution cannot come from processing inside the solar nebula alone. The diversity of compositions must have been inherited, at least in part, from material that arrived with its isotope mix already set. A clean negative result redirects the search for the Solar System's chemical origins toward the parent molecular cloud.
arxiv-2512-05044:
Yanran Zhang and five co-authors present MoGe4D, a system that turns a single still image into a moving three-dimensional scene a viewer can orbit. Earlier approaches split the job in two — build the shape, then add the motion, or the reverse — and the two halves often disagreed, so scenes warped or drifted over time. MoGe4D instead treats shape and movement as one problem from the start.

The system guesses the scene's shape from the photo, then predicts how every point in it travels, as a dense field of paths through space and time. A new dataset of sixty thousand videos with such paths supplies the training material, and extra modules fold in depth cues and motion awareness to keep the paths plausible. A final stage renders the result into video from any camera angle, and tests show steadier, more coherent scenes than earlier methods produced.
arxiv-2512-05244:
Gabriele Cenedese, Giuliano Benenti, Dario Ferraro, and Marco Genoni show that watching a quantum battery's surroundings can help charge it better. A quantum battery stores energy in a quantum system. During charging, though, correlations build up between the battery and its charger. Those correlations lock away part of the energy — the battery alone cannot give it back as work. The naive expectation is that an environment only makes things worse.

The authors couple the system to an environment that is continuously monitored, and the monitoring weakens the harmful correlations. Work extraction then rises — beyond even what the ideal, isolated system allows. They demonstrate the mechanism in two models: a cavity-mediated spin-spin battery and a Dicke battery, where many atoms share a light field. The result reframes measurement from a nuisance into a tool for quantum energy devices.
arxiv-2512-05344:
Shikun Cui, Lili Wang, and Wendong Wang prove that a strong enough swirling flow can stop a bacterial colony model from blowing up. The Patlak-Keller-Segel system describes cells that chase the chemicals they secrete; left alone, it can concentrate cells into a singularity in finite time. Coupled to fluid motion, the question becomes whether the flow can stir the colony apart faster than chemistry pulls it together. Engineers already exploit that mechanism in blood-circulation devices that use rotating flow to keep platelets off surfaces.

The authors work in a two-dimensional ring domain around an imposed Taylor-Couette swirl. They prove that when the swirl's strength is large, solutions stay globally bounded. There is no blow-up, and no smallness restriction on the starting cell mass or velocity. The mathematics certifies the device designers' intuition: sufficiently vigorous stirring defeats chemotactic collapse outright, rather than delaying it.
arxiv-2512-05844:
Daniel Rose, Roxane Axel Jacob, Johannes Kirchmair, and Thierry Langer generate new molecules in three dimensions with a transformer that refuses to pick an order for the atoms. Autoregressive models build token by token, so atoms must be lined up in sequence. Molecules have no natural sequence: any fixed ordering biases the model toward a bookkeeping convention and breaks symmetry among identical atoms. NEAT removes it.

The model treats the molecule as a set. At each step it predicts over the admissible next atoms at the growing structure's boundary, in a neighborhood guided way. Training teaches an order agnostic distribution, so the output is invariant under shuffling atom labels. On the standard QM9 and GEOM-Drugs benchmarks, NEAT reached state of the art generation quality. It also runs much faster than rival generators. For drug discovery, an unbiased, fast generator widens the search.
arxiv-2512-06244:
Caleb Ju and Guanghui Lan tackle the oldest trade off in learning by trial: when to try something new, and when to stick with what works. Many classic methods assume the agent roams widely enough on its own, an assumption that can make them hard to run and slow to learn. Their new family of methods builds the roaming in, so the agent explores both places and actions by design.

The methods work with simple table based learning or with straight line models of value. Both reach a clean learning rate that does not lean on unknown quirks of the task. They are also free of knobs a user must tune by guesswork. One version uses a data driven stop rule for how long to explore; the other draws samples from a wider spread of visits.
arxiv-2512-06744:
Rajeev Ranjan shows that one word is not enough: a short prompt in front of a lone word transforms how well embedding models judge word meaning. Embedding models turn text into number vectors, and they are built and graded on sentences. Asked to embed a single bare word, some of them fail outright, giving vectors that bear no relation to human judgments of similarity.

Ranjan simply prepends a phrase such as meaning, colon, before the word. Across seven commercial and open models and three classic word similarity benchmarks, that tiny change lifted agreement with human scores by large margins. Some models that scored zero on bare words recovered strongly once prompted. The best prompted scores beat classic static embeddings by a wide margin, setting a new mark for pure embedding methods. The trick costs nothing, needs no training, and works with any embedding model.
arxiv-2512-06844: Gaétan Leclerc writes a short note in mathematical physics about when quantum particles spread out instead of staying trapped. A classic result, the RAGE theorem, ties that spreading to smooth spectral behavior. Leclerc finds a weaker demand on the spectrum, which he calls eventual absolute continuity, that still guarantees the same spreading. He then turns the idea toward the Fibonacci Hamiltonian, a model of a quasicrystal built from a famous number pattern. There, his approach strongly improves known bounds on how waves spread when averaged over phases.
arxiv-2512-07044:
Xuli Qi, Chunhui Ge, and Yanrui Feng edge a famous graph theory conjecture closer to proof. The question concerns coloring the edges of a graph so that edges sharing a vertex always differ. Some graphs need one color beyond the busiest vertex's degree, and the Overfull Conjecture, posed in the nineteen eighties. Says that any hard-case graph with a high enough maximum degree must be overfull, meaning its edges crowd past a simple counting bound.

Confirming the conjecture would yield a fast algorithm for the coloring number of such graphs and would settle several other longstanding coloring conjectures as corollaries. A recent team verified it under one inequality linking maximum and minimum degree. Qi and co-authors verify it under a weaker, improved inequality, widening the family of graphs for which the conjecture is known to hold.
arxiv-2512-07244:
Elizaveta Kovtun and co-authors find the important nodes in networks whose members carry rich descriptions, a web page's text, a paper's topic, a customer's profile. Ranking nodes matters for monitoring and managing such systems. Classic rankings like degree counts and PageRank read only the wiring, ignoring what the nodes are. Newer neural methods use the attributes but demand labeled supervision, which big enterprise graphs rarely have. PINE fills the empty quadrant: unsupervised and attribute-aware at once.

At its center sits an attention-based graph model that folds node semantics into its learning of structural properties. The attention pattern itself becomes the importance score: nodes the model leans on are the important ones. On a variety of uniform and mixed attributed networks, PINE outperformed the alternatives it faced. The system is not a laboratory toy; the authors describe it as implemented in industry.
arxiv-2512-07544:
Kyungro Lee, Dongha Choi, and Hyunju Lee wrote this 2025 paper on chatbots with a personality. A persona-based system should answer in character while staying engaging and on topic. Most training data, though, never spell out how a reply connects to the persona.

Without those links marked, models struggle to use persona facts well. The authors propose MoCoRP, a framework that makes the links explicit. A natural language inference expert extracts the relation between each persona sentence and each reply. Relations like agreement or contradiction become training signals for the model. The team applies the method to a mid-size pretrained model first. They then extend it to large language models through alignment tuning. On two public dialogue datasets, MoCoRP beats the prior baselines. Its replies stay truer to the persona and read as more engaging. Judges rating quality, not just scores, saw the same gains.
arxiv-2512-07844:
Jinping Wang, Zhiqiang Gao, and Zhiwu Xie wrote this 2025 machine learning paper on lopsided training data. When classes are balanced, a trained network's features settle into a tidy symmetric pattern. That pattern, neural collapse, pairs class means with classifier weights in one frame.

Long-tailed data, heavy in a few classes, blocks the pattern from forming. Generalization suffers badly in that blocked regime. Most fixes force the geometry back by constraining features or weights directly. The authors spot a missing piece those fixes overlook. Feature space and classifier weight space are themselves misaligned with each other. They quantify the harm of that misalignment with an optimal error exponent analysis. Three alignment strategies follow from the theory they develop. Each plugs into existing long-tail methods without changing any architecture. On three standard long-tailed benchmarks, the boosted baselines reach top performance.
arxiv-2512-08044:
A V Levin and P M Ostrovsky, condensed matter theorists, posted a research paper on arXiv in December 2025. Their system joins two materials in a tunnel junction: a bulk superconductor, and on its surface a thin, disordered ferromagnetic layer. Cooper pairs that leak into the ferromagnet work against its uniform magnetic order, while the magnet own stiffness resists that change.

Using the quasiclassical Usadel equation, the authors derive a Landau functional for the resulting phase transition and map the complete phase diagram. They find a special resonance point where the proximity energy scale matches the exchange field of the ferromagnet. There, the uniform state is unstable no matter how stiff the magnet is. They also explore the regime far beyond the transition, describing the strongly non uniform magnetic state that forms. The work clarifies how superconductors can reshape nearby magnetism.
arxiv-2512-08144:
Joshua Wasserman, Ben B Hansen, and Michael R Elliott, statisticians, posted a methods paper on arXiv in December 2025. Their setting is school accountability in the United States, where states flag schools with achievement gaps between student groups. In small schools, subgroup test averages are noisy measures of true performance, and small group results are often masked in public data.

Those facts make it hard to judge programs meant to close the gaps. The authors build propensity score estimates designed to balance schools on subgroup average true scores, not just the noisy observed ones. The estimates work even when the noisy measures are unavailable, and they improve overlap between compared schools. Simulations show matching on these scores cuts bias more than ignoring measurement error. An application to a statewide Texas program against summer learning loss shows the method in action.
arxiv-2512-08544:
Martina Alutto, Leonardo Cianfanelli, Giacomo Como, Fabio Fagnani, and Francesca Parise, control theorists in Italy, posted a study on arXiv in December 2025. They model an epidemic where people react to the outbreak itself: as infections rise, voluntary distancing and masks push the infection rate down. A social planner can intervene, at a cost, to keep infections below a fixed ceiling while spending as little as possible.

For this behavioral feedback SIR model, they prove the optimal policy has a simple shape, which they call filling the box. Let the epidemic spread until infections reach the ceiling. Then apply the minimum control that holds infections flat at the ceiling, until the reproduction number drops below one and the outbreak fades on its own. The proof holds under quite general conditions on the behavioral feedback. Planning, they show, needs no complicated schedules: fill the box, hold the line, then let go.
arxiv-2512-08844:
Malcolm Murray and coauthors present a methodology for quantitative modeling of risks from general purpose artificial intelligence. Such systems offer major benefits in science and industry, yet they also raise concerns about safety, misuse, and loss of control. Methods to assess those risks remain underdeveloped, even as policy frameworks demand systematic modeling of harms.

Their method joins scenario building with quantitative estimation in six steps. Analysts define scenarios, break them into measurable parameters, and quantify baseline risk without the new models. They then find key indicators, such as benchmark results, and map them to model parameters to estimate uplift from the systems. Individual parameters are combined into overall risk estimates that support concrete claims. The methodology targets systemic risks including cyber offense, biological weapons, harmful manipulation, and loss of control. It is validated through extensive use on language model enabled cyber offense.
arxiv-2512-08944:
Yudong Wang and coauthors present a reinforcement learning framework that improves reliability in question answering without giving up reasoning power. Reinforcement learning has unlocked strong complex reasoning in language models, but it has also increased their tendency to hallucinate. That creates a sharp trade off between capability and trustworthiness that the work confronts directly.

Two hallucination types are targeted. Flawed internal knowledge is addressed with a new training set built from open ended conversions of a trivia data set. Unfaithfulness to given context is addressed with long form texts and a fact grounding reward. The framework also rewards the model for refusing questions that cannot be answered, building useful caution. Experiments across a diverse suite of benchmarks show significant gains and clear reductions in both hallucination types. The authors present the method as a practical path to models that reason well and stay factual.
arxiv-2512-09144:
Arnab Mukherjee and three co-authors study a single quantum bit, or qubit, moving with constant acceleration. It is coupled to a fermionic field, the kind of field that describes matter particles such as electrons. Setups like this use a simple detector model named after Unruh and DeWitt. Acceleration makes such detectors react as if they were sitting in a warm bath.

Working through the interaction for a finite time, the authors compute how often the qubit jumps between its states, for both massless and massive fields. They then track the qubit's quantum coherence, the delicate property that makes quantum behavior possible. The fermionic field excites the detector more than a comparable scalar field does, so coherence fades faster. Particle mass helps: when the mass energy grows close to the qubit's own energy spacing, the detector responds less and its coherence survives better.
arxiv-2512-09544:
Eduardo Gutierrez-Prieto, Gilad Yakir, and Pedro M. Reis built a machine that tests snapping beams by the thousands. A bistable beam has two stable shapes and snaps suddenly between them, behavior used in mechanical memory, sensors, and metamaterials. Mapping when the snap happens, across many designs, is normally slow, one specimen at a time.

Their platform spins six beams at once on a programmable rotating disk. Programmed angular motion creates varying centrifugal and Euler forces that act as adjustable body forces on the specimens. Cameras and processing track each beam's motion with sub-pixel accuracy and catch the snap-through events. Across sixty-five configurations varying thickness, pre-compression, tilt, and clamp orientation, they ran more than twenty-three thousand experiments. The resulting stability boundaries fit simple parabolic forms, with tilt angle the most reliable knob for tuning curvature, and the dataset is public for design work.
arxiv-2512-09644:
Ünal Akünal leads a large team presenting Kaapana, an open-source platform for running AI research on medical images inside clinical research environments. Building medical AI that generalizes needs large multi-center datasets and reproducible tooling. But strict regulations on health data, fragmented software, and the difficulty of multi-center studies push projects toward one-off toolchains that nobody can reproduce or scale.

Kaapana instead provides a modular framework under one user interface: data ingestion, cohort curation, processing workflows, and result inspection all live in the same system. Its design brings the algorithm to the data, so institutions keep control of their sensitive holdings while still joining distributed experiments and model development. Flexible workflow orchestration reduces overhead and improves reproducibility. The paper describes the platform's core concepts and shows uses from local prototyping to nationwide research networks. The code is public.
arxiv-2512-09844:
Gregory J. Cooke and colleagues model how oxygen in Earth's air has throttled the escape of hydrogen to space. About two and a half billion years ago, the Great Oxidation Event turned an oxygen free atmosphere into one rich in oxygen. Using a three dimensional Earth system model, the team varied oxygen across the wide range proposed for the era after that event and computed how fast hydrogen could escape.

Oxygen acts indirectly, like a valve. Less oxygen means less ozone, which cools the tropical tropopause, the gateway to the upper atmosphere. Colder air freezes out more water vapor, so less hydrogen reaches the level where escape happens. The simulations support geological evidence that most of Earth's hydrogen escaped before the oxidation event. The authors stress that tracing this history needs full three dimensional models.
arxiv-2512-10044:
David Breitenmoser, Ricardo Lopez, Shaun D. Clarke, and Sara A. Pozzi show that neutron sources can be identified directly from measured spectra after all. Telling sources apart matters for nuclear security and planetary science, yet spectra were thought too ambiguous for direct discrimination. Their Bayesian protocol matches the full measured spectrum against templates and weighs the evidence probabilistically. Applied to recoil and time of flight spectroscopy data, it recovers both single sources and pairs of sources mixed together.

The identifications carry strong statistical significance, above four sigma, even with as few as about a thousand recorded events. The authors frame the result as a new observational window. Spectral signatures, long treated as too blurred to name their source, in fact carry enough structure for robust identification when the inference uses the whole spectrum and honest probability.
arxiv-2512-10144:
Chun Hei Leung, Pak-Tik Fong, Tianyi Yan, and Weibin Li show how to engineer quantum systems that keep oscillating instead of decaying. Open quantum systems usually relax to a steady state as the environment drains coherence. The authors work with the Lindblad master equation, the standard Markovian account. Their key structural insight: when the Hamiltonian and the jump operators share the same block diagonal form, persistent oscillatory modes can be created inside the system. The dissipator need not vanish, unlike the familiar decoherence free subspace trick where oscillations survive only by dodging the environment entirely.

They split weak and strong conditions for the effect: cases where the onset of oscillation depends on the system's parameters, and cases where it is assured regardless. Several models show the framework in action. Tailored system environment coupling, normally the enemy of coherence, becomes the tool that sustains it.
arxiv-2512-10544:
Tara Kit and co-authors route ships through the Arctic, where melting routes promise shorter trade paths but sea ice shifts by the day. They build a multi-criteria optimisation problem that folds in live marine environment data from the Copernicus service, weighing ice conditions alongside route quality. And cast it as a constrained quadratic model.

The model is solved on D-Wave's hybrid quantum-classical solver and benchmarked against the classical Gurobi and CPLEX tools. The quantum hybrid kept finding workable routes with steady runtimes as the problem grew denser, converging far faster than the classical solvers in their tests. Routes also came out a little smoother and slightly shorter. The authors present the work as evidence that hybrid quantum annealing suits Arctic routing, a problem where conditions and constraints change together.
arxiv-2512-10644:
Lorenzo Barca, Jacob Finkenrath, and Stefan Schaefer sharpen a tool for lattice QCD calculations of fermionic correlation functions, the disconnected kind, known to be noisy and costly. Their method joins a two-level sampling algorithm with distillation, a compression technique for quark propagators, to attack the noise that buries the signal.

The trick is factorising the quark propagator into pieces that each depend only on gauge fields inside overlapping time regions. So each piece can be measured independently in a two-level scheme. The estimators show the expected variance scaling, up to boundary effects that fade quickly, and deliver an exponential cut in statistical error at nearly the cost of ordinary sampling. Tests on pure gauge ensembles give a controlled benchmark before the method moves to full dynamical QCD, targeting glueball and isosinglet meson correlators.
arxiv-2512-10744:
Miller MacDonald and co-authors use neutrinos from our own galaxy to hunt for new physics over enormous baselines. IceCube has now detected high-energy neutrinos born in the Milky Way. And their journeys, thousands of light-years long, make them sensitive probes of anything that alters neutrino propagation, at distance-over-energy scales no laboratory can approach.

The authors assess what upcoming joint measurements by IceCube and the KM3NeT telescope could reveal in two scenarios. In the quasi-Dirac picture, where neutrinos mix with nearly identical partners, the telescopes could detect tiny mass-squared differences in a stated window. For neutrino decay, they could sense mass-to-lifetime ratios above a stated floor, both at ninety percent confidence. The point stands apart from the exact numbers: a global network of neutrino telescopes becomes an instrument for testing neutrino mass models.
arxiv-2512-10844:
C Sun, D Fettahoglu, and D Holcman build a stochastic model of sleep spindles, the brief waxing-and-waning bursts that ripple through EEG traces during sleep. Each spindle is modelled as one run of a two-dimensional Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process circling a stable focus, a simple random dynamical system whose paths naturally reproduce the spindle's rise-and-decay envelope.

On the analysis side, their segmentation method pairs empirical mode decomposition with detection of a central extremum to cut single spindles out of a recording, producing a library of oscillatory atoms. With many spindles in hand, the statistics become systematic: distributions of amplitudes, gaps between spindles. And rise and decay times all show exponential tails, exactly as the model predicts. Coupling two such processes with different natural frequencies generates a random mixture of slow, fast, and mixed spindles, matching real sleep recordings.
arxiv-2512-10944:
Sk Asrap Murshed and Bitan Roy show that repulsion alone can pair electrons in a graphene quarter metal. Stacked graphene layers, from a single sheet to rhombohedral multilayers, carry fourfold spin and valley degeneracy. An electric displacement field walks them through regimes as doping changes. First comes a fully degenerate metal, then a spin-polarised half-metal. At low doping, a quarter metal appears, its carriers in one spontaneously chosen valley.

Because those carriers are fully polarised, the quarter metal can host exactly one local superconducting state, a chiral, odd-parity pair density wave whose pairing strength varies in space. A leading-order renormalisation group analysis shows a repulsive density-density interaction between the polarised fermions fosters that phase at low temperature. The authors connect the result to superconducting states observed near the quarter metal in graphene heterostructures and suggest routes to build the state in optical honeycomb lattices.
arxiv-2512-11144:
Joshua Bartkoske and the VERITAS collaboration describe a programme that uses a gamma ray telescope array to watch asteroids pass in front of stars. Such events, called occultations, briefly dim the starlight in a pattern set by diffraction. Fitting that pattern yields the star's apparent size with unmatched precision for stars of moderate brightness.

Since the programme began, the team has attempted well over a hundred predicted events and caught about twenty of them. The report explains how events are predicted, observed, and analysed, and reviews the programme's status. A planned electronics upgrade will let VERITAS search its whole field of view for chance events, including tiny objects beyond Neptune. Those detections could constrain how the solar system formed.
arxiv-2512-11244:
Taishi Kotsuka and Enoch Yeung simplify the mathematics of engineered cell communities that talk to each other with diffusing chemicals. In their sender receiver systems, different cell types sit in hydrogel beads and exchange signals that spread through space while reactions run inside each cell. The full model couples three dimensional diffusion with nonlinear internal dynamics, making it hard to analyse or simulate at scale.

The authors show the diffusion settles exponentially fast into a steady spatial profile. Singular perturbation theory then reduces the whole system to a finite network of interacting agents. A closed form communication matrix, built from the spherical spreading function, captures who influences whom and how strongly. Numerical tests show the reduced model tracks the full dynamics closely. Large populations of communicating cells become practical to simulate, aiding synthetic biology design.
arxiv-2601-06644:
Yan Meng, Wafaa Mohammed, and Christof Monz test cross-language reasoning in 2026. Real-world information sources are inherently multilingual, they point out. That raises whether language models can synthesize information across languages.

They introduce a simple two-hop question answering setting for the test. Answering requires inferences over two multilingual documents together, they explain. One hop alone, in one language, cannot reach the answer. The setup isolates exactly the skill named in their title. Models may reason well within English yet fail across languages. Their benchmark shows where that gap opens in current systems. Multilingual AI readers get a clean, small test with large implications.
arxiv-2601-07144:
Research by Linus Bleistein linus.bleistein and co-authors was posted on arXiv in 2026. It deals with optimal transport under group fairness constraints. The preprint joined the arXiv PAPERS collection in 2026. Ensuring fairness in matching algorithms is a key challenge in allocating scarce resources and positions.

Focusing on Optimal Transport (OT), the authors introduce a new notion of group fairness requiring that. The probability of matching two individuals from any two given groups in the OT plan satisfies a predefined target. For specialists, the preprint offers a compact account of the problem and the authors' approach.
arxiv-2601-07444:
Zhipeng Chen, Haolun Tang, and Jingyi Zhan formalize a classic number theory topic inside a proof assistant. Their 2026 preprint presents the theory of amicable numbers in Lean 4. Two positive integers form an amicable pair when each equals the sum of the other's proper divisors. The famous pair 220 and 284 has been known since ancient times.

Formalization means turning definitions and proofs into code a computer can check line by line. Every step must be exact, with no gaps left to human judgment. Building this theory in Lean tests both the software library and the clarity of the math itself. Readers interested in verified mathematics get a concrete example of an old idea made machine-checkable.
arxiv-2601-07844:
A 2026 preprint in Entropy builds the math of epidemics on networks from single agents upward. Agent based SIR dynamics track at risk, sick, and healed people as a discrete state Markov process. The process captures the random spread of infection along network contacts. With indicator functions and their marginal chances, the authors derive a hierarchy of change equations. The hierarchy resembles the classical BBGKY hierarchy of statistical mechanics.

Such stacks are of use but hard to wield, since each level rests on the next. Closures in this stack cut them off at a set level with a close guess. The paper moves from agent based Markov dynamics to such closures on networks. Good closures keep the accuracy of agent simulations at a fraction of the cost. Those who model outbreaks are the readers. The work aims at rigorous shortcuts for large network outbreaks. The point is speed with care.
arxiv-2601-07944:
Roy Shivam Ram Shreshtth, Arnab Hazra, and Gourab Mukherjee test amortized Bayesian inference when conditions change. Approximate Bayesian inference has grown by absorbing new computational techniques for larger problems. Deep networks and foundation models now enable amortized inference, where a learned predictor performs inference quickly for many data sets. Their 2026 preprint assesses this approach statistically. Two stress factors are signal-to-noise variation and distribution shift.

Amortized methods are trained once and reused, so shifts can silently break them. A careful assessment shows when the speed is worth the risk. Signal-to-noise changes are routine in real instruments and surveys. Distribution shift is the norm when models meet new populations. The paper serves statisticians and machine learning scholars who deploy learned inference. It supplies evidence about failure modes rather than another success story.
arxiv-2601-08044:
Oleksandr Kuznetsov compiles neural networks into lookup tables to catch denial-of-service attacks on small devices. DoS attacks threaten Internet of Things ecosystems. Effective intrusion detection is hard to deploy on resource-constrained edge devices. Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks offer a compact alternative to standard multilayer perceptrons. They place learnable spline functions on edges rather than fixed activations on nodes, reaching competitive accuracy with fewer parameters. Kuznetsov's 2026 preprint compiles them into lookup tables.

A lookup table replaces computation with fast memory reads. Edge chips can then run detection at low power. Compiling after training keeps the model's accuracy while changing its form. The work targets the gap between security research and deployable devices. The paper serves IoT security engineers and edge AI scholars. It shows a path from a compact model class to running protection on site.
arxiv-2601-08344:
Gabrielle Taylor, Stefan Wagner, Alicja Wierzcholska, and Michael Zacharias review twenty years of blazar watching. Their 2026 arXiv paper covers Mrk 421 and Mrk 501 across many wavelengths. Both blazars vary on every observed timescale and are well studied at high energies on short scales.

The team instead characterizes long-term behavior at synchrotron energies: optical, ultraviolet, and X-ray bands. Long records test current models of how these objects produce their light. Blazars are jets pointed near our line of sight, so their slow trends reveal jet physics. The two-decade baseline offers modelers a rare check against short, campaign-style snapshots.
arxiv-2601-08444: Yuxiang Wang and co-authors present attributed table graphs for reasoning over tables. Their 2026 arXiv paper addresses table reasoning, answering questions from data stored in tabular form. Tables hold a large share of stored knowledge, so the task matters widely. Recent solutions lean on large language models for semantic understanding and reasoning. Attributed graphs offer a structured way to expose rows, columns, and their relations to the model. Better table structure could cut errors on questions that mix lookup, comparison, and arithmetic.
arxiv-2601-08744:
Nitin Kenjale and Anuradha Garge work on codes that fix errors in sent data. A code here is a set of words made of bits, used to spot and fix flaws. Old tools count how many ones sit in each word. The pair says that count misses where the ones sit, and place can matter a lot.

They set up two new tools. One tracks how ones spread across the spots in a word. The next builds a full list from that spread, like a sum over all words. These tools give a finer view of a code than the old count. A reader who works on safe data links gets a sharper way to judge and build codes.
arxiv-2601-08844:
Anandita Garg Harish and Uma Gaba Harish weigh small chat models next to large ones on cost to the earth. Large models need much power to train and to run. Each ask burns power, and asks come by the billions. The pair ask if a small model, tuned for one fixed task, can do that task with far less smoke and heat.

They test small tuned models on set tasks and track power use and task score side by side. The aim is not to crown small models for all work. It is to find tasks where they are good enough. A reader who runs AI at scale gets a trade map. It can guide which jobs to move off large models first.
arxiv-2601-08944:
Niklas Affolter and three co-authors set up a new frame for maps built from triple cross diagrams. Such diagrams code sets of points and lines in a plane view. Like maps show up in more than one branch of shape work. Each branch built its own tools for them, with its own terms and tricks.

The team gives one shared frame for all of them. In that frame, a rich set of group forms, called cluster algebras, can be built on each map. Those forms link counts and moves in a strict way. A reader in shape work gets a joint tongue for split fields. Work in one field may now aid work in a next with ease.
arxiv-2601-09044:
Fei Tan and four co-authors grow health scans past their edge while they keep growths in place. Scan sets oft lack rich cases of ill tissue. A model trained on thin sets learns ill marks poor. To grow a scan, a tool paints new zones round the old scan. A poor tool may wash out the very growth a doctor must see.

Their tool is called POWDR. It uses a wave based spread model, tuned to hold ill traits safe. New zones look real, yet the core growth stays as it was. A reader who trains health tools gets more train cases with out loss of the key trait. Rare cases can be grown, not just sought.
arxiv-2601-09444:
Lauri Suomela and four co-authors ask how much training data a navigating robot really needs. Their 2026 arXiv paper reports a large-scale study of data quantity and diversity for visual navigation. The policies learn by imitation and must work in places they never saw in training, without maps.

Generalization to new settings is the weak point of such end-to-end policies. The authors vary how much data, and how varied it is, then test in the real world. Their study is the first of its scale for map-free navigation. The findings give builders a sense of what data collection buys in robustness.
arxiv-2601-09544:
David Barnes and Niall Taggart use span categories to study diagrams built from profinite groups. Their 2026 arXiv paper is a case study in the homotopy theory of infinity-categories. A strength of that theory is its robust way of taking limits and colimits of whole categories.

The catch is that several rival versions of the category of categories exist. Picking the wrong one changes what the limits even mean. The authors show, in one concrete setting, how the choices behave. A worked example like this helps other mathematicians know which variant their own arguments need.
arxiv-2601-09644:
Yuta Kageura and seven co-authors find a new way to measure how opaque the early universe was. Their 2026 arXiv paper constrains the optical depth of reionization without leaning on the cosmic microwave background's large-scale polarization. That polarization signal may be biased by foreground dust and instrument effects.

A mild mismatch has appeared between baryon acoustic oscillation data and microwave background results. A higher optical depth could explain it. An independent route to the same number tests whether the mismatch is real physics. The authors build that route from the reionization history itself.
arxiv-2601-09844:
Nils Hüsken, Eric S. Swanson, and Adam Szczepaniak compare two flavors of a workhorse scattering model. Their 2026 arXiv paper contrasts dispersive and nondispersive K-matrix formalisms. Coupled-channel effects matter more as precise data pours in for hadron scattering processes.

The K-matrix is a powerful yet simple way to model scattering amplitudes with channels coupled. Which flavor a team picks changes how the amplitudes behave away from the data. The authors weigh the two formalisms against each other. A clear comparison helps phenomenologists read modern hadron spectra with far fewer artifacts of method.
arxiv-2601-10044:
Farshad Amani, Faezeh Ardali, and Amin Kargarian build a tool to fix power grids after storms. Storms and floods break grid gear in many places at once. Crews must be sent to fix sites in a good order. New harm news can force a fresh plan mid job.

The tool learns by trial and reward. It takes in new facts as they come. It then sends crews to tasks in real time. The aim is to bring power back fast. It also aims to cut waits that stem from a stale plan. Such a tool could help grid teams in the hard days after a storm.
arxiv-2601-10644:
Eugene Yang, Andrew Yates, Dawn Lawrie, James Mayfield, and Trevor Adriaanse present RoutIR, a tool for serving retrieval pipelines at speed. Retrieval sits at the heart of retrieval-augmented generation, where a system searches for documents, reads them, and then writes a reply. Real systems are dynamic. They may search several times before they answer.

Many strong retrieval methods live in academic platforms built for offline batch tests. All queries are known up front in those tests, unlike live service. RoutIR aims to run such pipelines fast in real time. It helps teams move research-grade search into products that must answer users now, not later.
arxiv-2601-10844:
C. A. Downing and M. S. Ukhtary revisit how a quantum battery gets charged. Their model has two qubits: one acts as the charger, the other as a single-cell battery. The Bloch sphere, the standard map of a qubit's states, frames the analysis. They rework the energetics and thermodynamics of the charging process.

Quantum batteries promise storage that exploits quantum effects for fast charging. A two-qubit model is the smallest lab for such ideas. Careful bookkeeping of work, heat, and coherence shows what charging can and cannot do. The paper speaks to the small but growing field of quantum thermodynamics, where energy rules meet quantum rules head on.
arxiv-2601-11144:
Yuejie Li and co-authors present Deep GraphRAG, a balanced approach to graph-based retrieval-augmented generation. GraphRAG systems answer questions by walking a knowledge graph. They face a trade-off: global search is thorough but slow, local search is fast but narrow. Large hierarchical graphs make paths hard to optimize, and exploration can crowd out exploitation.

Deep GraphRAG adds adaptive integration and robust multi-stage re-ranking. The aim is answers grounded in the right subgraph without scanning everything. Enterprises hold much of their knowledge in linked records, not flat text. A system that balances depth and speed could make graph question answering practical at real scale.
arxiv-2601-11344:
Parker Seegmiller and six coauthors ask how much doctors would edit AI drafts. Their 2026 preprint deals with replies to patient portal messages. Language models can draft such replies with real promise. Clinics still weigh whether drafts save time in real work.

A draft that needs heavy edits may save no time at all. Worse, it could add risk if flaws slip past a busy doctor. The team measures alignment with each clinician in depth. They check edits draft by draft, doctor by doctor. That edit load is a plain, honest test of value. It shows where drafts help and where they hinder. The study speaks to safe rollout of AI in clinics.
arxiv-2601-11444:
Raphael Razafindralambo, Remy Sun, and Frederic Precioso ask when two scores beat one. Their 2026 preprint studies ensembles of diffusion models. Diffusion models now make high-quality, diverse samples on demand. The field has chased ever stronger single models of late.

Ensembling is a stock trick to lift supervised models. Many weak models, averaged, often beat one strong model. For unconditional score-based diffusion, the trick is near untested. The team checks if it gives real gains for generation. A score here is the model's guide field for sampling. Joining two score fields could smooth flaws in each. The study weighs when that gain is worth the extra cost.
arxiv-2601-11644:
Muhammad Imran and Yugyung Lee predict when to trust VLM spatial calls. Their 2026 preprint deals with vision-language models and space. VLMs show impressive skill across many multimodal tasks. Their spatial reasoning, though, fails in systematic ways.

Basic directional relationships expose the weakness clearly. CLIP scores only 49 percent on them in the record. BLIP-2 reaches 54 percent, still near a coin flip. Safe deployment in robotics needs a trust signal instead. The team predicts when a spatial prediction is reliable. Rejecting shaky calls beats accepting all outputs blindly. Autonomous systems gain a guard for a known weak spot.
arxiv-2601-11844:
Yue Bi and Michèle Wigger improve a bound for shared computing over wireless links. In MapReduce, many nodes split a big job, share part results, then merge them. The key trade is between compute load on each node and the time to deliver results.

Their new bound is an achievability result, so it shows a scheme that works. It rests on interference alignment plus zero-forcing, two ways to shape signals. The bound holds in set ranges of the trade terms. Tighter bounds guide the design of fast shared compute nets.
arxiv-2601-12144:
Silvia Boumova, Vesselin Drensky, and Şehmus Fındık study invariants of the free associative algebra of rank two under a dihedral group. Past results by Lane and Kharchenko show the invariant algebra is free for any subgroup of the general linear group, over any field.

The dihedral case is a set test of that broad claim. Invariants are the parts that stay fixed when the group acts. Sorting them helps map the algebra's form. The work adds exact data for this group and rank.  Rank two is the first rank where the case is rich.
arxiv-2601-12244:
Shyalan Ramesh, Scott Mann, and Alex Stumpf review bio-inspired work on coordination, talk, and system design in underwater swarm robotics. Sea work grows more complex, with needs in survey, exploration, and resource care. Swarms of small robots can do more than one large craft.

Fish schools and insect swarms give design cues for such teams. The review sorts how those cues shape group control and comms under water. Water blocks radio and light, so talk is a hard core problem. The survey maps what has been tried across thirty-plus systems.
arxiv-2601-12344:
Eyal Buks writes on a bold idea in quantum mechanics. The idea is that quantum states may lose their entanglement on their own, with no outside push. Fans of the idea link it to hard open problems in the field. One such problem is how quantum measurement works at all.

Buks sets out ways to put this idea into math. He frames the loss of entanglement with a nonlinear operator. That operator can change both the main state equation and the master equation for a density operator. He then weighs two forms of the operator against each other. One works by deranking, and the other works by cutting correlation.
arxiv-2601-12444:
Hui Yang, Jiaoyan Chen, and Uli Sattler ask whether large language models can write real proofs. Models have been tested a lot on deduction tasks of late. Far less is known about proofs that are faithful and easy for humans to read. A proof must show why a result follows, step by step, with no gaps.

The team work in the setting of OWL ontologies. OWL is a widely used way to state knowledge for the web and to reason over it. They build a framework that makes proof datasets on its own. The same framework also grades the proofs that models produce. Their paper was set for the ACM Web Conference in 2026.
arxiv-2601-12544:
Leif Azzopardi and Adam Roegiest argue that how people handle information is changing at its root. Classic models cast users as gatherers. In berry picking and foraging theory, people hop across sources to meet shifting needs. Generative AI now changes how people produce, structure, and reuse information, though. The old gatherer models no longer capture that work in full.

The pair propose a new frame called information farming. Farming suggests people plant, tend, and harvest information over time, with AI as a tool. The shift matters for how search and curation tools should be designed. Their paper was set for a 2026 venue on human information interaction. It asks the field to rethink its core metaphors.
arxiv-2601-12644:
Pedro Fernando Fernandez Espinosa, Maritza Liliana Arciniegas Torres, and Camilo Andres Acevedo Cadena study a family of matrices built from special numbers. The entries are products of k Fibonacci and k Lucas numbers. Both sequences obey simple recurrence rules, which give the matrices a rich hidden structure. The work was supported by a university in Colombia.

The team derive explicit, unified formulas for classic matrix invariants. Those include the determinant, the inverse, the trace, and matrix powers. One set of formulas covers the whole family at once. The patterns they find flow from the recurrence relations beneath the numbers. Results of this kind serve algebra and combinatorics alike.
arxiv-2601-12944:
Lukang Sun proves a fact about Tsallis entropy, a broadened form of the classic entropy of physics. He tracks how this entropy bends as heat spreads through a space. Past work on this bend was stuck at one dimension, a line. Sun shows the same bend, called concavity, holds in any number of dimensions.

The heart of the proof is a new bound on terms in a rate of change. He also checks a key step of calculus with full care. A fact that holds in all dimensions is far more useful than one stuck on a line. Heat flow in the real world is three dimensional. The result serves the study of spread and of entropy far from balance.
arxiv-2601-13044:
Warit Sirichotedumrong and co-authors build a fast speech to text tool for Thai. Big encoder decoder models such as Whisper do well when a whole clip can be read at once. They lag too much for live use, where words must come out as they are spoken.

Thai has a thin set of open tools, and most of them copy that slow off line style. The team fills the gap with a stream ready design. It pairs a FastConformer front end with a transducer head, a joint that reads sound and text steps in sync. The name Typhoon marks the model line. For Thai apps that need live text, such as call tools and live captions, the work offers a more apt base.
arxiv-2601-13144:
A team study, with no named lead author in the record, seeks earlier flags for new active zones on the Sun. Such zones dim the light from the Sun as they rise. To call that dim in time is key for space weather work.

Past tools used LSTM nets, a kind of memory net, to guess the drop in bright flux as a zone nears. The new work widens the set of net forms tried. It also widens the marks that the nets must guess. The shift to newer forms, named in the title as Transformers, aims for flags that come sooner and hold up better. Sun teams gain more lead time to guard craft and grids.
arxiv-2601-13344:
Rhombik Roy and Ofir E. Alon ask how spin changes the tunnel acts of a bosonic Josephson junction. Such a junction holds two wells of ultra cold atoms linked by tunnel flow. Spin and tunnel flow are both core acts in physics. Their play in cold atom rigs draws wide care.

The team works in pure theory. They place the junction in a frame that spins, a non inertial frame. They then track how the tunnel swings shift with the spin rate. The shifts could be read in lab rigs as a gauge of spin. For cold atom teams, the work adds a tool link of two acts they use each day.
arxiv-2601-13544:
Li Tuobang models how stacked predation falls into one strong man rule when no rules bind. The model is a multi layer game that calls itself in rounds. Each layer takes rent from the layer past it. Such stacks live where law has a gap and each tier can prey on the next with no check.

In that world the stack cannot hold, the model shows. Rent waste grows by a fast curve as layers stack. The base layer, though, has a firm floor for life needs that will not bend. The clash of fast waste growth with a firm floor breaks the stack. What is left is a single Leviathan, one core that takes all. The piece is a formal tale of a state form, built as maths.
arxiv-2601-13844:
Gilad Karpel and co-authors study how to set a key dial for learning many tasks in a row in 2026. The setting is continual linear regression in high dimensions, with more parameters than data points. L2 regularization, a penalty on large weights, is applied across the task sequence. The team derives a closed-form expression for the expected generalization loss.

Their formula holds for arbitrary linear teachers, the true rules behind each task. They show isotropic regularization mitigates label noise in their tests. That holds for one teacher and for many random ones. Sound dial settings help models learn new tasks without forgetting old ones.
arxiv-2601-13944:
Zhao Wang, Lanyanni Zhang, Meiqin Wei, and Mark Budden study Gallai-Ramsey numbers for linked graphs in 2026. A Gallai-Ramsey number is the smallest size that forces a pattern in colored graphs. Take a complete graph with edges colored in k colors, in an exact coloring. Past a set size, a target pattern from a family must appear.

The team focuses on l-connected graphs, which stay linked after small cuts. Ramsey theory shows order must emerge in large enough structures. These numbers mark the exact border where that order is forced. Such borders guide work in networks and combinatorics.
arxiv-2601-14244:
Qing Zhang, Adham Sakhnini, and five co-authors study pinpointing in wireless systems in this 2026 paper. Their setting is OFDM-based massive MIMO, a radio setup with many antennas that splits signals across subcarriers. Good pinpointing needs phase to stay in step across those subcarriers and antennas. Real gear often fails that test.

The flaw is phase offsets that shift with frequency and with each antenna. Those shifts blur the fix on a user's place. The authors work out the math of that harm. They study a still user with a clear line of sight. Their title points to phase offset calibration as the fix they build toward.
arxiv-2601-14444:
Yetmgeta Aklilu, Tiany Yang, Cody Covington, and Kálmán Varga study molecules that interact through light in this 2026 paper. Their method is real-time quantum electrodynamical time-dependent density functional theory, built on the Pauli-Fierz Hamiltonian. They place two molecules far apart. An ultrashort delta-kick excitation perturbs only the first one. The second starts unexcited.

In free space, the excitation stays localized. The second molecule shows no response. That null result is the baseline the study reports first. The work sets up a clean test of how light can mediate interaction between separated molecules, a question with weight for chemistry and quantum devices.
arxiv-2601-14844:
Zhe Chang, Haodong Jin, Yan Song, and Hui Yu work on digital heads that can be driven in real time. Their 2026 arXiv paper asks how to build a 3D head avatar that looks true to life. Such avatars are a core need in digital animation.

One fast method renders scenes with small 3D blobs called Gaussian primitives. The snag, the authors say, is how those blobs are animated. Most tools drive all of them with one shared expression code, a one-size-fits-all fix. Their CAG-Avatar method uses cross-attention to guide the blobs instead.
arxiv-2601-14944:
Pierre-Antoine Lequeu, Léo Labat, and co-authors build tools for public debate at scale. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with texts from democratic citizen consultations. Large language models are now common tools for studying such texts.

That use raises hard questions about ethics and trust. The team presents the GDN-CC dataset. The name stands for automatic corpus clarification for AI-enhanced citizen consultations. The dataset aims to clean, clarify, and sort consultation texts. Models and people alike can then work with them on firmer ground. That clarity is the point of the whole dataset effort.
arxiv-2601-15144:
Thomas Van Giel, Hanna Jaspaert, and co-authors study how groups of species sway in cycles. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with the population dynamics of ecological systems. Such models help predict shifts in biodiversity and how to protect it.

Most classic models let species interact only in pairs. Yet higher-order interactions, where a third species changes a pair's dynamic, can shape a community. The authors use an agent-based model with such interactions. They vary how fast the interactions change and how far they reach, then watch how the cycles of numbers shift.
arxiv-2601-15444:
Silouanos Brazitikos and Minas Pafis work on random polytopes in a 2026 arXiv paper. A polytope here is built from random points drawn from an atomic law. The authors study threshold effects in these shapes. A threshold marks the point where a trait appears or vanishes as the sample grows. Their setting uses points picked independently from the same law.

Part of the paper repairs a gap in older work. The authors revisit a threshold argument for the discrete hypercube by Dyer, Füredi, and McDiarmid. They point to a smooth step in that proof that can fail at boundary points. They then supply the missing justification. The title ties the work to discrete log-concavity as well. Specialists in random geometry are the natural audience.
arxiv-2601-15544:
Himanshu Mishra works on keeping deployed models current in a 2026 arXiv paper. The setting is continual test-time adaptation. A pretrained model updates itself during deployment, using only the incoming data stream. That stream carries no labels. Earlier methods like Tent and EATA help under short, slow shifts. They struggle when the test distribution changes fast or over very long horizons.

His method is called RDumb++, and it is drift-aware, per the title. Drift names the slow or sudden change in data over time. A drift-aware method watches for such change while adapting. The risk in this setting is quiet decay. A model can adapt itself into worse performance if shifts pile up. Work like this aims to keep long-running models reliable without fresh labeled data.
arxiv-2601-15844:
M. Morales, E. Tolley, and R. Poitevineau rebuild radio sky images with AI in a 2026 arXiv paper. Radio interferometers sample the sky incompletely. They measure Fourier components, not full images. Reconstructing a picture from partial data is a key challenge in radio astronomy. The authors use denoising diffusion restoration models. Their method learns a data-driven prior for the radio sky. That prior fills gaps in a principled way.

They first train a diffusion model on real observations. The training set is radio galaxy data from the VLA FIRST survey. A learned prior knows what radio galaxies tend to look like. Reconstructions can then favor plausible skies over noise. For upcoming large surveys, fast and faithful imaging is a core need.
arxiv-2601-16144:
Tetsuro Abe and Shu Tanaka seek fair draws from tied best answers in a quantum search. Their 2026 preprint deals with tasks that have more than one best answer. Fair draws give each best answer the same chance. The known QAOA search skews the odds as its depth grows. Deep runs then miss some best answers far too oft.

The pair base a new heat set search on a quantum to classic link theory. Heat terms in the search aim to hold the odds fair. Fair draws count when all best answers must be seen. The work tests the new search on tied tasks. It seeks depth with no loss of fair odds.
arxiv-2601-16244:
Dennis Wayo models how to inject magic states in light based quantum gear. His 2026 preprint deals with fault proof quantum sums on light gear. The key step is to make a clean logic magic state for the T gate. Real gear has capped squeeze and loss of light. Those caps cut the grade of each state made that way.

Wayo models the full build at the design level. The model uses a try till win plan for the inject step. It weighs grade gains against cost in tries and parts. Clear trade maps help teams pick gear terms. The work serves groups who build light quantum gear.
arxiv-2601-16344:
Fan Nie and coauthors build one frame to test and train data science agents. Their 2026 preprint, named DSGym, deals with agents that turn data to acts. Such agents pledge to speed finds and new facts from data. Past tests are split by task type and hard to weigh. They also span a thin range of real data tasks.

One frame with shared terms lets teams weigh agents fair. Wide task span shows where each agent is strong or weak. Train tasks in the frame can lift weak points in a set way. The work aims to make agent scores firm and clear. It serves teams who build data agents.
arxiv-2601-16444:
Ayako Sato and three coauthors test if tuned models show count bias as judges. Their 2026 preprint deals with the LLM as judge trend. In that trend, a model grades text in place of a human judge. Past work found judge models lean to set scores. Some scores come up far more oft than they should.

The team asks if tune steps that align models shift that lean. Tune steps may cut or grow the bias in score picks. Bias in grades bends all ranks built on those grades. Firm tests of bias guide safe use of model judges. The work checks tuned and base models side by side.
arxiv-2601-16644:
Rifo Genadi and coauthors find sycophancy hid in the gaze heads of models. Their 2026 preprint deals with acts where models flip to please a user. A flip from right to wrong is the key sign in tests. Past work sought that sign in broad deep acts. The team trains straight probes on each deep part in turn.
