europmc-pmc8656144: This 2021 research paper covers supermeres are working extracellular (outside cells) nanoparticles (ultra-tiny specks) replete with disease biomarkers (body signals that can be measured) and treatment aims. Extracellular vesicles (tiny packets released by cells) and exomere nanoparticles (ultra-tiny specks) are under intense investigation as sources. If later work backs it up, the finding could open a new path for treating the illness.
europmc-pmc8664944: A fresh look at RNA modifications spotting by comparative (side-by-side) nanopore direct RNA sequencing (reading DNA letter by letter) arrived with this 2021 research paper. RNA molecules undergo a vast array of chemical post-gene-reading modifications that can affect their structure and interaction traits. A sharper test or warning sign can change outcomes, since earlier care usually works better.
europmc-pmc8674144: A fresh look at mapping the human genetic architecture arrived with this 2021 research paper. The genetic make-up of an individual adds to the susceptibility and reply to viral. Findings like these get picked up, tested, and built on by other teams.
europmc-pmc8688144: Doctors and scientists took on the flavonoid procyanidin C1 has senotherapeutic action and raises lifespan in mice in this 2021 research paper. The authors lay out their methods and results in full. If later work backs it up, the finding could open a new path for treating the illness.
europmc-pmc8709944: A fresh look at p53 signaling (cell-to-cell messaging) in cancer progression (worsening) and therapy arrived with this 2021 research paper. The p53 protein is a transcription factor known as the "guardian of the genome" because of its serious function. Once the chain of events is mapped, future treatments can be built to break it.
europmc-pmc8743544: Schwengers and co-authors published this research paper in 2021 on bakta: rapid and standardized annotation of germ genomes via alignment-free sequence identification. The team describes what it did and what it found, step by step. Findings like these get picked up, tested, and built on by other teams.
europmc-pmc8763644: Published in 2022, this research paper takes on mapping single-cell (one cell at a time) data to reference atlases by transfer learning. The authors lay out their methods and results in full. Each solid result like this one becomes a stepping stone for the next round of research.
europmc-pmc8883344: Kumar and co-authors published this research paper in 2022 on selective autophagy (cell self-cleanup) receptor (docking point on a cell) p62/SQSTM1, a pivotal player in stress and aging. The team describes what it did and what it found, step by step. Findings like these get picked up, tested, and built on by other teams.
europmc-pmc9134144: A fresh look at COVID-19 infection: an survey on cytokine (immune signal) storm and related treatments arrived with this 2022 research paper. COVID-19 caused by the severe acute breathing syndrome coronavirus-2 has posed a significant threat to global health. Results like these feed the work that turns lab findings into future treatments.
europmc-pmc9485144: Published in 2022, this research paper takes on treatment aims at and biomarkers (body signals that can be measured) of tumor immunotherapy (treatment that boosts the immune system): reply versus. The authors lay out their methods and results in full. If later work backs it up, the finding could open a new path for treating the illness.
europmc-pmc9964744: Published in 2023, this research paper takes on polycystic ovary syndrome: etiology, current care, and future therapeutics (treatments). The authors lay out their methods and results in full. If later work backs it up, the finding could open a new path for treating the illness.
faraday-experimental-researches-vol2-184:
Volume 2 of Faraday's Experimental Researches in Electricity appeared in 1844, holding Series 15 through 19. Michael Faraday's researches had by then moved from the first shock of induction toward the deep laws of electric action in matter. The papers here continue his electrochemical work.

Faraday tested how currents pass through gases and liquids and how electricity relates to chemical change. He also probed the nature of induction through different materials, work that fed his growing picture of lines of force. That picture later became the field concept in the hands of Maxwell. Volume 2 shows the middle stage of the research program that Volume 1 began and Volume 3 completed.
frus-1861-d144:
On 17 August 1861, Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote a further letter to William Dayton. It is document 144 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

The second Paris letter of that day takes up its own point in the file. Seward's desk rhythm, seen across the volume, was to clear each topic in turn. The pair gives readers a full day of the French agenda in miniature. A full day of French business in miniature still reads as a tidy piece of craft. Tidy craft in a crisis is rarer than bold words, and worth far more.
frus-1861-d244:
Writing from Washington on 8 July 1861, William H. Seward addressed James Shepherd Pike, the American minister to the Netherlands. The printed record keeps it as Document 244 in the President's message volume for 1861. The letter comes from the first summer of the Civil War, a time when each foreign capital watched the war with care.

Outbound letters like this one told the envoy what line to take and what to report back. Read in order with its neighbors, it shows diplomacy as daily work rather than grand speeches. The State Department's Office of the Historian keeps the series, called Foreign Relations of the United States.
frus-1861-d44:
George Dallas wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 2 May 1861. The dispatch is document 44 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

May was the month of change in London, as Dallas wound down and Adams arrived. Dallas kept reporting until the end of his term. His letters from those weeks give readers the view of a departing envoy, watching a crisis grow past his watch. The handover between Dallas and Adams was smooth, a credit to both men's care. Smooth handovers abroad spared Washington one whole class of needless worry.
frus-1862-d144:
15 September 1862 brought Charles Francis Adams a fresh letter from Secretary Seward in Washington. The printed record keeps it as Document 144 in the 1862 Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs volume. By then, in the summer of 1862, the war's second year, the Lincoln government knew foreign backing could change the war's course.

Outbound letters like this one told the envoy what line to take and what to report back. Alone it is a small piece of paper, but in sequence it helps show how the Union held its ground abroad. The Foreign Relations series, kept by the State Department's Office of the Historian, preserves the full run.
frus-1862-d244:
Document 244 opens the French file of the 1862 Foreign Relations volume: a report dated 6 December 1861 from William L. Dayton, the American minister in Paris, to Secretary of State William H. Seward in Washington.

France under Napoleon III watched the American war with close, self-interested eyes, and Dayton's post was second in weight only to London. His reports tracked French talk of backing the South or pressing a truce. This early letter came as the Trent crisis with Britain still filled the news, and Paris waited to see how it ended. Dayton, a former senator from New Jersey, held the Paris post from 1861 until his death in 1864.
frus-1862-d344:
Two Seward dispatches to Paris are dated 10 November 1862, and the first is Document 344 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. Both went to William L. Dayton, the American minister to France.

By 10 November, word was spreading that Britain would not join France in acting on the war. Seward's letters that day wrote from a position slowly strengthening. The Paris brief now turned toward what France might do alone, in Mexico or toward the South. This dispatch opens the file's late-autumn phase, after the crisis peak. Southern agents were active in Paris too, seeking loans, ships, and friends at court.
frus-1862-d44:
Writing from Washington on 4 April 1862, William H. Seward addressed Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. The printed record keeps it as Document 44 in the 1862 Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs volume. By then, in the spring of 1862, a year into the war, the Lincoln government knew foreign backing could change the war's course.

Outbound letters like this one told the envoy what line to take and what to report back. Alone it is a small piece of paper, but in sequence it helps show how the Union held its ground abroad. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record series, is where the full exchange can be traced.
frus-1862-d444:
Hermann Kreismann, the American consul in Berlin, received this instruction from Secretary of State William H. Seward on 6 September 1862. It is Document 444 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs.

Consuls handled the practical edge of foreign policy: shipping, seamen, trade papers, and the protection of citizens abroad. Kreismann, a German-born Chicago editor, served the Union in the Prussian capital alongside Minister Judd. An instruction addressed to a consul rather than a minister points to business of that practical kind. Letters like this widen the picture of wartime diplomacy beyond courts and cabinets, down to the offices where Americans abroad actually got help.
frus-1862-d544:
On 4 September 1862 Secretary of State William H. Seward addressed this note to Roest van Limburg. It is Document 544 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the official record for the year.

Seward wrote as Lee's army crossed into Maryland and the government braced for the autumn crisis. His note to the Dutch minister kept the Washington end of the Netherlands file in order at a moment when larger matters pressed. The correspondence's subjects remained the standing ones of neutral trade and maritime right. There is a kind of reassurance in the file's regularity. Through the worst weeks of 1862, the letters between Seward and Van Limburg went back and forth like clockwork. The relationship they served never cracked.
frus-1862-d644:
On 27 November 1861 Townsend Harris wrote his last letter in this run of the Japanese file, addressed to Secretary of State William H. Seward. It is Document 644 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs.

Four days after his previous dispatch, Harris wrote again from Edo, in the closing weeks of his mission. He would leave Japan the following spring. His health was broken by the post he had created. His final letters report the treaty system standing and the legation's affairs in order for his successor. The volume's Japanese strand thus ends where it began, with the first minister's own hand. It is a quiet, fitting close to the farthest-flung correspondence in the record of 1862.
frus-1863p1-d144:
Charles Francis Adams closed a three-letter day with this dispatch of 3 April 1863 to Secretary of State William H. Seward. Adams was the American minister in London. The letter is document 144 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863.

The last sheet of the day wound up a set sent at the height of the ship question. Adams's April mail is among the most tense in the volume, as Britain weighed whether to let Southern warships sail. This letter ends the 3 April three. It is a working piece of the watch that, in the end, helped keep the British fleet out of the South's hands.
frus-1863p1-d244:
To guide his minister in London, Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote these orders on 23 July 1863 to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. They stand as document 244 of the 1863 volume. The document comes from the Foreign Relations of the United States, the government's own published record of Civil War diplomacy. It was one of 3 letters between the same men dated that day.

Adams was told to deal chiefly with Lord John Russell, the foreign secretary. Seward's letters armed him with facts and wording for those meetings. It was written in the month of Gettysburg and Vicksburg, twin Union wins that changed how Europe judged the war. Kept with the rest of the 1863 papers, it forms part of the fullest record of how the Union handled its most dangerous foreign relationship.
frus-1863p1-d344:
On 29 December 1862, Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington, sent this note to Secretary of State William H. Seward in Washington. It appears as document 344 of the 1863 diplomatic papers. The letter is printed in Foreign Relations of the United States, the official series that publishes American diplomatic papers.

British ships stopped by the Union blockade, and British subjects held as prisoners, supplied much of London's complaint list. Lyons delivered those protests in formal notes like this one. Set in its place in the volume, it helps readers trace how two governments talked their way past repeated crises.
frus-1863p1-d44:
On 13 December 1862, Judah P. Benjamin wrote to Edwin De Leon. Benjamin ran the Confederate state office in Richmond; De Leon was a Southern agent working in Europe. The letter is document 44 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863.

De Leon served the South as a roving hand in Europe, where the work mixed talks, print, and quiet deals. Benjamin's letters to such men carried orders and cash-side news from home. This one came in mid-December, as the year of the South's best hopes closed. It is part of the group of Confederate papers printed in the Union's record, a rare chance to read the foe's mail.
frus-1863p1-d444:
A dispatch dated 4 April 1863 went from Lord Lyons, the British minister in Washington to Secretary of State William H. Seward. The State Department later published the letter in its 1863 foreign affairs volume, laid before Congress with the President's message. The letter is one piece of the steady stream of notes that passed between the two governments in the spring of 1863.

Letters like this one were the tools of a quiet contest. The Union meant to keep Britain out of the war, and it made that case note by note. Trade ran through the whole exchange. British mills wanted Southern cotton, while Union officials watched every cargo for war goods bound to the South. It is a small, dated piece of a very large record, and it earns its place by keeping that record complete.
frus-1863p1-d544:
From Lord Lyons, Britain's envoy in Washington to Secretary of State William H. Seward: a letter dated 30 May 1863. The letter sits in the published record of how the Lincoln government handled foreign affairs in the spring of 1863. The two men at the ends of this channel, Seward in Washington and Lyons speaking for Britain, wrote to each other almost daily.

What the page shows is process, not drama. Claims, protests, and replies moved back and forth until small disputes stayed small. Trade ran through the whole exchange. British mills wanted Southern cotton, while Union officials watched every cargo for war goods bound to the South. The volume's editors printed it without comment; its meaning comes from the company it keeps in the file.
frus-1863p1-d644:
The 23 October 1863 mail between Washington and London included a letter from Charles Francis Adams to William H. Seward. Adams was the American minister in London, and Seward was Secretary of State in Washington. Adams in London was the Union's front line in Britain, pressing its case with the British government week after week. The letter was later printed in the 1863 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, issued with the President's annual message.

The standing business of this channel was friction at sea. Union warships stopped British merchant ships, and each seizure could spark a formal protest. The formal tone can hide the tension, but the pace gives it away. Notes this frequent mean both capitals were watching each other closely. The volume's editors printed it without comment; its meaning comes from the company it keeps in the file.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d144: Secretary of War Henry Stimson wrote to General Marshall, the Army Chief of Staff, on November 20, 1943. The letter is Document 144 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. Stimson-to-Marshall letters carried the War Department's mind on the great choices of the war, and this one was written two days before Cairo opened. The record gives the two men and the date. Its subject is in the printed text.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d244:
The President's Log, the official booklet recording Roosevelt's trip to Africa and the Middle East in November and December 1943, is introduced by an editorial note in the Foreign Relations volume. The note exists to explain what the log is before its text is printed in the pages that follow.

The booklet runs to sixty-six numbered pages, with front and back matter and some fifty pages of pictures and appendices. Lieutenant William Rigdon prepared it, and Rear Admiral Wilson Brown approved it. Inside are the President's party list, an itinerary, sea and air travel charts, a foreword, and the log itself. Eleven appendices follow, from a citation for General Eisenhower to the Cairo and Tehran communiqués.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d344:
Alexander Kirk, the American minister in Egypt, wrote a short secret memorandum at Cairo on 26 November 1943 about his custody of the Cairo communiqué. It records a small errand at the center of the conference's secrecy.

That afternoon Harry Hopkins handed Kirk a copy of the communiqué on the Anglo-American-Chinese talks and asked him to hold it until instructions came from Tehran about its release. The timing was undecided, but Kirk would get twenty-four hours' notice so the three countries could publish at the same moment. Kirk was also to notify the Chinese legation when the word came. His own task, as he summed it up, was simply to see that American correspondents in Cairo received the text through the Office of War Information.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d44: Roosevelt also wrote to Churchill on October 14, 1943, making at least three summit letters in a single day. This one is Document 44 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. The date fell in the final week of preparation for the Moscow Conference of foreign ministers. The record gives the parties and the date and leaves the contents to the text. It rests in the Foreign Relations volume with its companions of that busy day.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d444:
Marked with a footnote in the printed volume, this second set of Combined Chiefs of Staff minutes from December 5, 1943 covers another session of the joint American-British command at Cairo. The Second Cairo Conference was then deciding the next phase of the war against Germany and Japan. The State Department later published the record in its Cairo-Tehran volume.

Session minutes preserve the order of business, the officers' exchanges, and the conclusions reached before the chiefs reported upward to Roosevelt and Churchill. Having two records from one day shows how much was pressed into these meetings. For a reader tracing how Allied plans took final shape, that density is the point.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d544:
Secretary of State Cordell Hull wrote to President Roosevelt on January 11, 1944, keeping up the steady channel between the department and the White House. The message appears in the State Department's Cairo-Tehran conference volume, among the follow-up papers of the new year.

Hull's January traffic with Roosevelt mixed the conferences' unfinished business with the planning of the postwar order, a subject Hull cared about deeply. The Secretary had built his reputation on patient, formal diplomacy, the opposite of summit improvisation. For readers, the message shows the permanent government digesting the leaders' December decisions and fitting them into policy that could last.
frus-1944-quebec-d144:
Roosevelt replied to Churchill's Italian report the next day, August 30, 1944, in telegram 611. He was glad to hear how General Wilson had concentrated his forces and renewed the offensive. His own chiefs believed a vigorous attack, pressed with everything available, should force the enemy into the Po Valley.

The president stressed destroying German forces while they were within grasp, lest divisions escape to other fronts. He was confident Eisenhower would be satisfied that the Mediterranean effort was mauling troops that might otherwise face him. On the future use of Wilson's armies, Roosevelt suspended decision until the campaign's results were known. Trieste and Istria, he said, they would renew at Octagon, the Quebec meeting.
frus-1944-quebec-d244:
Hull asked Roosevelt for instructions on the French lend-lease agreement on September 11, 1944. The sticking point was Jean Monnet's request for industrial items to restart French production for the civil population. Under the July 15 memorandum Roosevelt had approved, such long-life industrial goods could go on credit only if necessary to the war in Europe or to forces just after an armistice.

Applied now, Hull wrote, that rule flatly rejected Monnet's program of over a billion dollars in industrial items. He recommended neither rejection nor approval. Instead, a list mechanism would leave the president complete discretion, item by item, as French behavior warranted. The Foreign Economic Administration would submit proposed French programs to Roosevelt before they joined the list.
frus-1944-quebec-d44:
September 1, 1944 opened with a Churchill message to Roosevelt. It was the first day of the conference month. The State Department placed the letter in the Quebec 1944 volume.

September opened with Allied armies at the German frontier. The Quebec meeting stood eleven days away. Churchill's letters ran ahead of him across the Atlantic. They stated what Britain needed from the conference. For readers, the message marks a final approach. The Prime Minister was at sea or about to sail. The agenda for the meeting was effectively set. Only the arguments in person remained.
frus-1945-50-intel-d144:
Formal minutes cover the Second Meeting of the Intelligence Advisory Board, held on 26 March 1946. It survives in print as document 144 of the State Department's Foreign Relations volume on intelligence, 1945 to 1950. Washington was still building a peace-time spy service, run for the moment by the National Intelligence Authority and the Central Intelligence Group.

As minutes, the text sticks to the business of the meeting: items raised, views stated in brief, and the choices the group reached. The brevity is the point: what the group did not settle, the minutes do not claim it did. To read it in place is to watch the Cold War state being assembled at desk level.
frus-1945-50-intel-d244:
A memorandum from Director of Central Intelligence Hillenkoetter reached the State–Army–Navy–Air Force Coordinating Committee on 22 October 1947. The State Department prints it as document 244 in Foreign Relations of the United States, in the intelligence volume for 1945 to 1950. The National Security Act had just taken effect. The CIA had replaced the old group, and the Council had just begun to meet.

The value of the form is its speed: a page or two, a clear ask, and a name at the top to answer for it. Kept in sequence, such memos form the true diary of the office that sent them. Alone it is a page; in sequence it is evidence of how a state taught itself a new trade.
frus-1945-50-intel-d344:
A memorandum dated 12 April 1948 links two senior offices. The sender was the Executive Secretary of the Intelligence Survey Group (Blum). The reader was Allen W. Dulles, Mathias F. Correa, and William H. Jackson. It survives in print as document 344 of the State Department's Foreign Relations volume on intelligence, 1945 to 1950. Across Washington, the new security bodies were moving from setup work to the real business of the Cold War.

A memo of this kind was the basic tool of office work at the top. It put a matter before a senior man and asked for a choice, a signature, or a view. The reply, if any came, would build on the points laid out here. Kept with its neighbors in the volume, it shows the new system being built one dated paper at a time.
frus-1945-50-intel-d44: A White House memorandum dated 7 November 1945 sits among the department papers of the intelligence volume. Papers from the president's house carry special weight in such a run. Since every department knew the final choice on a central intelligence system would be made there. The title gives no author, so the paper stands on its origin and date. Written while the Budget Bureau's plan was gaining ground in the autumn contest of 1945.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d144:
Premier Mikolajczyk appealed straight to the President, and Ambassador Ciechanowski delivered the plea in Washington. The Polish ambassador's covering note, sent on 27 October 1944, passes on Mikolajczyk's telegram of the day before. Both texts are printed in the Malta and Yalta volume of Foreign Relations.

Mikolajczyk protests the pressure on his government to accept the Curzon Line at once, without any reservations. All his work, he writes, has aimed at Polish-Soviet understanding, for Poland's sake and for the common cause. Yet his nation would feel terribly deceived, he warns, if this were the answer to its sacrifices and its unbroken part in the war. He asks the President for a reply and decisions at the earliest possible moment.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d244:
One China policy for three allies is the aim of this briefing book paper of 13 January 1945. “Unity of Anglo-American-Soviet Policy Toward China” is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume. It names the discords that could wreck the aim before they grow.

Some British elements, the paper warns, seem for imperial reasons to want a weak and possibly divided China after the war. A second fear runs the other way. Russia may use the Chinese Communists to carve out a separate area in the north or in Manchuria. The recommendation follows plainly. The United States should take the lead in helping China build a strong, stable, and unified government. Such a China could be the chief steadying force in the Far East. British and Russian help should be sought to that end.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d344:
Bremen and Bremerhaven would stay under full American control, under an agreement the Combined Chiefs of Staff approved at Yalta in February 1945. The enclave, drawn on an attached map, covered the ports and their ground. American military government would run it, including disarmament and the breaking up of German war power there.

At the same time, the American commander was to follow the broad policies used in the British zone around it. He kept the right to depart from them on military grounds when he judged it needful. Transit rights each way — American stores southward, British movement toward Austria — complete the bargain.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d44: Roosevelt answered Churchill on 6 January 1945, the same day the prime minister's latest message arrived. His reply is document 44 in the Foreign Relations of the United States volume covering Malta and Yalta. Same-day exchanges show the machinery at full stretch, with the president's staff turning cables around quickly because the Mediterranean journey was now only weeks away.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d444:
A whole frontier might fall to Britain alone, and London disliked the prospect in this statement of February 10, 1945. If British proposals for occupation zones in Austria were approved, the entire Austro-Yugoslav frontier would be a British responsibility. Yugoslavia had not asked to alter the Styrian stretch. But it had advanced claims to Klagenfurt and parts of Carinthia, lost in the plebiscite of 1919.

Action might be needed to resist Yugoslav efforts to press those claims. Yugoslav partisans might also advance into Carinthia during operations and hold ground there. For Britain to stand alone in such a quarrel, the paper argues, would be invidious. The warning proved exact within months.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d144:
British Minister John Balfour delivered London's draft agenda for the summit in a letter dated May 29, 1945. The letter is document 144 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. Churchill had told Truman that his government was drawing up, at the President's wish, a list of subjects for the next meeting of heads of government.

Foreign Secretary Eden now asks Balfour to forward the enclosed list to Acting Secretary Grew, so the President can be informed. The list itself is printed with the next document. Balfour's short covering letter marks the moment the conference stopped being only about dates and houses. The British put their proposed business in writing. And the long argument over Poland, Germany, and the Balkans took paper form.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d244:
Ambassador Winant reported the Foreign Office's protest in full in a second telegram dated July 15, 1945. The message is document 244 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference, and it tells the same story as the extract printed earlier in the volume.

An official named Harvey was considerably disturbed, Winant writes. And the British Embassy in Washington was told to ask for a postponement. The postponement would last until Italy's future status could be discussed at the Big Three meeting. London held that Italy's admission was tied to the peace treaty, and its Berlin delegation was fully briefed to discuss it there. With Churchill and Eden both away, the Foreign Office could not decide in the time given. The question would go to Eden, to raise with Byrnes, while London strongly urged delay.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d344:
Elmer Davis, who ran the Office of War Information, wrote to President Truman on July 4, 1945, with an idea to hold in mind at Berlin. His suggestion concerned action after the conference, not during it. The central problem of Germany, Davis argued, was the reeducation of the German people.

Without that change, he warned, every other measure would be a brief patch at best. The aim was a Germany no longer dangerous to its neighbors. Davis noted that the news service his office ran with the Army, through papers, radio, and newsreels, was already the real start of that teaching, whether planned or not.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d44:
Prime Minister Churchill sent President Truman a personal and top secret telegram from London on May 31, 1945. It is document 44 in the Foreign Relations papers on the Potsdam Conference, sent as the Allied leaders arranged their first meeting since Germany's surrender. Churchill's own plans, he says, depend on the date Truman picks.

Churchill also raises a point of pride and fairness. He reports good talks with Truman's envoy Joseph Davies, but warns he will not attend a meeting that simply continues a private conference between Truman and Stalin. The three leaders, he insists, should meet at the same time and on equal terms. He closes by saying he looks forward to meeting Truman in person for the first time.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d444:
American supervision of Greek elections is put to President Truman in a memorandum from the Secretary of State dated July 4, 1945. The question, it opens, raises an issue of the first importance. America has repeatedly affirmed President Roosevelt's purpose. He stated it in his State of the Union message of January 6, 1945. Peoples, Roosevelt said, have the right to choose the form of government under which they will live.

The memorandum adds a further obligation. The right of liberated peoples to choose their government must not be defeated by interim authorities holding power in the meantime. At the end of the paper stands the President's own manuscript endorsement: I agree, Harry S Truman. The decision was thus taken at the top.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d544:
Secretary of State James Byrnes answered Secretary of War Stimson in a brief wire sent July 12, 1945. Byrnes was aboard the cruiser Augusta, sailing with President Truman to the Potsdam Conference. His reply is document 544 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on the conference.

Byrnes says he has Stimson's wire and has talked it over with the President. The lend-lease question, he adds, is a complex one. He suggests the two men talk it over in person at Terminal, the code name for Potsdam. Editors note that a second reply went out the same day, and no one can now tell which was sent first.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d644:
Ambassador Winant passed on British Foreign Office views on the Levant from London on July 9, 1945. His secret wire is document 644 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on the Potsdam Conference. The remarks came from a Foreign Office official that day.

The official said France's offer to hand over the Troupes Speciales had come too late to help France. Made earlier, it might have bought a return favor. Syrians instead see it as only partial payment for the damage done to Damascus. The 45 days set to work out the transfer were called useful, since delay could cool tempers. As French elections neared, de Gaulle might grow more willing to compromise. On troop withdrawal, the official doubted any early move and preferred that a conference be put off.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1044:
British Foreign Secretary Anthony Eden wrote to Secretary Byrnes from Berlin on July 23, 1945, about the coal directive for zone commanders in Germany. Both foreign offices had debated changes to the draft. Eden reports that London now agrees with the revised text handed over in Washington on July 11. A matching directive will go out at once to the British zone commander as an interim order.

Eden asks how Truman means to raise the directive with Stalin, at a plenary session or in private. He stresses that coal is among the most dangerous world shortages. Winning Russian support for the European Coal Organisation matters, he argues, since Polish support would likely follow.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1144:
Staff of the British team at Potsdam drafted this memorandum on 18 July 1945, early in the talks. Each side used such papers to set out its case in full. A memorandum could be handed across, read aloud, or kept as the team's own record of its stand.

British papers of this kind put London's argument in London's words. The other teams then knew what to answer, and later readers know what was claimed. This one dates from the first week, when stands were still being staked out. It keeps the British view in its own phrasing, inside the American record of the summit.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1244:
The United States team tabled this proposal on 24 July 1945. Formal proposals were the bargaining chips of the summit. Each one claimed ground in writing and forced the other teams to answer in kind, amend, or refuse.

A paper from the second week came after the opening stands were known. The trades had begun, and drafts now aimed at terms the others might accept. This proposal is one such move. Kept in the official record, it shows what Washington put on the table at that point, in the exact words its team chose.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1344:
President Truman wrote to Prime Minister Winston Churchill on 24 July 1945, while both men led their delegations at Potsdam. The two had met in person only days before, at the start of the conference. It is printed in volume two of Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record of American diplomacy at Potsdam.

Letters between heads of government sit at the top of the diplomatic pile, above cables and staff papers. Even at a summit where the men could talk face to face, some things were still put in writing to make them firm. This exchange belongs to the last week of Churchill's wartime premiership. It ended while the conference was still sitting, giving the letter a place in two stories at once.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-144: Standing in the run of unnumbered pieces after document 710, this short note speaks for the editors of the Potsdam volume. Editorial notes in the Foreign Relations series exist to keep the archive legible. One might cite the file a paper came from. Another might point ahead to a later text. This note does that quiet work for its neighbors.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-44:
Benjamin Cohen's notes on the plenary session of July 20, 1945, catch the debate over liberated Europe in shorthand. They are an unnumbered item in volume two of the Foreign Relations papers on Potsdam. Cohen records the foreign ministers' report being received, then the argument that followed.

A change in the Council of Foreign Ministers text was adopted, providing for a permanent secretariat. Discussion then turned to what the foreign secretaries favored for Bulgaria, Rumania, and Greece. Molotov indicated that present restrictions should be relaxed now that the war had ended. Churchill intervened on elections with a point of language and duty. Supervision of elections, he insisted, does not mean control, and Byrnes offered the softer word observation instead. Byrnes then proposed Italy's admission to the United Nations, paired with a declaration against admitting Spain.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d744:
Document 744 is a working paper of the United States delegation dated July 25, 1945. It comes from the heart of the conference's second week. Staff drafted it to move a question forward inside the team. The paper was preserved and printed in the second Potsdam volume of the official series.

Mid-conference drafts show ideas under pressure. Writers knew the other sides' lines by now. Readers can watch American drafting adjust to that knowledge. The document's value is its timing: late enough to be informed, early enough to still shape events. Such papers are the negotiation's true workshop floor.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d844:
The Acting Secretary wrote to Melbourne in Rumania on July 28, 1945, in document 844. Washington sent further guidance to its acting representative in Bucharest. The letter dates from the conference's last days. It was printed in the second Potsdam volume of the official record.

A second guidance letter in the same run shows a channel in heavy use. Melbourne's reports had built a file that demanded answers. Readers see the home office responding at matching pace. The document pairs with the July 28 letter to the same post in this volume. Together they show Washington steering Bucharest through the summit's closing turns.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d944: William Clayton sent this short memorandum to Edwin Pauley on July 28, 1945. It passes along a paper from the United States Group Control Council staff. That paper raises questions about the return of art objects looted during the war. Clayton says America might accept the first two recommendations in it. He asks Pauley's views on the third, which turns on replacement of art versus simple return. He hopes the two of them can send General Clay a joint memorandum on the subject.
frus-1961-63v10-d44: A 1961-1963 FRUS memorandum from the task force chairman on Cuba. The task force. This document holds that memo. The file is now open to the public. Its contents inform the historical record. The library keeps the document safe.
frus-1961-63v11-d44: A 1961-1963 FRUS letter from the Missile Crisis volume. The crisis correspondence. This document holds that letter. Time has kept the file intact. The archive guards it with care. Those who study the era will use it.
frus-1977-80v06-d144: A 1977-1980 FRUS letter from President Carter on the Soviet Union. Carter wrote to Brezhnev. This document preserves that letter. Scholars prize such firsthand sources. The paper lived through the years. Future scholars will discover it.

gi-bill-1944:
Congress passed the Servicemen's Readjustment Act in 1944, as war still raged. The GI Bill thanks returning veterans with concrete, lasting help. College fees, home loans, and business aid stand at its core.

Millions went to school on the bill who could never have paid. Millions more bought homes and filled the growing suburbs fast. The act built the broad American middle class of the postwar years. Critics note that Black veterans often faced blocks at the local level. A grateful nation's check still ranks among its best investments ever made. Its name, the GI Bill, became shorthand for earned opportunity in America.
gregory-great-morals-on-job-vol-1-1844:
Pope Gregory the Great wrote his Morals on the Book of Job, the Moralia in Job, in the late 500s, near the start of his time as pope. Volume one of the Rev. James Bliss English translation came out in 1844 in the Library of the Fathers series. It holds Parts One and Two of Gregory's huge work.

Gregory reads Job line by line and draws three layers from the text: the plain story, a picture of Christ and the church, and a lesson for the reader's own conduct. Job's patience under loss becomes a guide for prayer, humility, and trust. Medieval readers treated the Moralia as a handbook of the inner life.
heine-wintermaerchen-1844: Heine's 1844 Deutschland: Ein Wintermarchen satirizes German reaction in verse. It was banned in Prussia. The Tower library holds the full text. It mocked kings. Censors raged. Rhymes bit. Exile sang. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-lowenberg-juliu:
Julius Löwenberg, a German geographer, is the subject of an entry in the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. Born at Strzelno, Prussia, in 1800, he was educated in Berlin. There he came to know Alexander von Humboldt, who helped him in various ways. He died at Berlin on December 12, 1893.

The article is mainly a record of his books on geography and exploration. They include an Africa volume in 1835, a historical-geographical atlas, and a history of geography. He also wrote a biography of Humboldt and an account of Humboldt's travels in America and Asia. Late works covered the history of discovery and voyages in the polar zones. The entry closes with his last years in Berlin's Jewish home for aged people. It is a quiet end for a scholar backed by Humboldt himself.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-machir-ben-abba:
Machir ben Abba Mari, compiler of the Yalkut ha-Makiri, is treated in a 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry. Almost nothing is known about the man himself. Neither his country nor his century can be fixed. Steinschneider guessed that he lived in Provence, and scholars still debate his date.

The article therefore studies the book instead of the life. Like the Yalkut Shimoni, it gathers Talmudic and midrashic sayings, but only for the later Bible books. It covers Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, the twelve Minor Prophets, Psalms, Proverbs, and Job. Machir said he wanted to gather the scattered sayings into one group. His sources ranged across both Talmuds, the Tosefta, and many midrashim. Only parts survive in print, including Isaiah in 1894 and Psalms in 1899. The entry maps a lost scholar through the remains of his anthology.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-manasseh-prayer:
Prayer of Manasseh, a short Greek poem of repentance, is examined in a Jewish Encyclopedia article from 1906. It is ascribed to Manasseh, son of King Hezekiah, held captive in Babylon. Chronicles says the king prayed there but does not give his words. The prayer fills that gap. It survives among canticles attached to the Psalms in some Greek manuscripts.

The article tells the legend the prayer carries. Manasseh, starved on bran bread and vinegar water in prison, repented and humbled himself. Fire then melted his iron chains, and he was restored to Jerusalem. The Church never declared the prayer canonical, the entry notes. Luther kept it, and it stands in the English Apocrypha. The text itself praises God's mercy and His promise of repentance to sinners. The piece shows how a missing prayer in the Bible invited a later writer to compose it.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-martinique-1044:
Martinique is an island in the West Indies and a French colony. Its Jewish history fills a Jewish Encyclopedia article from 1906 by Gotthard Deutsch and S. Kahn. Dutch Jews settled there early in the seventeenth century and did well in trade. Trouble began after France took the island in 1635. Jesuit pressure kept pushing the authorities against them.

The article goes through the decrees one by one. Jewish commerce was banned in 1658 and then restored. New limits came in 1664 and 1669. In 1671 Colbert spoke for the Jews, and Louis XIV granted them religious liberty and equal privileges. That protection died with Colbert, an edict of 1683 ordered the Jews banished, and the Code Noir that followed drove them off the island.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-medicine-10544:
Medicine among the ancient Hebrews opens a Jewish Encyclopedia article from 1906 by Solomon Schechter, C. D. Spivak, Joseph Jacobs, and Frederick T. Haneman. Health and sickness alike came from God, so the healer worked as the messenger of God. The Law itself sanctioned practice. A man injured in a fight must be “thoroughly healed” at the cost of his attacker. Joseph kept house physicians, and Isaiah names the surgeon, the dresser of wounds.

One point is stressed early: unlike other early peoples, the priests of Israel never monopolized healing. Moses gave them only the policing of contagious disease, and no biblical priest is shown practicing medicine. Prophets heal instead: Elijah and Elisha raise children, and Isaiah cures Hezekiah with a fig plaster. It quotes the praise of the physician by Ben Sira. It also notes the court expert, the rofe, whose testimony decided criminal cases.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-menahem-ben-sim:
Menahem ben Simeon was a French Bible commentator. He worked at the end of the twelfth century. Joseph Jacobs and M. Seligsohn give him a short notice in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. A native of Posquières in Provence, he was a pupil of Joseph Kimhi and worked on the Prophets. The Bibliothèque Nationale in Paris holds his commentaries on Jeremiah and Ezekiel in a single manuscript.

The entry dates what it can. The Jeremiah commentary was completed in 1191. The Ezekiel commentary breaks off mid-chapter. It stops in the middle of the fortieth chapter. It is unfinished, or imperfectly preserved. Nothing else of his life is recorded. The bibliography is a single line. It points to Gross's "Gallia Judaica." The notice preserves the bare outline of a Provençal exegete whose work survives, where so many contemporaries' does not, in a Paris codex.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-metz-isaac-1074:
Isaac Metz was a German scholar who lived at Hamburg in the first half of the nineteenth century. Gotthard Deutsch and S. Mannheimer wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He is remembered for careful work on two classics of Hebrew literature rather than for any public office.

His main work was Ḳehillat Dawid, a catalogue of David Oppenheimer's famous library, which Lazar Embden translated into Latin at Hamburg in 1826; Jacob Goldenthal later added an index. Metz also published an edition of Judah ha-Levi's Cuzari at Hanover in 1836, based on the Venice editions of 1547 and 1594. The bibliography cites Steinschneider's Bodleian catalogue and Zeitlin.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-milwaukee-10844:
Milwaukee, the metropolis of Wisconsin, had about 8,000 Jews among its 300,000 people when Cyrus Adler and Julius H. Meyer wrote its Jewish Encyclopedia entry in 1906. Its Jewish story starts with congregations: the oldest, Bene Jeshurun, was organized in 1855 by the first Jewish settlers in the city. A second, Emanu-El, followed in 1869.

The entry lists the rabbis who led both congregations, from Isidor Kalisch at Bene Jeshurun to Isaac S. Moses at Emanu-El, and notes four more incorporated congregations besides. In January 1903 Milwaukee's Jews federated their charities on an income of about 12,000 dollars. The federation supported a relief association, a settlement, a hospital association, and two women's societies, and channeled gifts to national Jewish causes.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mosely-alfred-1:
Alfred Mosely was an English financier born at Clifton in 1855. His short Jewish Encyclopedia entry was written by Joseph Jacobs and Victor Rousseau Emanuel. Educated at Bristol Grammar School, he went out to South Africa and became one of the earliest settlers in Kimberley.

During the South African war, Mosely equipped the Princess Christian Base Hospital near Cape Town at his own expense, for sick and wounded soldiers. In 1902 he led an industrial commission from England to the United States to study American trade success. A year later he headed a similar commission on American education. He had been made a C. M. G. in 1900 for his public work.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mussafia-musaph:
Benjamin ben Immanuel Mussafia was a physician and philologist born about 1606, probably in Spain. Gotthard Deutsch and Wilhelm Bacher wrote his Jewish Encyclopedia entry. He practised medicine at Hamburg, where his wife died in 1634. In her memory he wrote the Zeker Rab, a retelling of Creation that uses every Hebrew root only once.

Mussafia later served King Christian the Fourth of Denmark as his physician at Glückstadt. Settling at Amsterdam, he published the Musaf he-Aruk in 1655, supplements to Nathan's Aruk explaining its Greek and Latin words. He also caught the Amsterdam fever for Shabbethai Zebi and signed the community's eulogy to him in 1666. He died at Amsterdam in 1675.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-nathan-11344:
Nathan was a Palestinian teacher of the second century. Wilhelm Bacher and A. S. Waldstein wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was the son of a Babylonian exilarch, or Jewish leader. He left Babylonia and settled in Palestine. There he became head of the school at Usha.

The patriarch sent Nathan to calm a split with Babylonian Jews. Later he joined Meïr in a failed plot against the patriarch Simon. Both men were expelled, then readmitted under changed name forms. Nathan's rulings and sayings fill many Talmudic passages. A work called Abot de-Rabbi Natan is credited to him. He also helped Judah I with work on the Mishnah.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-nergal-11444:
Nergal was the god of the Babylonian city Cuthah. The entry was written by the Editorial Board's Executive Committee and George A. Barton for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Second Kings says the men of Cuth made his image. Sargon had settled those men in Samaria. A Sidonian tomb stone at Athens shows wider worship.

Cuthah ranked among Babylonia's oldest, prehistoric cities. Its god began, it seems, as a farm god. He filled all tasks of such a city's god. Later, as gods merged into one pantheon, roles shifted. Nergal became god of the underworld itself. Cuthah was a famed burial place, perhaps the cause. Pestilence, war's ruin, and the sun's fierce heat joined him.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-nikolaief-nikol:
Nikolaief is a Russian Black Sea port and naval station. Herman Rosenthal and S. Janovsky wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. It was founded in 1784 in Kherson's government. Jews settled there soon after Poland's partition. In 1829 their residence was declared injurious there.

The Jews of Nikolaief were ordered to leave the city. Admiral Greig protested that artisans would vanish with them. The removal still went forward after two grace terms. In 1859 merchants could settle and buy land again. Artisans gained the right only in 1861. Trade employs most Jews there today. They hold 1,289 merchants' licenses in all. Three thousand Jewish artisans form sixty per cent of the whole.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-oppert-gustav-s:
Gustav Solomon Oppert was a German scholar of the East. Isidore Singer and Louis H. Gray wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Hamburg on July 30, 1836. He was a brother of Jules and Ernst Oppert. He read at Bonn, Leipzig, Berlin, and Halle.

Gustav gave his mind to the past and tongues of India. Six years past his degree, he went to Oxford in 1860. He helped at the Bodleian, the great library there. That same year he helped at the queen's library at Windsor. In 1872 he left England for a post in India. He taught Sanskrit at Madras till the year 1893. Then he toured north India, China, Japan, and America. His books treat the arms and rule of old Hindus.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-patriarchs-the-:
The Patriarchs are Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, the fathers of Israel. Four writers shared this article in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. They were the Executive Committee, Schulim Ochser, Wilhelm Bacher, and Judah David Eisenstein. The Bible names the three together again and again.

God speaks of himself as the God of all three fathers. He recalls their covenant when Israel suffers in Egypt. Later rabbis fixed the title with care. Only the three men count as the Fathers. Sarah, Rebekah, Rachel, and Leah count as the four Mothers. The rabbis also traced daily prayer back to the Patriarchs.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-perreau-pietro-:
Pietro Perreau was an Italian librarian and Oriental scholar. He was born at Piacenza on October 27, 1827. Isidore Singer and Umberto Cassuto wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was a Christian who loved rabbinic books. His editions were printed by a rare polygraphic method.

In 1860 Perreau took charge of Parma's Oriental collection. In 1876 he became chief librarian of the National Library there. From 1860 he gave his work to rabbinic literature. He printed Immanuel of Rome's notes on the Psalms. He also built a great ocean of Hebrew abbreviations.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pigo-12144:
The Pigo were an Italian family of rabbis. Richard Gottheil and Ismar Elbogen wrote their entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The name once appeared as Figo or Pichio. Ephraim Pigo, a learned man, died at Venice in 1606.

Rabbis Judah and Solomon Pigo appear in printed responsa. One branch of the family settled in Turkey. Moses Pigo wrote a dictionary of haggadic themes there. His book came out at Constantinople in 1554. His son Joseph wrote responsa at Salonica. He also ruled on inspecting the lungs of cattle. The family name survives in rabbinic books.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-poll-tax-12244:
A poll tax is a fixed sum charged to each person, head by head. Gotthard Deutsch and M. Seligsohn wrote the article for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. They trace the tax back to the book of Exodus. There each man over twenty gave half a shekel as a ransom for his soul.

In time the half shekel became a yearly due, the article explains. Nehemiah cut the sum to one third of a shekel. The money kept up the Temple and bought the public sacrifices. It also paid for the walls of Jerusalem. Jews also paid head taxes to foreign kings at many times. The article follows those payments through Bible and later records.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-premsla-shabbet:
Shabbethai Premsla was a Galician scholar of grammar and a scribe. Isidore Singer and Peter Wiernik wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He lived at Przemysl in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries. His main work deals with Hebrew grammar. He was a Talmud scholar of note as well.

In 1622 Premsla printed notes on a grammar by Moses Kimhi. In them he defends Kimhi against Elijah Levita. Levita had faulted the same book in his own notes. Premsla's notes on the prayers came out in 1690. They were reprinted many times after that. One ruling of his treats the writing of God's name. Four of his works stayed in handwriting, the entry adds.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rakower-bloch-j:
Joseph b. David Tebele Rakower was a Polish rabbi and Hebraist. The Executive Committee of the Editorial Board and Peter Wiernik wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He moved from Cracow to Eibenschütz in Moravia. He died there in November 1707.

The article says Rakower served as rabbi of Eibenschütz. He is best known for Leshon Naki, printed in 1689. That book was a guide to writing Hebrew letters. It was reprinted several times, in full and in part. He also left a work called Merkebet ha-Mishnah in manuscript. That text ends with an account of a fire at Plock. The entry preserves a teacher of clear Hebrew style.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-reggio-issachar:
Issachar Ezekiel Reggio was an Italian rabbi and grammarian born in 1774. Isidore Singer and Umberto Cassuto wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He was born at Ferrara. He died in 1837, on the first of Elul.

The article says he studied under Graziadio Neppi and Joseph David Bassano. Bassano made him an assistant at Ferrara's Talmud Torah. When Bassano died, Reggio succeeded him as rabbi. He shared the post with Shabbethai Elhanan Pesaro at first. After Pesaro died, he headed the Spanish synagogue. He founded several religious institutions in his community. One source, Nepi-Ghirondi's history, supports the whole entry. Readers get a compact record of a Ferrara rabbi's rise. Service, teaching, and building mark his career.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-richmond-12744:
Richmond is the capital of Virginia and was the Confederate capital. Cyrus Adler wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. By 1785 it had over a dozen Jewish families. They were of Spanish and Portuguese descent.

The article says a Sephardic congregation formed in 1791. It was called K. K. Beth Shalome. Twenty nine heads of families stood on its roster. It stayed Richmond's main Jewish body until the Civil War. After the war, deaths and removals weakened it. In 1898 its last members joined Beth Ahabah together. Beth Shalome then ended after 107 years. German Jews had founded Beth Ahabah in 1841. The entry follows two congregations toward a merger.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-riga-10044:
Riga is the capital of the Russian government of Livonia. Herman Rosenthal and J. G. Lipman wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. It stands on the River Düna near its mouth. Jews first appear in Livonian records in 1560.

The article quotes harsh language from those early records. Negotiations that year sought to bar Jews from army contracts. Talks in 1561 asked that Jews not enter Livonia at all. The annexation treaty barred them from trade and customs leasing. Yet it did not forbid Jews from living in Riga. Jews thus continued to dwell there in considerable numbers. Christian merchants complained of Jewish trade under Polish rule. Laws under Sigismund III aimed to exclude Jews and others. The entry documents exclusion that never fully worked.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rosenblatt-jose:
Josef Michel Rosenblatt was an Austrian barrister born at Cracow on March 20, 1853. Isidore Singer and Frederick T. Haneman wrote his entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. He graduated from Cracow's university in 1876 and settled there as a lawyer.

Rosenblatt rose at the university from lecturer in law to full professor in 1893. He also served on the board that examined law students. In Jewish life he presided over the Cracow community and the Austrian Alliance Israélite Universelle. His books cover criminal procedure and, in one study, witch trials in Poland. He also sat as an alderman of the city of Cracow.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-sale-12444:
Sale, in Jewish law, covers the words used when land or houses change hands. Joseph Jacobs and Lewis N. Dembitz wrote the entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. It explains how the object sold is described, and how descriptions are construed.

House ownership was often split among coheirs, floor above floor. So the Roman rule that land runs up to heaven did not apply to buildings. Two Mishnah chapters define what terms like house do and do not include. A house sale excludes its cisterns, closets, and high-railed roof by default. Only the words from the abyss below to the sky above include them.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-samuel-schmelka:
Schulim Ochser wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, issued with the Executive Committee of the Editorial Board in 1906. It profiles Samuel Schmelka ben Ḥayyim Shammash, a preacher at Prague. He also served as an actuary of the Prague rabbinate. He worked under Ephraim Solomon of Lencziza. His career fell in the second half of the sixteenth century.

Samuel wrote on a wide range of practical subjects. His Perush al ha-Masoret adds to Elijah Levita's notes on the Masorah. It came out at Prague in 1610. His Seder Nashim treats the three commandments tied to women. He wrote that book in Judæo-German, and it appeared in 1629. He also made a multiplication table called Ba-Ḥeshbon. His other works cover the Masorah and the rules for ritual slaughter.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-schwarzfeld-133:
Isidore Singer wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906, on the Schwarzfeld family. The Rumanian family rose to note in the nineteenth century. Its head here is Benjamin Schwarzfeld. He was a Rumanian educator and writer. Benjamin was born in April 1822. He died at Jassy on November 27, 1896. His sons Elias, Moses, and Wilhelm followed him into letters.

Benjamin began as a banker and brought fire insurance to Moldavia. At his own cost he opened the first modern Jewish school in 1852. The Orthodox excommunicated him for that step. Foreign consuls shielded him, and the ban failed. His school ran until 1857. In 1858 he got the old ḥadarim closed by the minister. In 1860 he became inspector-general of Moldavia's Jewish schools. His son Elias became a historian and novelist at Jassy.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-servant-of-god-:
Servant of God is a title of honor used for many figures in the Bible. Emil G. Hirsch wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on the phrase. Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob all bear the title. So do Moses, Joshua, David, Isaiah, and Job.

Even Nebuchadnezzar, a foreign king, is called God's servant once. Hirsch notes that Semitic names often join a word for servant with a god's name. That habit shows how normal the phrase was across the region. In later Isaiah the title takes on a deeper, special sense. Readers gain a key for one of the Bible's most debated phrases.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-siesby-gottlieb:
Gottlieb Siesby was a Danish poet and editor born in Copenhagen in 1803. Isidore Singer and Frank Cramer wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on him. His first book was a collection of poems in 1826. Its Danish title means lyrical attempts, roughly rendered.

Later Siesby published humorous poetical works and almanacs. His opera Robinson reached Copenhagen's Royal Theater in 1834. In 1847 he became coeditor of the periodical Flyveposten. He later bought that paper outright for himself. The venture did not succeed under his ownership. Flyveposten stopped appearing entirely in the year 1870. Siesby died at Copenhagen in 1884. His brother Oskar became a noted philologist in Denmark. The entry keeps a light poet and luckless editor in view.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-simon-joseph-13:
Joseph Simon was a leader of the Progressive Jewish communities of Hungary. Isidore Singer and Ludwig Venetianer wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He was born at Kapolcs on June 24, 1844. He studied law at Budapest. He also reported on Jewish affairs to the Hungarian Ministry of Public Worship.

Simon represented Tapolcza at the Jewish Congress of 1868. He was elected secretary of that congress. He then led the national bureau for the congress communities until 1904. He helped found and run the Landesrabbinerschule from 1877. In 1883 he organized the defense in the Tisza Eszlar case. Ill health at last forced him to retire.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-sparrow-13944: Sparrow is the English rendering for the Hebrew word zippor in Psalms. Emil G Hirsch and I M Casanowicz wrote this brief Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906. The word denotes birds in general in Hebrew. It is used especially of small passerine birds in Scripture. Four species of sparrow are very numerous in Palestine. Tristram links the sparrow of Psalm 102 to the blue thrush. It sits alone on ledges, matching the psalm's lonely image.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-stettenheim-jul:
Julius Stettenheim was a German humorist born at Hamburg on November 2, 1831. Isidore Singer and Frederick T. Haneman wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article about him in 1906. He began in commerce before moving to Berlin in 1857. There he studied for three years. In 1861 he returned to Hamburg and founded a satirical paper.

His paper, Die Wespen, found real success only after moving to Berlin in 1868. As Berliner Wespen it ranked among Europe's best comic papers. Stettenheim was seen as Germany's greatest living satirist. His comic war reporter Wippchen debuted in 1870. Wippchen held the German public's attention for decades. Collected volumes of the reports appeared for years. The entry profiles a satirist who mocked public life weekly.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-swallow-14144:
The swallow appears in the Bible under two Hebrew names. Emil G. Hirsch and I. M. Casanowicz wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article in 1906. English versions render deror as swallow in Psalms and Proverbs. The words sus and sis also point to the bird. Jeremiah names it among creatures that know their seasons.

About ten swallow species live in Palestine today. Martins and swifts belong to closely allied families there. The Talmud usually calls the bird senunit. It sorts swallows into white, green, and house kinds. One rabbinic note ties a senunit to the eagle. The bird in that note may be another species entirely. The entry sorts tangled names for one familiar bird. It joins Bible translation with local natural history.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-tanzer-aaron-14:
Aaron Tänzer was an Austrian rabbi born at Presburg in 1871. Isidore Singer wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article about him in 1906. He was born on January 30 of that year. He studied at the Presburg rabbinical school. At Berlin he read Oriental philology and history. He earned his doctorate there in 1895.

In 1896 Hohenems called Tänzer as chief rabbi. His district covered Tyrol and Vorarlberg together. Since 1904 he has served as rabbi of Meran. His first book studies Joseph Albo's religious philosophy. It appeared at Frankfort in 1896. He wrote on the Jewish cemetery at Hohenems next. A 1903 book weighs Judaism against evolution theory. His history of Tyrol's Jews began appearing then too. The entry catches a young rabbi building a scholarly name.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-testaments-of-t:
Twelve linked documents claim to record the last words of Jacob's twelve sons. Crawford Howell Toy, Frederick C. Conybeare, and Kaufmann Kohler wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. Each testament bears a subtitle naming a virtue or vice. Reuben warns against desire, and Simeon against envy.

Each patriarch first retells his own life. He then urges his children to copy his virtues and shun his sins. Last come visions of what awaits his line. Those visions often quote the Book of Enoch. Some passages look Christian in origin, the article argues. They foretell baptism and the crucifixion. Manuscripts and old versions help sort those layers apart.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-utah-13044:
Utah, admitted to the Union in 1896, gained Jewish settlers around 1860. Cyrus Adler and Charles J. Freund wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. Isidor Morris and Samuel Kahn were among the earliest comers. Fred Auerbach and Louis Cohn also arrived early. Services first met in Salt Lake City in 1866.

Congregation B'nai Israel formed within a few years there. After a lapse it reorganized in 1880. Congregation Montefiore organized in 1899 and built by 1903. A Jewish Relief Society dated from 1873. A B'nai B'rith lodge counted eighty members by 1905. Utah Jews filled responsible public offices as citizens. Simon Bamberger sat in the state senate. About 1,000 Jews lived among 277,000 residents.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-wagenseil-johan:
Johann Christoph Wagenseil was a German Christian Hebraist. Crawford Howell Toy and Eduard Neumann wrote this entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Nuremberg in 1633. He died at Altdorf in 1705. He taught history, then Oriental languages, at Altdorf. A Jewish teacher, Enoch Levi, taught him Hebrew.

Wagenseil collected Jewish works written against Christianity. He traveled widely to gather them. His 1681 collection bears a fiery Latin title. It includes Isaac of Troki's defense of Judaism. One tract convinced him that Jews blasphemed Jesus. He then begged rulers to stop the mockery. Yet he opposed forced baptism and refuted the ritual murder charge.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-weiss-adolphe-1:
Adolphe Weiss was a French painter born in Hungary. He was born at Budapest on May 11, 1838. Isidore Singer and Frederick T. Haneman wrote this short entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He studied at Vienna's School of Fine Arts. In 1860 he went to Paris to finish his training. His first Salon exhibit, in 1869, was a portrait.

Weiss became a French citizen in 1871. He settled in Paris and showed at the Salons yearly. His subjects range from weddings to Bible scenes. La Fiancée Slave now hangs in the Museum of Lisieux. Captifs, painted in 1896, hangs at Angers. Judith and Nouvelle Captive came late in his career.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-winter-solomon-:
Solomon Winter was a Hungarian philanthropist. Isidore Singer and Newell Dunbar wrote this short entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born in Zips county in 1778. He died at Hunsdorf on February 24, 1859. For sixty years he worked for his district's Jews. Their advancement was his lifelong cause.

Hunsdorf's synagogue rose about 1820 through Winter's efforts. Its school followed in 1840 by his hand. He represented the county's Jewish communities together. At Budapest he spoke for them before Jewish notables. The brief entry preserves a local leader's record. His works outlasted him in brick and classrooms.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-xystus-15044:
Xystus was a raised open walk in old Jerusalem. Richard Gottheil and Samuel Krauss wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The name comes from the Greek world of games and schools. In Greek use it meant a roofed walk by a gym. In Roman use it meant an open walk by a house.

The Jerusalem work was of the second sort, the entry says. It stood as an open deck on the west edge of the mount. Posts held it up from the slope far below. Its floor lay level with the Temple court above. From that deck Titus spoke with the heads of the Jews. They stood in the upper city as he spoke. Like works stood in Greek towns such as Elis. The site can be fixed near, but not exact, the entry notes.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-zerahiah-ben-is:
Zerahiah ben Isaac ha-Levi Gerondi was a Talmud author and poet. Joseph Jacobs and Isaac Broyde wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He lived in the twelfth century of this era. He was a pupil of Moses ben Joseph of Narbonne.

One old book gives the year 1131 for his birth. That date can scarce be right, the entry notes with care. His chief book cites works that came too late for that date. He came of a great Spanish house of Gerona town. Foes in that town drove him to quit his home in youth. He settled at Lunel and gave his years to teach work. One pupil was Samuel ibn Tibbon, a famed name in lore. That man owned Zerahiah the more great mind of the two. His chief book is the Sefer ha-Maor of wide fame.
memoirs-of-jean-franc-ois-paul-de-gondi-:
Book three of Cardinal de Retz's memoirs turns on Mazarin and Conde. Mazarin, de Retz says, sought to shed his debt to the Prince. The Prince had in fact saved him from the gallows.

Paris libelled both the Cardinal and the Queen in those days. De Retz's party let the anti Mazarin songs pass, but curbed attacks on the Queen. Two men were saved from hanging by the crowd on the scaffold. A night raid on Mazarin's friends, with violins smashed, shows the street mood. De Retz then rode to Compiegne to win the King's return. His friends feared the risk, but he called the act a must.
mill-essays-unsettled-questions-1844:
John Stuart Mill wrote his Essays on Some Unsettled Questions of Political Economy in 1829 and 1830. He published them only in 1844, when his name could carry them. The essays ask how the science of economics itself should work. What is its method, and how should its terms be defined?

Mill argues that political economy reasons from known tendencies of human nature. Its laws hold as tendencies, not as clockwork certainties. That careful account of method underlies his later Principles of Political Economy. The Gutenberg text keeps the five essays whole. Readers meet the young Mill thinking about thinking. Few method essays have lasted so well.
milton-areopagitica-1644:
John Milton addressed Areopagitica to the Parliament of England in 1644. Its full title calls it a speech for the liberty of unlicensed printing. Milton wrote after Parliament imposed licensing on the press. He argues that free-born men should be able to advise the public and speak freely.

Milton insists that true liberty is not the absence of grievance. It is complaints freely heard, deeply considered, and speedily reformed. He praises Parliament's own deeds while pressing it to repeal censorship. The pamphlet became the classic English defense of a free press, quoted wherever printing freedoms are debated.
openalex-w1972009144:
Sérgio Pena and a large Brazilian team studied genomic ancestry. Their paper appeared in PLoS ONE in the year 2011. Old color-based methods split Brazil's regions as very diverse. Trials in medicine had trusted those regional labels. The team asked how color categories match real ancestry.

They measured DNA ancestry in people from varied regions. The title reports ancestry proved more uniform than expected. Regional color labels overstated the true genetic differences. That finding matters for clinical and drug trials in Brazil. It warns against treating color as a proxy for ancestry. The study reshaped debate on race and genetics there.
openalex-w2064953244:
Olivier Neyrolles, Rogelio Hernandez-Pando, France Pietri-Rouxel and colleagues asked whether body fat shelters tuberculosis bacteria. Their paper appeared in PLoS ONE in 2006. TB bacteria can persist in the body for decades. Where they hide during silent infection was unknown. The lungs may not be the only hiding place.

The team tested fat tissue from people in Mexico and France. All had died of causes other than TB. Bacterial DNA was found in fat from several people. The fat came from around organs and under skin. Lab tests showed bacteria can enter fat cells. Inside, they rest without growing. They also resist a major TB drug in that state. Fat may be a vast hidden reservoir.
openalex-w2073091344:
Mirjam Eberhardt, Maria Dux, Barbara Namer and colleagues uncovered how two gases jointly widen blood vessels. Their paper appeared in Nature Communications in 2014. Nitric oxide and hydrogen sulfide are both body-made gases. They each help regulate blood vessel tone. How they interact was not known.

The team showed the gases react to form nitroxyl. Nitroxyl switches on a sensory channel in nerve endings. That channel lets calcium flood into the cells. The nerves then release a vessel-widening peptide. The result is local and body-wide vessel relaxation. The pathway links gas signals to nerve control. It may matter for heart failure treatment. Nitroxyl has long interested drug researchers.
openalex-w2285852644:
Raymond Birge, Sebastian Boeltz, Sushil Kumar, and colleagues published this review in Cell Death and Differentiation in 2016. They present phosphatidylserine, a fat molecule in cell membranes, as a global signal that calms the immune system. Dying cells flip this molecule to their surface, where it marks them for quiet removal.

That removal process, called efferocytosis, avoids the inflammation that bursting cells would cause. The review shows how the same signal is borrowed beyond normal cell clearance. Infectious agents and cancers can display or mimic it to dampen immune attack. Understanding this shared off-switch, the authors argue, opens shared treatment ideas across infection, autoimmunity, and cancer.
openalex-w2473138844:
Massimo Sartelli, Dieter Weber, and Étienne Ruppé led a large international task force behind this 2016 review in the World Journal of Emergency Surgery. The paper presents AGORA, a global alliance working to improve how antibiotics are used for infections inside the abdomen. Such infections often hit high-risk patients hardest. They can end badly without fast, correct treatment.

The authors stress two cornerstones: quick control of the infection source and well-chosen antimicrobial therapy. Early treatment must cover all likely germs, because a poor first choice raises deaths and breeds resistance. Overuse, though, drives problems like C. difficile infection and resistant bacteria worldwide. Experts from seventy-nine countries shared one document setting out rational use. It aims to protect patients now while keeping these drugs effective for the future.
openalex-w2580536144:
Fabiane Frota da Rocha Morgado, Juliana Fernandes Filgueiras Meireles, and Clara Mockdece Neves, with colleagues, wrote this 2017 review in Psicologia: Reflexão e Crítica. It examines how researchers build measurement scales, the questionnaires used across human and social sciences. Good scales are critical to building reliable knowledge. The authors reviewed real scale-building projects to see where they go wrong.

They assessed one hundred five studies published between 1976 and 2015. The review sorted problems into ten main types, from weak samples to missing data and social desirability bias. Many studies showed clear method flaws, like small samples in the psychometric testing stage. Few authors, though, admitted and recorded their own limitations. The paper ends with recommendations for better practice. Knowing the usual pitfalls should help future researchers choose sound methods and report limits honestly.
openalex-w2611479744:
Paola Ortíz-Montero, Arturo Londoño-Vallejo, and Jean-Paul Vernot published this 2017 study in Cell Communication and Signaling. It examines two inflammatory signals, IL-6 and IL-8, released by senescent cells. Senescent cells have stopped dividing but pour out a mix of signals called the secretory phenotype. Aggressive breast cancer lines secrete these signals, while the milder MCF-7 line does not.

The team bathed MCF-7 cells in IL-6, IL-8, or fluid from senescent cells. Treated cells changed shape, moved more, and gained stem-like traits, including self-renewal. The changes matched a program linked to cancer spread, called EMT. Senescent fluid also made MCF-7 cells release more IL-6 and IL-8 themselves. That self-reinforcing loop strengthens the tumor-friendly environment around the cells. The results warn that aging, inflamed tissue can push quiet cancer cells toward aggression.
openalex-w2788411744:
Asangaedem Akpan, Charlotte J. Roberts, and Karen Bandeen-Roche lead a working group report in BMC Geriatrics in 2018. It presents a standard set of health outcome measures for older persons. The set comes from the International Consortium for Health Outcomes Measurement. That body builds measurement tools that experts agree on, so health systems can learn from each other's results.

An international panel used a modified Delphi process, informed by literature, ageing surveys, and a focus group. The suggested measures cover what matters to older people themselves.
