They include taking part in decisions, autonomy, mood, loneliness, pain, and daily activities. Frailty, hospital time, survival, carer burden, many medications, and falls also appear. The set targets everyday care providers and payers, not researchers. Shared measures should help systems improve care pathways and quality for ageing populations.
openalex-w2885005744:
Hyun Soon Lillehoj, Yanhong Liu, and S. Calsamiglia lead this 2018 review in Veterinary Research, on plant chemicals as substitutes for antibiotics. Drug-resistant superbugs are rising while new antibiotics lag behind. Farm animals, especially poultry and livestock, urgently need growth promotion without antibiotics. The review grows out of a global symposium on alternatives held in Paris in 2016.

Over two hundred seventy experts from more than twenty-five countries came to that meeting. Sessions spanned vaccines, microbial products, plant chemicals, immune products, and new drugs. Plant-derived compounds, called phytochemicals, are this paper's focus. The symposium weighed policy differences and hurdles to selling each option. Its goal was a workable plan, not just promising science. Substitutes must protect production levels while slowing resistance. The review reports a field pulling together around that hard demand.
openalex-w2921196544:
Lisbeth Bethelmy and José Corraliza wrote this 2019 research article in Frontiers in Psychology. Both study how people relate to the natural world, with a focus on spiritual experience. Their subject is transcendence in nature: feelings of awe and of inspiring energy that people report in wild places.

The article places awe within wider research on spirituality and human wellbeing. It notes that spirituality can mean an inner experience or belief system that gives life meaning and lifts a person beyond the present moment. Feelings of awe have drawn growing experimental study in recent years. Bethelmy and Corraliza examine how such sublime experiences in nature arise and what they involve.
openalex-w3040309044:
Madhu Gupta, Brian Wahl, Binita Adhikari, and colleagues wrote this commentary in Global Health Research and Policy in 2020. It argues that COVID-19 research in low- and middle-income countries is urgently needed. In the pandemic's early months, most reported cases and deaths sat in rich countries.

Weak testing, the authors warn, may have hidden the true toll in poorer countries, leaving the pandemic's full impact there uncertain. They propose research in three broad areas: how the virus transmits, how the disease presents, and what response measures do. Such work should be led by local investigators and draw on many fields. It must also avoid draining staff, funds, or supplies from the response itself.
openalex-w3091814244:
Maricelis Acevedo, Kevin Pixley, Nkulumo Zinyengere, and colleagues published this scoping review in Nature Plants in 2020. It asks what leads small-scale farmers in poorer countries to adopt climate-resilient crops. Such crops are often recommended for coping with climate change, yet uptake varies widely.

Following a standard protocol, the team reviewed two hundred two papers covering thirty years. Farmers adopted hardy crops mainly to withstand drought, heat, flooding, and salty soils, with drought tolerance the most common trait. The strongest drivers of adoption were good extension services and outreach, schooling of the household head, and access to seeds and fertilizer. Social traits such as sex and age also shaped who adopted, in about half the studies.
openalex-w3124179444:
Usama Bilal, Philipp Hessel, Carolina Pérez Ferrer, and colleagues of the SALURBAL group published this study in Nature Medicine in 2021. It compares life expectancy and causes of death across three hundred sixty-three cities in nine Latin American countries. Talk of an urban health advantage hides wide gaps between cities, they argue.

Life expectancy differed a great deal even among cities in the same country. Injury deaths varied most within countries, while infection and chronic disease shares varied mostly between them. Cities with better schooling, water, and sanitation, and less crowding, enjoyed longer lives. Their death mix leaned toward cancer and heart disease and away from infections and newborn deaths. City policy, the results imply, shapes health powerfully.
openalex-w3194040044:
Lina Ruiz, Allan Libedinsky, and Álvaro Elorza review the role of copper in mitochondria, the cell's energy-producing structures. Their review appeared in Frontiers in Molecular Biosciences in 2021. Mitochondria do far more than make energy: they help decide whether a cell grows, changes role, or dies. Their inner machinery runs on a chain of protein complexes that pass electrons along.

Copper is a small but vital part of that machinery, needed by key enzymes in the chain. The review explains how cells obtain copper, deliver it safely, and place it where it works. It also covers what goes wrong when copper is missing or builds up. That balance shapes metabolism in health and in diseases such as cancer.
openalex-w4406633044:
Viktoria Cologna, Niels Mede, Sebastian Berger, and colleagues survey trust in scientists across sixty-eight countries. Their paper appeared in Nature Human Behaviour in 2025. Claims of a crisis in trust spread after the COVID-19 pandemic. Hard evidence from beyond wealthy Western countries was scarce.

The team ran a large preregistered survey with local research partners. It measured trust in several dimensions and recorded demographic, political, and country-level factors. The survey also asked what role people want scientists to play in society and policymaking. It further asked which problems people want scientists to prioritise. The results test whether the distrust narrative holds worldwide.
openalex-w7204564944: A premature baby in intensive care strains the bond between parent and child before it can form. This study looks at how psychologists in neonatal ICUs help parents become parents under extreme stress. The authors review the mediator role: building attachment through glass and tubes. Tender and clinical, it treats bonding as something medicine can protect.
openalex-w7206160644: Starting in the 2000s, Brazil massively expanded free federal universities, opening doors in poor regions like Alagoas. This study follows student trajectories from 2020 to 2024 to see who got in, who stayed, and who finished after the REUNI expansion program. It asks whether expansion alone delivered on the promise of fair access. A data-driven check on one of Brazil's biggest education bets of the century.
openalex-w7207835744: Brazil's federal institutes promise job training for everyone, including students with disabilities. This paper asks whether that promise holds in real classrooms. The authors review how schools for technical careers try to include these students, and they list what gets in the way and what helps. Framed as an open question, are we prepared, it calls on schools to close the gap between policy and daily practice.
openalex-w7212081144:
Daiane de Lourdes Alves Velho leads a team on how learning and growth link, in the view of Lev Vygotsky. The Russian thinker held that the mind is made in social life. We take in tools and signs from our culture, and speech has the lead role in that shift. The team read past work on his thought and on how schools have used it.

To learn, in this view, is not to store facts or to react to cues. A child grows through talk and joint work with others. The teacher's part is planned and active. She sets tasks, picks the knowledge, and lends support at the right point. One key tool is the zone just past what a child can do alone. Good tests and plans, the authors argue, should look at that zone.
openalex-w7212281544:
Challes Henrique Soares Romeiro, Davi Beserra Gomes, and Valeria Maciel Cordeiro de Oliveira review slip-ups in drug orders at Brazilian wards. A drug order is the hinge of drug care. When it holds the wrong dose, the wrong drug, or thin facts on the patient, harm can flow down the line. The team read studies from 2020 to 2025 in three databases. They sorted the kinds of slips, their roots, and the ways to stop them.

To stop such slips, they find, takes more than care by one hand. It takes shared work: sound skill, clear steps, and checks built into the path of the drug. The ward pharmacist earns a lead place in that chain. That expert reads each order with a trained eye and can catch a flaw in time. The review gives wards a plain map of where orders go wrong, and who can set them right.
openalex-w7213439644:
Rodrigo Alber Alves de Vasconcelos and co-workers review a combined therapy for rebuilding large jaw bone defects. Such defects can follow removal of maxillary cysts, where natural regrowth is not enough. Their 2026 review examines platelet-rich fibrin together with a bone growth protein.

Studies in national and international sources were analysed. The combination favoured new blood vessel growth, bone induction, and new bone training. Clinical and X-ray results improved in the reports reviewed. The authors see relevant promise for maxillofacial bone regeneration. They also warn that more clinical studies are needed before treatment protocols can be standardized for routine surgical use.
openalex-w7213495244:
Thiago Francisco Costa Solak leads a team characterising wild animals admitted in Curitiba, Paraná. Their 2026 study covers a city wildlife support centre from January 2019 to October 2024. Records were mapped by place and tested for seasonal and taxonomic patterns.

Nearly twelve thousand admissions were analysed. Birds made up more than three quarters, followed by mammals and reptiles. Admissions peaked in spring and summer, and young animals were the majority. Most animals arrived by voluntary delivery, and about a quarter returned to nature. Threatened species appeared among the cases. The authors present the centre as a key source for conservation medicine and city wildlife planning.
openalex-w7213876744:
An integrative review on physical activity and childhood obesity forms this 2026 article. The review itself, in a Brazilian journal, treats childhood obesity as a major public health challenge. Sedentary habits, screen time, and ultra-processed food drive the account.

Activity helps through energy use, better body composition, motor growth, and self-esteem, the review argues. Obese children tend to spend less total time active, the studies show. Causes are many-sided, so responses must join family, school, and health workers together. The physical education professional holds a named role in that shared effort against excess weight in childhood.
openalex-w7214069144:
Jozadake Petry Fausto leads an integrative review on long-term benzodiazepine use in Brazilian primary care. Their 2026 review, run in August and September 2026, covers PubMed and two regional sources for 2021 to 2026. Eleven studies of varied design were selected and synthesized.

Long-term use was relevantly frequent, the review finds, and tied to adverse events. Older people and patients on many medicines need special attention. Dependence and withdrawal symptoms sit among the consequences. Gradual dose reduction, health education, and user participation made deprescribing strategies work better, though results varied. Rational use, safety, and steady therapeutic follow-up are presented as collective health duties, not private matters alone.
openalex-w7215120844:
Andréa Navarro Vieira Nery, Matheus Garcia Coelho, and Renato Marcelo Resgala Júnior wrote a 2026 article on meaning in atypical motherhood, read through logotherapy, Viktor Frankl's meaning-centered approach to psychology. A child's autism diagnosis reshapes family routine, parental expectations, and daily life. Mothers can face insecurity, overload, anxiety, guilt, and isolation under continuous care demands, and the authors ask what logotherapy can and cannot offer them.

Concepts such as meaning, freedom, responsibility, self-transcendence, values, and self-distancing can frame psychological listening for these women, the review indicates. Yet the authors are careful: the review cannot prove clinical effectiveness, and meaning-making must never shift responsibility onto mothers or replace support networks and public policy. Logotherapy can contribute, they conclude, when it respects each mother's singularity, welcomes her suffering, and preserves her autonomy rather than romanticizing hardship.
openalex-w7220696744: Tyrosine hydroxylase deficiency is a rare disorder that disrupts dopamine production. This paper traces the disease from its clinical signs and treatments to its genetic roots. The authors mapped the variants and their effects. A rare-disease review connecting genes to symptoms.
openalex-w7220715044:
Nauana Sandrelly Ferreira Lima and Vinícius Denardin Cardoso wrote, in a 2026 experience article, a guided physical education placement at a clinic serving children and teens with autism spectrum disorder. Autism brings lasting differences in communication and social interaction, with narrow, repetitive behavior patterns. Early help across fields supports the child's whole growth, and PE with adapted bodily work helps motor growth, social inclusion, and quality of life. Their account looks at what PE and adapted bodily work did inside that clinic.

Joining PE with ABA mattered: such strategies can make motor work better. Yet although motor work sat inside the therapy protocols, it often lacked structured planning, pedagogical progression, and individualization. Working with autism demands competences beyond traditional movement teaching, they conclude, including broader formation and multiprofessional practice aimed at whole development. The report speaks to PE teachers joining clinical teams that rarely plan their work with teaching intent.
phrenology-proved-illustrated-and-applie: Phrenology Proved, Illustrated, and Applied, 1844. Another edition. This book preserves that work. The library keeps the document safe. Writers of history may cite it later. The paper lasts as a quiet witness. Time has kept the file intact.
plos-pbio-0020044:
Gregor Rainer, Han Lee, and Nikos K. Logothetis studied how learning changes vision in monkeys for PLOS Biology in 2004. They recorded from the extrastriate visual cortex, an area that processes what the eyes see beyond the first entry point. The monkeys learned a visual task while the team tracked nerve cell responses.

As skill grew, the way these cells fired changed with it. That shows learning does not just add facts in high brain areas. It also retunes mid-level vision itself. The work helps explain why practice makes sights easier to pick out and judge. It gives a concrete case of the adult brain reshaping its own wiring through experience.
plos-pbio-0020244:
Justin Gage Crump, Mary E. Swartz, and Charles B. Kimmel studied throat cartilage in zebrafish in PLOS Biology in 2004. The hyoid cartilage supports the tongue area in fish and, in changed form, in humans too. It forms near a pouch of gut tissue called the endoderm.

The team found that this pouch must use integrins, the anchor proteins that grip surrounding material, for the cartilage to form right. That is a case of one tissue guiding another's growth through its anchors. The work shows development is a team effort between tissues, not a solo program in each one. Faults in such guidance may underlie some human jaw and throat birth defects.
plos-pone-0000044:
Barbara Davids, David Reiner, Shanda Birkeland, and co-authors catalogued a fresh family of genes in a gut parasite in 2006. Giardia makes people sick with diarrhea worldwide, and it survives outside the body as a hard cyst. Its surface proteins, the VSPs, were well studied; this team looked beyond them.

They found a new family of giardial genes coding for cysteine-rich proteins that are not VSPs, plus a novel cyst protein involved in the parasite's survival shell. New surface and cyst parts are candidate targets for drugs and diagnostics, since they sit where the parasite meets its host. The paper extends the known toolkit of one of humanity's most common parasites.
plos-pone-0000144:
Daniel A. Beard and Hong Qian published this theory paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. It works on a question in thermodynamics, the physics of energy and heat, applied to chemical reactions. Specifically, it examines how the driving force behind a reversible process relates to the one-way flows of molecules in each direction.

These relationships sit under much of biochemistry, since cells run on reversible reactions near equilibrium. The authors sort out exactly how force and flux connect. The result gives modelers of metabolism and other chemical networks a firmer theoretical base, and it corrects loose assumptions that can creep into textbook treatments.
plos-pone-0000244:
Thomas Clausen and Katharina Ribbeck published this theory paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. During cell division, the spindle, a scaffold of microtubules, separates the chromosomes. Some spindles form without centrosomes, the usual organizing hubs, and are called anastral. The authors model how such spindles organize themselves.

Their model combines three ingredients: microtubules that grow and collapse, autocatalytic production of more microtubules, and a spatial signaling gradient. Together these produce an organized spindle from disorder. The work shows how cells can build precise machinery by self-organization, without a blueprint or a foreman.
plos-pone-0000344:
Clarence C. Tam, Sarah J. O'Brien, Irene Petersen, and colleagues published this epidemiology paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. Guillain-Barré syndrome is a paralyzing autoimmune condition often triggered by infection. Using the UK General Practice Research Database, the authors examine how often it follows infection with Campylobacter, influenza, or Epstein-Barr virus.

Campylobacter food poisoning was the prime suspect, but numbers per infection were fuzzy. A huge practice database gives rates grounded in routine care records. The estimates help doctors counsel patients and help researchers weigh how much of the syndrome each infection explains.
plos-pone-0000444:
Gregory M. Mikkelson, Andrew Gonzalez, and Garry D. Peterson reported a link between wealth gaps and species loss, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Their study found that economic inequality predicts biodiversity loss, meaning places with wider gaps between rich and poor tend to lose more of their species.

The connection runs against the hope that growth alone saves nature. If inequality itself drives loss, through land pressure, weak protection, or short-term extraction, then social policy becomes conservation policy. Cross-country patterns like this one are early evidence, not proof of cause. Still, they reframe the problem. Protecting species may require narrowing inequality, not just funding parks.
plos-pone-0000544:
Santhi K. Ganesh and colleagues searched blood proteins for a signature of dangerous clots, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. Venous thromboembolism, clots forming in veins, can travel to the lungs and kill, yet diagnosis often needs imaging that is slow or unavailable. The team worked on detection by proteomic serum biomarkers, patterns of proteins in blood serum.

A blood test for clots would speed triage of patients with chest pain or swollen legs. Proteomics screens thousands of proteins at once to find the pattern that separates patients with clots from those without. Studies like this are the discovery phase of test development, where candidate markers are found before validation.
plos-pone-0000644:
Lee Shaish, Avigdor Abelson and Baruch Rinkevich used a branching coral to ask how far flexibility can go, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Phenotypic plasticity is the ability of one genotype to adjust its shape and life traits to changing conditions. Their model animal is Stylophora pistillata, a coral that builds colonies by branching.

The researchers propagated colony pieces and watched how new branches formed, a process called astogeny. Some architectural rules stayed fixed while others bent with conditions. Sorting the fixed rules from the plastic ones shows what a colony can change and what it cannot. Reef biologists get a sharper sense of how corals cope with varied seas.
plos-pone-0000744:
Jon E. Brommer, Mark Kirkpatrick, Anna Qvarnström and colleagues measured whether fit parents of one sex predict fit offspring of the other. In PLOS ONE in 2007, they tackled the genetic benefits of mate choice in the wild. Those benefits are limited by how strongly male and female fitness are genetically correlated. A small or negative correlation breaks the logic of choosing a fit mate.

Their subject is lifetime fitness, total reproductive success across a life, measured outside the lab. If high-fitness males tend to produce low-fitness daughters, sexual selection faces a genetic tug-of-war. Knowing the correlation's true size changes what mate choice can and cannot achieve in evolution.
plos-pone-0000844:
Sushant K. Kachhap, Dennis Faith, David Z. Qian and colleagues assigned a new job to a gene whose loss tracks with spreading cancer, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Cell-to-cell adhesion is mediated by molecules on the cell surface, and downregulation of adhesion complex molecules is a characteristic of metastatic cancer cells. Downregulation of the gene NDRG1 increases metastasis in prostate and breast cancers, as background work showed.

Their title reports that NDRG1 is a Rab4a effector involved in vesicular recycling of E-cadherin, the main adhesion molecule between epithelial cells. Recycling returns E-cadherin to the surface after use. If NDRG1 helps that loop, losing it loosens cells for metastasis.
plos-pone-0000944:
Shojiro Kitajima, Yasusei Kudo, Ikuko Ogawa and colleagues showed how a chemical tag can stabilize a cancer linked protein, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Aurora-A is an enzyme that helps cells divide, and it is overproduced in many human cancers. Extra copies of its gene explain only part of that excess.

The team report that steady phosphorylation, a phosphate tag at one site, Ser51, keeps Aurora-A from being broken down. A stabilized protein piles up even without extra gene copies. That mechanism widens the list of ways a cancer cell can boost a growth driver. It also marks the tagging step as a point where a drug might intervene.
plos-pone-0001044:
Ravi Kolla, Suresh Chintalapati, Mojgan Sabet and colleagues boosted an anthrax vaccine by attaching an immune helper, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Anthrax is caused by Bacillus anthracis, and its toxins enter cells through a part called protective antigen. The standing vaccine relies on that antigen with an aluminum adjuvant and gives a slow response.

The team conjugated protective antigen to C3d, a fragment of the complement system that flags material for immune attention. Their title reports a rapid, sustained and protective antibody response. A faster anthrax vaccine matters for responders after an exposure, when weeks of waiting are not available.
plos-pone-0001144:
Cells constantly take in material from their surroundings through a process called endocytosis. Michela Felberbaum-Corti and co-authors examined one protein involved in the fluid-phase version of this uptake, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. The protein is TXNL1, which the authors describe as a redox sensor, a molecule that reacts to the cell's oxidation state.

The paper also touches on Rab proteins, small switches that organize membrane traffic and are handled by a carrier called GDI. The authors report that TXNL1 plays a regulatory role in fluid-phase endocytosis. The work ties the cell's redox balance to its basic housekeeping of taking in fluid.
plos-pone-0001244:
High blood pressure runs in populations, and modern migration mixes ancestries in ways that can help locate the responsible genes. Xiaofeng Zhu and Richard Cooper used that strategy, called admixture mapping, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. They genotyped a panel of 2,270 ancestry-informative markers in a random sample.

The authors report evidence associating the VNN1 gene with hypertension. VNN1 codes for an enzyme called pantetheinase, not an obvious blood pressure suspect. Admixture mapping exploits the fact that a disease commoner in one ancestral group points to genome regions inherited from that group.
plos-pone-0001344:
Many obese people try diets; some lose weight and many do not, and nobody can tell in advance who will respond. David Mutch and colleagues asked whether gene expression in fat tissue, measured before weight loss, can make that prediction, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. The ability to identify dietary responders in advance would change disease management.

The authors report that adipose gene expression prior to weight loss can differentiate and weakly predict dietary responders. Weak prediction is still a proof of principle: the fat's transcriptional state holds information about the future. Their study is an early step toward personalized diet advice based on biology.
plos-pone-0001444:
Jesús Lemus and co-authors published a 2008 PLOS ONE study on drug residues that reach wild birds. Drugs given to farm animals can stay in dead stock left in fields. Scavenger birds that feed on those bodies may take in the drugs. The team checked blood of wild scavengers for residues of a common class of germ drugs.

They found marks of these drugs in the birds, tied to disease in some cases. The work warns that farm drug use can harm wild life far from the farm. Vultures and like birds have crashed in some regions for drug linked causes. The study adds proof for tighter rules on which drugs dead stock may carry.
plos-pone-0001544:
Takashi Hiroyama and co-authors wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE study on making red blood cells in the lab. Donor blood supply falls short in many lands. A cell line that could make transfusable red cells in bulk would be a prize. No such line yet existed. The team tested whether mouse embryo stem cells could yield one.

They built lines of young red cell stock from the stem cells. Those lines could make working red blood cells on demand. That is a proof of concept for lab grown blood. Much work stays before human use, but the path is now shown to exist.
plos-pone-0001644:
Marcel M. Daadi, Anne-Lise Maag, and Gary K. Steinberg built a human neural stem cell line for stroke repair research, described in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. The cells came from human embryonic stem cells, which can supply nerve cells in near-limitless amounts. Grown in a flat, adherent culture, the line could renew itself and still mature into nerve cell types.

The team tested the cells in an experimental stroke model, grafting them into damaged brain tissue. The full text gives the culture method, the markers the cells carried, and how the grafts fared in the injured brains. A stable, well-defined cell line matters because stroke trials need cells that behave the same way in every batch. This work is an early step toward cell therapy for stroke damage.
plos-pone-0001744:
Philip E. Higuera, Linda B. Brubaker, Patricia M. Anderson, and their co-authors read ancient fire records in Arctic Alaska in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Feedbacks between land and atmosphere matter for predicting global change, above all in the fast-warming Arctic. Fire is a key process, but what altered fire regimes do to tundra was poorly known.

From paleorecords, traces preserved in lake sediments, the team found that fires were frequent in ancient shrub tundra. The full text gives the sediment cores, the fire dates, and how past fire frequency compares with today. A fiery past for the tundra suggests modern warming could bring back frequent burns, with large effects on carbon stores and northern ecosystems.
plos-pone-0001844:
Keng Boon Wee and co-authors studied how RNA folding affects a Duchenne muscular dystrophy therapy in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Antisense oligonucleotides, short synthetic DNA-like strands, can make cells skip faulty exons in the dystrophin gene, a potential therapy for Duchenne. Finding effective target sites was unsatisfactory because binding accessibility could not be predicted precisely.

The team shows that the dynamics of co-transcriptional pre-mRNA folding, how the RNA folds as it is being made, influence the induction of exon skipping. The full text gives the folding analysis and the skipping efficiencies. Better target prediction could turn exon skipping from trial and error into a designable drug approach.
plos-pone-0001944:
Daisuke Matsuzawa and co-authors measured a protective chemical in the brains of people with schizophrenia, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. The chemical, glutathione, is a major guard against cell damage inside cells. It also plays a part in signaling through NMDA receptors, a path thought to go wrong in this illness.

Using a strong magnet scan that can read brain chemistry, the team measured glutathione in a rear midline area of the frontal lobe. As the title states, lower levels tracked with worse negative symptoms, such as flat affect and low drive. A chemical link to symptom load could guide new treatment ideas.
plos-pone-0002044:
Peter Ungar, Frederick Grine, and Mark Teaford read diet from the tooth wear of an ancient human kin, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Paranthropus boisei, a hominin from the Plio-Pleistocene, had huge flat cheek teeth with thick enamel. It also had a robust skull and jaw, and signs of massive chewing muscles. That build earned it the nickname Nutcracker Man.

The trio examined dental microwear, the tiny pits and scratches meals leave on teeth. Wear can test whether the teeth were used as nutcrackers in daily life, or only as a fallback for hard foods in lean times. Fossil diet is read from such marks.
plos-pone-0002144:
Deborah French, Wenjian Yang, Leo Hamilton, and co-authors compared gene activity in cancer cells and healthy blood cells, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. They asked how far gene activity matches between unlike tissues inside the same person. Their idea was that genes whose activity rises and falls together across tissues are more likely to be steered by inherited DNA differences.

The team looked at leukemia cells alongside normal white blood cells from the same people. Shared patterns pointed them to nearby DNA variants, called cis-SNPs, carried from birth. Findings like these help explain why the same gene can behave in unlike ways in different patients.
plos-pone-0002244:
Marjolijn Hoekert, Leonie Bais, René Kahn, and co-authors timed the brain's response to emotion in the voice, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Tone of voice, or prosody, tells listeners a speaker's feelings and intent beyond the words themselves. Earlier studies had pointed to the right frontal and right temporal parts of the brain as key sites for reading that tone.

The team mapped the time course of activity in the right anterior superior temporal gyrus and the right fronto-parietal operculum. Knowing which area acts first helps model how the brain builds an emotional read of speech, step by step, within fractions of a second.
plos-pone-0002344:
Paolo Sordino, Nikos Andreakis, Euan Brown, and co-authors used natural variation in a sea squirt to map mutant traits, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Ascidians such as Ciona intestinalis are simple chordates whose study has taught much about the origin of vertebrates. Forward genetics in Ciona, finding genes from their effects, needs richer information on how traits vary.

The team combined natural variation with model mutant phenotypes, traits from known laboratory mutants, to support that mapping. Wild populations carry ready-made differences that can pinpoint the genes behind a trait. The approach strengthens Ciona as a genetic model for the earliest branches of our own phylum.
plos-pone-0002444:
Research by Qi and co-authors came out in PLOS ONE in 2008. The author list runs from Zhen Qi, Gary W. Miller, Eberhard O. Voit, and others. Its subject is computational Systems Analysis of Dopamine Metabolism. A prominent feature of Parkinson's disease (PD) is the loss of dopamine in the striatum.

What the team did, and why they did it that way, forms the core of the piece. It stands as one careful step in a longer line of work, with its question and approach laid out in full. PLOS ONE is an open journal, and the full text can be read free by anyone who wants to check the work.
plos-pone-0002544:
Gratwicke and colleagues set out their study in a 2008 PLOS ONE article. The author list runs from Brian Gratwicke, Judy Mills, Adam Dutton, and others. Its subject is attitudes Toward Consumption and Conservation of Tigers in China. A heated debate has recently emerged between tiger farmers.

Each part of the study builds on the part before it, in the order the team carried it out. In short, the piece gives a clear, short route into a field that can seem hard to enter from the outside. PLOS ONE is an open journal, and the full text can be read free by anyone who wants to check the work.
plos-pone-0002644:
Work by Irene Sendiña-Nadal and colleagues appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008, dealing with phase locking induces Scale-Free topologies in networks of coupled oscillators. The catalog record names Irene Sendiña-Nadal first among the authors, and the source is the open journal PLOS ONE.

The opening of the abstract sets out the basis for the work. An initial unsynchronized ensemble of networking phase oscillators is further subjected to a growing process where a set of forcing oscillators. For readers, the value lies in how plainly the abstract sets out the problem and what the authors set out to test or describe.
plos-pone-0002744:
Research from Carsten Matz and co-authors, published in PLOS ONE in 2008, covers marine biofilm bacteria evade eukaryotic predation by targeted chemical defense. Authorship is credited in the record to Carsten Matz and co-authors, with PLOS ONE as the journal of publication.

The opening of the abstract sets out the basis for the work. Many plants and animals are defended from predation or herbivory by inhibitory secondary metabolites. Its abstract frames the work for later readers, who can judge the full text against the aims stated at the start. No results or figures are claimed in this summary beyond what the title and abstract themselves state.
plos-pone-0002844:
Work by Barbara Köhler and colleagues appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. Their subject was bid participates in genotoxic Drug-Induced apoptosis of HeLa cells and is essential for death receptor ligands' apoptotic and synergistic effects. The full author list in the catalog record begins with Barbara Köhler, and the article appeared in the open journal PLOS ONE.

The opening of the abstract sets out the basis for the work. The BH3-only protein Bid is an important component of death receptor-mediated caspase activation. The authors add a further point. Bid is cleaved by caspase-8 or -10 into t-Bid, which translocates to mitochondria and triggers the release of caspase-activating factors. Anyone studying the topic can use the article to see how the authors framed the problem at the time of publication.
plos-pone-0002944:
Luiz Corrêa, Diego Riaño-Pachón, Carlos Schrago and co-authors traced bZIP proteins across green plants in 2008. These transcription factors switch genes on and off and exist in all eukaryotes. In plants they govern leaf and seed formation, light responses, and energy balance, among other jobs.

The PLOS ONE paper argues that many adaptive features of plant bZIPs grew from just four founder genes. Tracing that expansion shows how a small starter set can diversify for many tasks. Plant biologists gain a family history that helps predict what untested bZIP genes in crops may do.
plos-pone-0003044:
Rossella Ventura, Emanuele Latagliata, Cristina Morrone and co-authors linked prefrontal norepinephrine to motivational salience in 2008. Giving rewards intense importance, called high salience, is thought to play a major role in several mental disorders. Many brain areas join normal salience attribution, and whether they share one mechanism was unclear.

Norepinephrine in the prefrontal cortex determines attribution of high motivational salience, the title reports. Published in PLOS ONE, that singles out one chemical in one region as a deciding factor. The finding frames a target for research on addiction and related conditions. Readers can follow the full methods and data in the complete text of the article.
plos-pone-0003144:
Beihua Dong, Robert H. Silverman and Eugene S. Kandel study two related retroviruses in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Murine leukemia virus, a rodent virus, forms the backbone of common tools that deliver genes for experiments and therapy. A newer infectious virus of the same family, XMRV, had lately been found in prostate cancer patients.

The title reports that this natural human retrovirus can efficiently complement vectors based on the mouse virus. Readers learn how parts from one virus can make up for missing parts in the other. The work bears on the safety and design of gene delivery tools built from retroviruses.
plos-pone-0003244:
Laura Temime, Pierre-Yves Boelle, Lulla Opatowski and colleagues model capsular switch in pneumococcal disease in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Despite the dramatic decline in invasive pneumococcal disease observed since conjugate vaccination began, it is feared that several factors may undermine future effectiveness of the vaccines. In particular, pathogenic pneumococci may switch their capsule type to escape vaccine coverage.

The team assess the impact of capsular switch on disease incidence in a vaccinated population. Readers see a key vaccine risk tested in a model before it fully emerges. Planning for strain replacement is part of keeping vaccine gains over decades.
plos-pone-0003344:
Mark D. Alter, Daniel B. Rubin, Keri Ramsey and colleagues link brain gene patterns to behaviour in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Despite sharing the same genes, identical twins demonstrate substantial variability in behavioural traits and in their risk for disease. Epigenetic factors, DNA and chromatin modifications that affect levels of gene expression without affecting DNA sequence, are thought to be important in that variability.

The title reports variation in large-scale organization of gene expression in the hippocampus relates to stable epigenetic variability in behaviour. Readers see differences arise without DNA changes. That finding helps explain twin differences and why behaviour can be stable yet not strictly genetic.
plos-pone-0003444:
Maxim I. Lutskiy and co-authors watched immune cells evolve inside two brothers in this 2008 paper. Both siblings had Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome, a genetic immune disorder. Their faulty gene raised the cost of living for immune cells. Any cell that found a workaround gained an edge over the rest.

Over time, many compensating changes arose in their T cell populations. Cell groups became highly varied as new fixes spread. The process was evolution running within a single body. It shows how strong pressure can reshape cell lines in one lifetime. Few studies catch that process at work inside one family.
plos-pone-0003544:
Giovanni Zito and co-authors hunted stem-like cells in a deadly thyroid cancer in this 2008 paper. Anaplastic thyroid carcinoma grows fast and responds poorly to treatment. Its cells are highly dedifferentiated, having lost mature traits. A small subset of cancer stem cells may drive such tumors.

Working in cell lines, the team identified CD133-positive stem-like cells. Those cells carried the marker linked to tumor-starting power. Finding them in this cancer points therapy at the root population. Bulk killing alone may miss the cells that regrow tumors. Rare and fierce cancers like this one get few trials, so each clue counts.
plos-pone-0003644:
Martin D. H. Teichmann, Frederic v. Wegner, Rainer H. A. Fink, and colleagues published this muscle study in PLOS ONE in 2008. It concerns muscle that lacks dystrophin, the protein missing in Duchenne muscular dystrophy. In such muscle, control over small calcium release events, called sparks, breaks down.

The team found that stretch-sensitive channels normally help keep these sparks in check, and that this control fails without dystrophin. Giving the muscle a shortened form of dystrophin restored the control. The result links a missing brake on calcium to the damage seen in dystrophic muscle.
plos-pone-0003744:
Michael C. Wimberly, Michael B. Hildreth, Stephen P. Boyte, and colleagues published this disease ecology study in PLOS ONE in 2008. West Nile virus rates stayed high in the northern Great Plains while they fell elsewhere in the United States. The reasons for that lasting risk were not determined.

The team mapped the ecological niche of the 2003 epidemic in that region. They assessed which landscape and climate conditions suited the virus's spread. The niche map explains a regional hotspot of a national disease and can guide where surveillance and mosquito control matter most.
plos-pone-0003844:
Lindsey N. Shaw, Catharina Lindholm, Tomasz K. Prajsnar, and colleagues published this bacteria study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Staphylococcus aureus is a highly successful pathogen, perhaps the most common cause of human bacterial disease. Its success rests on adapting gene activity to each environment it meets during infection.

The team identified and characterized sigma S, a new component of that adaptive machinery. Sigma factors direct which genes are read under set conditions. This one shapes both the stress response and virulence of the bacterium, adding a master switch to the portrait of a formidable pathogen. A new switch also means a new point where drugs might act.
plos-pone-0003944:
Satoshi Habuchi, Hidekazu Tsutsui, Anna B. Kochaniak, and co-authors presented a switchable glowing protein in 2008. Glowing proteins that turn on and off with light had lately widened cell imaging. Such proteins let scientists tag one set of molecules and track them alone. Most early versions worked as paired units, which can distort tagging.

Their PLOS ONE article describes mKikGR, a single-unit version that switches with light. A single-unit tag behaves more like the protein it labels. The new tool aids fine imaging of movement inside living cells. It adds a cleaner option to the molecular biology toolkit.
plos-pone-0004044:
Adrian L. Melott searched fossil records for long cycles in life history in a 2008 PLOS ONE article. The Paleobiology Database holds marine invertebrate fossil counts through time. Time series analysis can reveal hidden rhythms in those counts. Earlier work on another database suggested a long biodiversity cycle.

Melott reports a significant cycle near 63 million years. The result agrees with the earlier Sepkoski database analysis. He also explains why the cycle was missed in one prior study. A real cycle would link Earth's history to life's ups and downs. It was printed in PLOS ONE, where the full text stays free to read.
plos-pone-0004144:
Feng-Ping Lu, Kun-Pei Lin, and Hsu-Ko Kuo published this review in PLOS ONE in 2009. Earlier observational studies had linked diabetes to many problems of ageing, from memory loss and dementia to depression, falls, disability, and bladder trouble. How strong and how broad that link really was stayed uncertain.

The authors gathered the existing studies and combined their results in a meta-analysis, a method that pools data across papers. They weighed diabetes against the risk of this whole set of ageing-related conditions at once. The review gives doctors and planners a clearer sense of the extra burdens diabetes adds in later life.
plos-pone-0004244:
Esteve Fernández and colleagues published this public health study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Spain's smoke-free law took effect on 1 January 2006 and covered all enclosed workplaces. Hospitality venues were the exception: owners could choose a full ban, partial restriction with smoking areas, or no restriction at all.

The team followed hospitality workers over time, measuring their exposure to second-hand smoke and their respiratory health. The cohort study tests what a partial law does for the workers it leaves unprotected. Its evidence bears on whether exemptions undo the benefits of smoke-free laws.
plos-pone-0004344:
John Kenny and colleagues published this microbiology study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Staphylococcus aureus is a common human commensal and opportunistic pathogen behind a wide range of infections. Long chain unsaturated free fatty acids are found on skin. They form a barrier to colonisation and infection by this bacterium, acting as an antimicrobial part of innate immunity.

The team studied how S. aureus responds to these fatty acids and survives them. Understanding the bacterium's survival tricks matters for its virulence. Skin's natural antibiotics only work if the target cannot adapt, and this study checks that adaptation.
plos-pone-0004444:
Fat tissue in obese mice draws in stem-like cells with help from an inflammation signal, report Beatriz Galvez, Nuria San Martin, and Carlos Rodriguez in PLOS ONE in 2009. Most adult tissues hold a small pool of mesenchymal precursor cells. These cells can mature into several tissue types, and fat tissue holds many fat cells among them.

The signal in question is TNF-alpha, a protein the immune system uses to raise alarms. Using ob/ob mice, a strain prone to obesity, the team showed the signal is required to pull the precursor cells into white fat tissue. That finding links inflammation to how fat tissue grows and renews itself. It may also matter for using these flexible cells in repair medicine.
plos-pone-0004544:
Cancer signatures from different studies may converge on the same biology even when their gene lists differ, argue Xavier Sole, Nuria Bonifaci, Nuria Lopez-Bigas, and co-authors in PLOS ONE in 2009. Gene expression profiling had produced signatures that predict cancer outcomes better than standard clinical measures. Such signatures were entering clinical practice and were set to shape everyday decisions.

A puzzle followed: signatures for the same cancer often shared few genes. The authors test for biological convergence, whether unlike gene lists point to the same underlying processes. If they do, the signatures agree more deeply than their lists suggest. That would rescue many studies from the scrap heap and help doctors trust gene tests built on different patients.
plos-pone-0004644:
A pilot study asks whether a huge trial of epidural anesthesia in surgery is even feasible, report Peter Choi, W Scott Beattie, Gregory Bryson, and co-authors in PLOS ONE in 2009. Neuraxial blockade, anesthesia delivered near the spine, may reduce heart and lung complications after surgery outside the chest. Early randomized trials suggested a benefit, but recent larger trials were inconclusive.

The PeriOperative Epidural Trial pilot study assessed whether a large multi-center trial could actually be run. Recruitment, protocol adherence, and patient willingness all decide that. The authors conclude the effects may be difficult to study using large randomized trials. A frank feasibility verdict saves the field from spending years and millions on a trial that cannot answer its question.
plos-pone-0004744:
Marina Meli and colleagues surveyed viruses and other germs that threaten the Iberian lynx, in PLOS ONE in 2009. The lynx is viewed as the most at risk cat species in the world. Spain runs a captive breeding plan that brings wild lynxes in to save the species from dying out.

Bringing wild cats in can also bring in disease. The team looked back at how common feline leukemia virus and other germs were in the cats. Knowing the disease load helps vets screen and guard the breeding group. It also protects wild cats when bred cats return.
plos-pone-0004844:
Benjamin Fredembach, Anne Hillairet de Boisferon, and Edouard Gentaz studied learning of arbitrary links between visual, and Auditory stimuli in adults, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Human beings readily associate stimuli perceived in their setting. Children use this ability in reading acquisition when arbitrary links between visual and auditory stimuli must be learned. Linking letters to sounds through repeated exposure and active exploration of print materials.

Haptic exploration strengthened the bond between senses. Touch helps adults link sight and sound too. Multisensory learning applies to education and rehabilitation. The bond effect names that benefit. Replication in other settings will show how robust the findings really are.
plos-pone-0004944:
Burn wounds often get infected with stubborn bacteria. Two culprits are Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Staphylococcus aureus. Both often resist antibiotics. Maya Merabishvili and colleagues described a different weapon in PLOS ONE in 2009. They produced a cocktail of bacteriophages in the lab. Bacteriophages are viruses that kill bacteria. The cocktail was designed for burn patients.

Their phages were chosen to be purely lytic. That means they destroy their bacterial hosts. The small batch passed careful quality control. The paper sets out the production steps for human clinical trials. It is a practical step toward phage therapy for drug-resistant wound infections.
plos-pone-0005044:
Edelfosine is an experimental lipid drug. It kills leukemia cells by triggering apoptosis, programmed cell death. Consuelo Gajate and colleagues studied how it works in Jurkat leukemia cells. Their PLOS ONE paper appeared in 2009. The focus was the death receptor Fas, also called CD95. Lipid rafts are fatty patches in the cell membrane.

The team found raft aggregates enriched in the death-inducing signaling complex. Edelfosine herds Fas receptors into these rafts. There the killing machinery assembles. Genetic, biochemical and imaging evidence all supported the picture. The raft clustering explains the drug's antileukemic action. It shows how a lipid drug turns the cell's own death switch against cancer.
plos-pone-0005144:
Heart failure weakens the blood vessels' ability to relax. The relaxation signal is nitric oxide. Erhan Ararat and Frank Brozovich studied a drug's effect on that system. Their PLOS ONE paper appeared in 2009. The drug is losartan, a common blood-pressure pill. The team tracked a signaling pathway called p42/44 MAPK.

Losartan decreased that MAPK signaling. It also preserved expression of a key relaxation protein, the LZ-positive form of MYPT1. That protein sets how vessel muscle responds to nitric oxide. The drug protects the relax machinery at two levels. The finding reveals a benefit beyond blood-pressure lowering. It may explain part of losartan's value in heart failure. Familiar pills can hide fresh mechanisms.
plos-pone-0005244:
Enzymes that cut proteins, a process called proteolysis, are tightly controlled in healthy tissue. When control fails, cutting runs on in inflammation, tumors, cystic fibrosis, and pancreas disease. Mellet and colleagues built an imaging method to spot that cutting in PLOS ONE in 2009.

Their approach uses magnetic resonance imaging with a probe switched by an Overhauser effect. The probe lights up where proteolysis is active, without any cut into the body. Watching enzyme activity directly could help doctors judge disease activity and whether a treatment is working. A scan that shows where the wrong cutting takes place could help a doctor pick the right drug and see at once if it calms the site.
plos-pone-0005344:
Protein interaction networks contain hub proteins with very many partners, and hubs are thought to be especially important. Yet hubs are usually defined by an arbitrary cutoff on partner count. Vallabhajosyula and colleagues tackled that definition problem in PLOS ONE in 2009.

Most of these networks follow a scale-free pattern, with a few huge hubs and many small nodes. An ad hoc cutoff can mislabel which proteins count as hubs. A principled way to identify hubs sharpens every conclusion drawn from network maps of the cell. A hub list built on sand would waste years of lab work, so a strict rule for what counts as a hub is ground work that the whole field can stand on.
plos-pone-0005444:
Gregory Shearer and colleagues looked at blood fats and sudden heart trouble in a 2009 PLOS ONE study. Doctors judge heart risk by mixing standard measures such as blood pressure and cholesterol. The team asked whether the fat pattern inside red blood cells could pick out patients with acute coronary syndrome.

They compared red cell fat patterns in patients with the syndrome and in others. The patterns did help separate the groups beyond what standard factors show. A blood test based on cell fats might one day sharpen risk checks for people who reach hospital with chest pain.
plos-pone-0005544:
Han Liu, Richard Buus, and Michael Clague studied control of a cancer-related receptor in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. ErbB2 is a receptor that drives growth in some breast cancers and resists the normal process that destroys used receptors. Its partner, the EGF receptor, is destroyed more readily.

The team found that a protein called POH1, part of the cell's disposal machine, helps set how much ErbB2 a cell keeps. Changing POH1 changed receptor levels. That control point could become a new way to lower ErbB2 in cancers that depend on it.
plos-pone-0005644:
Richard Lester and co-authors studied immune responses in Kenyan female sex workers with HIV in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. Traces of gut bacteria leaking into the blood are reported in people with HIV and may drive constant immune activation. The response to those traces runs through a sensor called TLR4.

The team linked the amount of viral RNA in blood to how the natural TLR response behaved. Their results suggest the virus itself skews the response to bacterial traces. That skewing may feed the long-term harm HIV does beyond lowering cell counts.
plos-pone-0005744:
Luis Vidali and co-authors brought a new glowing probe to plant cells in 2009, revealing a lively web of actin at growing tips. Actin fibers drive tip growth in plants, but older probes distorted the very fibers they showed. They bunched fibers, slowed growth, or missed the finest strands.

The new probe, Lifeact joined to a green glowing protein, left growth normal. It showed a dynamic actin network at the apex that older methods blurred. Seeing true actin behavior opens the way to test how cells steer growth toward light, water, and support. Plant growth mechanics gains a clearer lens.
plos-pone-0005844:
Vanessa Deveaux and co-authors reported in 2009 that a cannabis-related receptor worsens obesity-linked inflammation and liver fat. In obesity, inflamed fat tissue drives insulin resistance and fatty liver disease. The CB2 receptor, found on immune cells, regulates innate immunity.

Activating CB2, the team found, made those problems worse, not better, in their models. That result surprised some expectations for cannabinoid drugs in metabolic care and weight control. It warns that CB2-targeted medicines could harm metabolic health. Knowing the receptor's true role in obesity helps set safe directions for drug development around the endocannabinoid system.
plos-pone-0005944:
One gene can steer many nerve cells, each in its own way. Leung-Hang Ma, Beena Punnamoottil, Silke Rinkwitz and colleagues traced that spread in the zebrafish hindbrain in a 2009 PLOS ONE study. They focused on hoxb4a, a guide gene, marking single cells with glowing labels in a fish line bred for this kind of tracking.

Their maps show the gene at work in a mosaic pattern, with varied effects from cell to cell in the rear brain. A careful count of those effects links one gene to a wide range of nerve cell fates. The work helps explain how genes and life experience together shape behavior, using a fish whose young brain can be watched cell by cell.
plos-pone-0006044:
A faster way to watch T cells switch on could speed the hunt for immune drugs. Kwangmi Kim, Lin Wang and Inkyu Hwang built such a tool in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper presents a high-throughput flow cytometry assay for studying how the T cell receptor turns on LFA-1, an integrin that helps T cells grip and move.

LFA-1 is a favored target for drugs against inflammation and autoimmunity. An assay that screens many conditions at once lets teams map the activation machinery step by step. The method turns a slow, one-at-a-time craft into a systematic search, which is what the paper's title promises and its design delivers.
plos-pone-0006144:
A cucumber plant can carry male flowers, female flowers, or both kinds at once. Adnane Boualem, Christelle Troadec, Irina Kovalski and colleagues found the switch behind one such form in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper studies andromonoecy, plants bearing male and bisexual flowers, in two Cucumis species, the genus of cucumber and melon.

A conserved ethylene biosynthesis enzyme leads to that form, the title reports. Ethylene is the plant kingdom's ripening and sex-setting gas, so its maker is a fitting switch. Knowing the exact enzyme lets breeders tune flower sex on purpose, a practical trait in crops where flower type decides fruit set and yield.
plos-pone-0006244:
Inositol is a building block for many fatty signals that cells need to live. Renee Guerin and colleagues studied fission yeast, which cannot make its own inositol, in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. When inositol runs out, the yeast cells die by apoptosis, a tidy form of cell death.

A protein called calnexin, which helps fold other proteins, regulates that death process. The study shows starvation death is controlled, not just a collapse. Controlled death in a simple yeast helps decode similar choices in human cells. It may also matter for fungi that infect people.
plos-pone-0006344:
Breakdown products of the amino acid tryptophan may contribute to Alzheimer's disease. Abdur Rahman and colleagues focused on quinolinic acid, an excitotoxin from the kynurenine pathway, in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. That pathway is overactivated in Alzheimer's brains, and quinolinic acid overexcites neurons.

Quinolinic acid induced tau phosphorylation in human neurons, the title reports. Tagged tau forms the tangles that mark the disease. Linking a metabolic toxin to tau changes names a possible disease driver. Blocking the pathway could become a treatment strategy worth testing. Drugs that block this path are one clear next step the work points to.
plos-pone-0006444:
Sreekumar Othumpangat and co-authors studied a lung virus that hits infants hard, in PLOS ONE in 2009. The virus is respiratory syncytial virus, or RSV. In infected infants, nerve growth factors in the airways rise. It was unclear which cells make them, where in the airways, and why the rise happens.

The team analyzed the pattern in detail across the respiratory tract. Their title gives the key result: nerve growth factor, NGF, is an essential survival factor for the cells lining the bronchial tubes during RSV infection. The finding reframes a nerve signal as a lung defense. It may inform care for severe infant RSV.
plos-pone-0006544:
Frederic Michon and Mark Tummers tracked how research topics rise and fall in PLOS ONE in 2009. The increase in the size of the scientific community created an explosion in scientific production. The authors analyzed the dynamics of biomedical scientific output from 1957 onward. They examined the dynamic interest in topics within the biomedical community.

Topics surge when tools, funding, and results align, then fade as fields mature. Mapping those waves helps funders and historians understand science itself. It can also warn young researchers about saturated areas. The study treats the literature as data about the community that makes it.
plos-pone-0006644:
Deepak Sharma and co-authors compared heat-shock proteins from yeast species in PLOS ONE in 2009. The cell sap of most eukaryotes holds many forms of Hsp70, a chaperone that helps proteins fold. These forms are highly conserved, kept alike across species, and differ mostly in when and where they are made. The team studied the SSA branch of this family. They asked how well each form can stand in for lost ones in baker's yeast.

Their title says the answer varies a lot: function differs widely both within one species and across species lines. Near-identical proteins thus turn out not to swap freely at all. That care in detail counts when one species is used to model the proteins of another.
plos-pone-0006744:
Deborah M. Sloboda and her team fed rats set diets to test how food shapes breeding in PLOS ONE in 2009. Food before puberty seems to set the pace of sexual growth. A mother's diet and a child's diet may each play a part. Which part each one plays was not clear. The team used a known rat model to pull the two apart.

They mixed diets before birth and after birth in set pairs. Then they tracked how fast the young rats matured and how their ovaries worked. Each food history left its own mark on adult breeding. The marks lasted long past the diets that caused them. The work shows that food in the womb and food in youth shape fertility in distinct ways.
plos-pone-0006844:
Anne E. Carlson and colleagues blocked a sperm channel to test its role in swimming power in PLOS ONE in 2009. The channels are called CatSper and occur only in sperm. They are required for hyperactivated motility and male fertility. They also admit calcium when conditions turn alkaline. Hyperactivation is the forceful swimming mode needed to reach an egg.

The team targeted native CatSper channels pharmacologically in sperm. Blocking them undermined maintenance of hyperactivation. That shows the channel is needed continuously, not just to start. The work confirms CatSper as a fertility control point. It is relevant to both contraception research and infertility diagnosis.
plos-pone-0006944:
Chaitali Dutta and Nicholas Rhind studied stressed DNA replication in fission yeast in PLOS ONE in 2009. When replication stalls, cells switch on a checkpoint response. In fission yeast, the checkpoint kinase Cds1 protects the normal S-phase program. It does this partly by regulating MBF, the transcription factor for S-phase genes.

The authors examined a specific set of transcripts switched on by the checkpoint. They tested which of them help cells resist replicative stress. Separating helpful transcripts from bystanders clarifies how cells survive stalled replication. That survival mechanism is relevant to cancer, where replication stress is constant.
plos-pone-0007044:
Mark Hester, SungWon Song, Carlos Miranda, and colleagues reprogrammed human stem cells in PLOS ONE in 2009. Turning adult cells back to pluripotency is a prized goal. Such cells could model human disease in a dish. They could also yield patient-specific stem cells for therapy. Mouse neural stem cells had recently been reprogrammed with few factors.

The team achieved the change in human neural stem cells with just two factors. Fewer factors mean a simpler, possibly safer recipe. Human neural cells start closer to pluripotency than skin cells do. Their result maps a shorter road back to the stem cell state.
plos-pone-0007144:
Marta Milo, Daniela Cacciabue-Rivolta, Adam Kneebone, and colleagues studied a hearing development gene in PLOS ONE in 2009. Gata3 is a zinc finger transcription factor. It helps direct how the mammalian inner ear forms. The team used conditionally immortal cell lines that model specific auditory cell types. These lines let them follow gene activity as cells differentiate.

Their genomic analysis mapped what gata3 controls during that process. Temporal profiles show which genes answer gata3 at each stage. The map aids understanding of inherited hearing loss, where this factor is one known player among many.
plos-pone-0007244:
Stefan Lim, Lilach Pnueli, Jing Hui Tan, and colleagues modeled hormone pulse decoding in pituitary cells in 2009. A brain hormone called GnRH arrives in pulses from the hypothalamus. Pulse frequency directs production of gonadotropin subunits, which control reproduction through hormones such as LH and FSH.

Different pulse speeds favor different subunit genes. The authors study how negative feedback governs this frequency decoding in gonadotrope cells. Their PLOS ONE paper builds a model of the process. Understanding the code matters for treating fertility problems and hormone disorders linked to pulse patterns.
plos-pone-0007344:
Ranji Singh, Joseph Lemire, Ryan J. Mailloux, and colleagues found a variant energy cycle protecting bacteria from aluminum in 2009. The tricarboxylic acid cycle is essential in almost all aerobic organisms. Its precise control and integration into wider metabolism were not fully understood, leaving room for surprises in how bacteria adapt it.

The authors report an alternative cycle in Pseudomonas fluorescens. This variant generates ATP energy and oxalate, a compound that binds metals. Both products counter aluminum toxicity for the bacterium. Their finding shows metabolic flexibility that could help bacteria survive metal-contaminated environments.
plos-pone-0007444:
Rabia Hussain and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on tuberculosis exposure among household contacts of TB patients. In countries where TB is common, half or more of healthy people test positive on the tuberculin skin test. That large group forms a reservoir for future cases. The immune signals marking a fresh conversion to positive were largely unknown.

The team followed exposed household contacts for two years. They tracked which immune biomarkers changed as people converted from negative to positive. Those changes flag recent infection more precisely than the skin test alone. Knowing them could focus preventive treatment on people most likely to develop disease. The study gives TB programs a sharper tool for finding risk early.
plos-pone-0007544:
William Gilliland and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on two division-regulating proteins in fruit fly eggs. Mps1 and Polo are kinases needed for proper cell division in both meiosis and mitosis. In fly oocytes, they gather on thread-like filaments during an early division stage. The team found that low oxygen changes this picture. Hypoxia drives the proteins onto those filaments in a temporary sequestration.

The filaments dissolve in collagenase, which identifies them as collagen-like structures. Sequestering key regulators is a way to pause or reroute division under stress. An egg short on oxygen may need exactly such a pause. The odd hideout reveals a stress response built into the machinery of egg formation. It also raises questions about how oxygen sensing reaches the division apparatus in other cells.
plos-pone-0007644:
Michael Hoffmann and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on ATAD-3, a protein of the mitochondria. In mammals, its relative is thought to help organize the mitochondrial DNA. The exact function remained unresolved. The team characterized the roundworm's version of the protein and tested its importance. Worms offer fast genetics for exactly such questions. Removing or reducing ATAD-3 showed what depends on it.

ATAD-3 proved essential. Without it, mitochondrial activity failed and development stalled. A protein of uncertain purpose turned out to be load-bearing for the cell's power plants. That verdict gives mitochondrial biology a firm fact to build on. It also validates the worm as a model for this corner of human cell biology. Power plant failures underlie many diseases, and each essential part is a clue.
plos-pone-0007744:
Alice Chang and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It asks what decides whether the heart restarts after cardiac arrest in rats. Fewer than half of arrest victims regain circulation, even with hospital resuscitation. One grim clue involves the brain stem, the control center at the brain's base.

When the brain stem dies, a flat heart rhythm tends to follow after a lag. The authors present brain stem death as the vital determinant of recovery. If the brain stem fails, circulation does not resume. The finding reframes what resuscitation must protect: the brain stem, not just the heart.
plos-pone-0007844:
Pu Zhang and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It profiles gene activity across the first days of human development. Preimplantation development, from egg to early embryo, is a crucial step. Its molecular basis in humans was poorly known.

The team applied microarrays to three hundred ninety-seven human oocytes and embryos. Samples covered six developmental stages. They charted how transcription rises and falls across those stages. That dynamic map shows when the embryo's own genome takes charge. It offers a reference for fertility research and embryo health.
plos-pone-0007944:
Li Guo and colleagues traced two families of tiny gene regulators across human groups in PLOS ONE in 2009. The regulators are microRNAs, short RNA strands that tune how strongly genes are used. The families, miR-17 and miR-124, are old and wide spread.

By mapping haplotypes, the linked sets of variants people inherit together, the team read how the families spread and changed. The patterns carry marks of selection as groups split and moved. The study shows even very small regulators have a rich past, shaped by the same forces that shaped the rest of our genome.
plos-pone-0008044:
Margarita Malakhova and colleagues mapped the working end of a cancer-linked enzyme in PLOS ONE in 2009. The enzyme, RSK2, is switched on by growth signals and helps cancer cells multiply. It carries two working ends; the team solved the shape of the front one while active.

The shape was not single or stiff. It came in several forms, which may matter for how the enzyme grips its targets. Drug makers aim at such pockets, and a moving pocket is harder to hit. Knowing the range of shapes should sharpen the aim.
plos-pone-0008144:
Kamraan Gill and Dale Purves argued that musical scales grow from the biology of hearing in PLOS ONE in 2009. Humans can tell apart hundreds of pitches in one octave, so countless scales are possible in principle. Yet cultures keep landing on a small set of like scales.

The authors tie that pull to how the ear and voice are built, above all to the sounds of speech. Scales that echo the pitch patterns of the human voice feel natural because the hearing system is tuned to them. Music, on this view, rides on gear built for talk.
plos-pone-0008244:
Thibaut Quillard and colleagues studied Notch signaling in vessel cells in a PLOS ONE paper from 2009. The Notch pathway controls key functions in endothelial cells, which line blood vessels. Most attention had gone to one receptor, Notch4. Little was known about what Notch2 contributes in these cells. The team investigated how Notch2 is regulated and what it does.

They found Notch2 signaling makes endothelial cells more prone to apoptosis, or programmed death. It does so by lowering survivin, a protective molecule. Balancing cell survival matters for healthy vessels. The result adds a missing piece to vascular biology.
plos-pone-0008344:
Jie Yang and colleagues studied diabetes recovery in mice in a PLOS ONE paper from 2009. Mouse beta cells, which make insulin, normally regenerate by copying themselves. Progenitor cells near pancreatic ducts may also exist. Whether other islet cells can become beta cells in the living body was open. The team used streptozotocin to damage beta cells and induce diabetes.

Overexpressing the protein p21cip in beta cells improved recovery from the induced diabetes. Better recovery suggests p21 helps the remaining cells rebuild. That finding bears on efforts to restore insulin production. It may inform future diabetes therapies.
plos-pone-0008444:
Ellen Nohr and co-authors use a large Danish birth study in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper on severe obesity. Little was known about fertility and birth health in women with severe obesity. The authors draw on the Danish National Birth Cohort. That study holds self-reported data from many young women. They sort the women by level of obesity.

They then link each level to a wide range of outcomes. Outcomes cover both mother and child. The paper shows where risks rise most sharply. It gives doctors and mothers clear facts for care and planning. It also shows why weight before pregnancy matters so much.
plos-pone-0008544:
Nicole Creanza and co-authors chart flu evolution within seasons in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Long-term influenza evolution has been well studied. Patterns of sequence diversity within a single season are less clear. The team analyze H3N2 influenza genomes from New York State. Samples span ten years of flu seasons. They use mean Hamming distance to measure sequence differences. That metric counts how many positions differ between genomes.

They find intraseasonal changes in evolutionary dynamics. Certain dominant sequences rise and sweep within a season. Diversity does not simply accumulate at a steady pace. Those within-season patterns matter for forecasting which strain comes next.
plos-pone-0008644:
Aline Oliveira and co-authors vaccinate mice against a foal pneumonia germ in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Rhodococcus equi causes pneumonia in foals that conventional vaccines fail to prevent. The team recently showed immunization with Salmonella expressing the VapA antigen protects mice. VapA is a key virulence protein of R. equi. Salmonella serves as a live oral vaccine vector. They now report the immune responses behind that protection in detail.

Vaccination induces mucosal and systemic Th1 responses against VapA. Th1 responses are the cell-mediated arm needed against intracellular germs. Those responses provide protection against R. equi infection in mice. The strategy may finally yield a working foal vaccine.
plos-pone-0008744:
Pablo Fernandez-Marcos, Cristina Pantoja, Agueda Gonzalez-Rodriguez, and colleagues removed a growth gene from mice. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. The gene, Sei1, helps assemble the machinery that pushes cells to divide. It also boosts a growth-driving transcription factor. Cancers often show too much Sei1, hinting at an oncogene role. A knockout mouse could test that hint directly.

Mice without Sei1 grew and formed tumors much like normal mice. Their pancreases, though, worked poorly. The split result shows one gene can matter greatly in one organ and little elsewhere. That nuance guides how Sei1 should be judged as a cancer target.
plos-pone-0008844:
Sascha Pust, Anne Berit Dyve, Maria Torgersen, and colleagues checked whether raft proteins guide toxins through cells. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Flotillins sit in fatty patches of cell membranes and inner compartments. Two toxins offered test cargo: bacterial Shiga toxin and a plant toxin. Toxins hijack normal transport routes to reach their targets. Whether flotillins help or hinder that ride was open.

Altering flotillin levels changed how the toxins were taken up and moved. Transport and flotillin placement influenced each other. The interplay reveals a route toxins exploit inside cells. Blocking such routes could blunt toxin damage.
plos-pone-0008944:
Jianhua Ruan reported a winning entry to a gene-prediction contest in PLOS ONE in 2010. The contest, called DREAM3, asked teams to predict gene activity from data. Systems biologists build computer models of how genes turn each other up and down. Judging those models fairly is hard, so the contest used hidden test data.

Ruan's algorithm ranked among the top performers at predicting expression patterns. The paper explains the method and how it handled the challenge data. Contests like DREAM give the field a rare honest scoreboard for its tools. Strong prediction methods help researchers guess which genes drive a cell's behaviour.
plos-pone-0009044:
Hendrik Weisser and co-authors tested whether a virus's predicted vigour helps forecast HIV therapy results, in PLOS ONE in 2010. A virus's replicative capacity is how well it copies itself in the lab. Clinicians sometimes blame odd treatment responses on a strain's fitness. But its true value for predicting outcomes was murky.

The team predicted replicative capacity straight from the virus's genes. They used support vector machines, a pattern-finding algorithm. Adding that prediction barely improved forecasts of therapy response. The modest result tempers hopes that viral fitness numbers guide treatment much.
plos-pone-0009144:
Haiyan Huang and Qiang Wu catalogued the full detox gene family of the zebrafish, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Ugt enzymes tag oily small molecules with a sugar acid to disarm them. Tagged molecules dissolve in water and can leave the body easily. This detox system handles many drugs and body wastes alike.

The team identified the complete Ugt set carried by the zebrafish. Comparing it with other species revealed the family's deep evolutionary variety. Fish carry their own expansions and losses of these detox genes. The catalogue supports using zebrafish to test how drugs break down.
plos-pone-0009244:
George Mtove and co-authors published this child health study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Invasive salmonella infections are a serious danger to African children. Yet hard numbers on how often they strike were scarce. The team ran fever surveillance at a rural hospital in Tanzania.

They tested children admitted with fever to estimate what share had invasive salmonellosis. They also compared their figures with earlier studies from other places. Reliable local numbers matter because treatment and vaccines depend on knowing the true burden. The study adds a rural Tanzanian measure to a map that is still mostly blank.
plos-pone-0009344:
Carina Banning and co-authors published this methods study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Proteins constantly meet and part inside living cells, and those meetings run the cell. A technique called FRET can detect such meetings under a microscope. But microscopy is fiddly and can only survey a few cells at a time.

The team built a FRET assay that runs on a flow cytometer instead. Flow machines stream thousands of cells past a laser, reading each one. Their assay can therefore identify and analyze protein interactions in large cell numbers. That scale turns interaction hunting from a craft into a screen.
plos-pone-0009444:
Marietta Keckeis and co-authors compared sleep disorders and blood sugar in PLOS ONE in 2010. Past work had linked short or broken sleep with poor handling of sugar. Yet no study had set the main sleep disorders side by side to compare them. The team measured how patients handled glucose, the main sugar in blood.

Patients with sleep disorders showed impaired glucose tolerance more often than expected. The pattern linked disturbed nights to a step toward diabetes. Clinics that treat sleep may thus be a place to catch sugar problems early. The authors argue that fixing sleep could also help protect against diabetes.
plos-pone-0009544:
David Silvestre and colleagues found a second job for a known protein in tumors in PLOS ONE in 2010. Most biologists know c-Fos as a gene switch in the cell nucleus. It can also sit at inner membranes and switch on fat molecule making. The team checked brain tumors from patients and from mice prone to such tumors. They looked at where c-Fos sat and what it was doing.

In these tumors, c-Fos in the cytoplasm was busy driving fat production. That activity helped tumors of both the central and peripheral nervous systems grow. A protein with a hidden second job offers a fresh target. Blocking that job might starve tumors of the fats they need.
plos-pone-0009644:
