poe-mesmeric-revelation-1844:
Edgar Allan Poe set Mesmeric Revelation in print in 1844. The form is a death bed talk held by art. A man in a mesmeric trance, close to death, speaks with the scribe. He tells what God, stuff, and the soul are past the veil of flesh.

Stuff is not dead, the voice holds, but one fine spread of force. Each grain of it can think, feel, and at last join the whole. Death is a shift, not an end, in this strange scheme. The tale is the most famed of Poe's works on the mesmeric creed.
quicherat-proces-jeanne-darc-vol2-1844:
Quicherat's second volume, printed in 1844, carries his Joan of Arc edition from sentence toward review. It completes the papers of the 1431 condemnation trial. It then opens the rehabilitation proceedings of 1455 and 1456, a full generation later.

The volume bridges the fire at Rouen and the inquiry that undid its verdict. Readers watch a famous case reverse itself in its own papers.
religion-natural-and-revealed-1844: Religion, Natural and Revealed, 1844. The two religions. The archive keeps it. Its contents inform the historical record. The library keeps the document safe. Writers of history may cite it later. The paper lasts as a quiet witness.
religion-natural-and-revealed-or-the-nat: Religion, Natural and Revealed, 1844. Another edition. This book preserves that work. History keeps its place secure. Such papers rarely see the light of day. The file is now open to the public. Its contents inform the historical record.
sandby-mesmerism-opponents-1844:
George Sandby answered mesmerism's first British critics in Mesmerism and Its Opponents, from 1844. Sandby was a clergyman who had watched mesmeric cures at close range. His narrative of cases replies to doctors and editors who scorned the practice. Detailed case histories carry the weight of his argument.

Patients relieved of pain and fits tell their own part in his pages. The book records the first wave of English controversy over mesmerism. Charges of fraud and folly met charges of closed minds. Sandby writes as a witness more than a theorist. His cases fed the movement's early defense. The volume is a primary record of a public fight.
schiller-poems-first-period-1844:
The Poems of Schiller: First Period gathers the young Schiller's lyrics in the Bohn Standard Library translation. The poems date from his stormy first years as a writer, before Weimar classicism calmed his style. Some of them stand inside his early play The Robbers, sung or quoted by its outlaws.

Love, rage at tyrants, and wild joy in nature drive these early pieces. The verse is rough, bold, and full of youthful excess by design. Readers can hear the voice that shocked Germany in 1781 taking shape. The Bohn set sorted Schiller's poems by period so English readers could trace his growth. This first volume gives the raw material of the later master.
schiller-poems-second-period-1844:
Schiller's middle years produced the poems in this second-period volume of the Bohn translation. By then Schiller had settled into study, friendship with Goethe, and steady fame. The Song of the Bell, his most loved long poem, belongs to this era of his work.

In that poem the casting of a church bell frames the whole course of a human life. Birth, love, work, loss, and death pass in its stanzas like scenes at a foundry. Other pieces here treat art, gods, and the dignity of man. The voice is calmer than the young rebel's, but the moral fire remains. Lyric readers rank this period at the height of Schiller's power.
schiller-poems-suppressed-1844:
Schiller chose not to reprint some of his early poems, and the Bohn editors gathered those pieces as the Suppressed Poems. They complete the four-volume English set of his poetry. In them the young writer speaks without the guard he later kept on his work.

The suppressed pieces show sharper satire, bolder feeling, and rougher craft than he later allowed. Some attack named targets of his youth with open scorn. Others try forms and tones he soon outgrew and disowned. Scholars value the set because it shows growth honestly, false starts included. English readers in the Bohn volumes could meet the whole Schiller, not only the polished classic. The volume rewards those who like a poet unbuttoned.
schiller-poems-third-period-1844:
The late poems in this third-period Bohn volume include Schiller's great ballads of his Weimar years. The Diver sends a young page to the sea floor for a king's golden cup, twice. The Glove tests a lady's love with a cruel and famous gesture among wild beasts.

Other ballads treat hostages, cranes, and rings, each turning on fate and honor. Schiller wrote these pieces in friendly rivalry with Goethe in 1797, their ballad year. The tales move swiftly, with clear scenes and ringing morals that never preach. Generations of German schoolchildren learned them by heart. In English they remain the easiest gate into Schiller's poetry.
sir-perceval-of-galles-thornton-1844:
Sir Perceval of Galles is a Middle English romance preserved in the Thornton manuscript. J. O. Halliwell edited it for modern readers in 1844. It gives the Grail hero Perceval a rough, funny English shape, quite unlike the solemn French versions.

Perceval grows up wild in the woods, knowing nothing of courts or arms. His blunders are comic, but his strength is real, and he fights his way toward knighthood. The poem is kin to the Welsh tale of Peredur, retold in a northern voice. Readers meet the innocent fool of the Grail story at his most boisterous and earthy.
siris-a-chain-of-philosophical-reflexion: Siris, a chain of philosophical reflexions, Berkeley's 1744 work. The tar-water philosophy. This book preserves that book. The archive keeps the paper open to all. Its pages add to the record of the past. Scholars prize such firsthand sources.
snorri-heimskringla-laing-1844:
Samuel Laing published The Heimskringla; Or, Chronicle of the Kings of Norway in 1844, the first English translation of Snorri Sturluson's kings' sagas. Snorri, an Icelandic poet and chieftain, wrote the Heimskringla in the 1200s. It tells the story of Norway's kings from mythic times to his own age.

Sagas of kings such as Olaf Tryggvason, Saint Olaf, and Harald Hardrada fill the chronicle, drawn from poems and oral memory. Battles, voyages, and feuds move at saga pace, terse and vivid. Laing's version founded the study of Norse history in English. Readers who want the Vikings in their own tradition's telling still start with Snorri.
synopsis-of-phrenology-presenting-genera: Synopsis of Phrenology, 1844. Another synopsis. This book preserves that work. Tomorrow's readers will find it. History keeps its place secure. Such papers rarely see the light of day. The file is now open to the public.
thackeray-barry-lyndon-1844:
William Makepeace Thackeray published Barry Lyndon in 1844, a novel in the form of a rogue's memoir. Redmond Barry is an Irish adventurer who tells his own story with great pride. He serves as a soldier, deserts, and becomes a gambler and cheat across Europe. He marries a rich widow to gain rank and wealth.

Barry boasts even as his schemes ruin others and himself. Thackeray lets the narrator expose his own vanity on every page. The book first appeared as The Luck of Barry Lyndon in a magazine. Its unreliable narrator was ahead of its time. Readers now prize its irony and pace.
the-trial-or-more-links-of-the-daisy-cha: Charlotte Yonge's The Trial continues the beloved story of the Daisy Chain. The sorely tried May family faces new sorrows and duties. Steadfast faith carries them through every loss. A cherished sequel for Victorian readers.
tob-13144:
Swami Vivekananda taught Bhakti Yoga, the path of devotion, in lectures later gathered as a book. Bhakti is love of God as the heart's way to the Absolute. Vivekananda spoke of it with the fire that marked all his teaching.

He treats prayer, ritual, images, and the guru, arguing that forms help love grow until it needs no props. Real bhakti, for him, asks nothing back and loves God for God's own sake. The talks move from outer worship to a love so full it ends all sense of separation, and they show the devotional side of Vedanta clearly.
tob-4144:
Griffith's verse Ramayana opens with volume one in 1870, and India's beloved epic found its English singer. Prince Rama, exiled from his father's court through a queen's demand, withdraws to the forest with his wife Sita and brother Lakshmana. There the demon king Ravana steals Sita away to Lanka.

The search for Sita, the alliance with the monkey hosts, and the march toward the island war all begin in this volume. Griffith's flowing lines carried Valmiki's Sanskrit to Victorian drawing rooms. Verified from the 1919 edition, his first volume still reads as the warmest entry into the great story of Rama.
tob-4244:
T. W. Rolleston retold the myths of the Celtic peoples for general readers in Myths and Legends of the Celtic Race. Cuchulain's boyhood deeds and last stand, Finn and the Fianna, the Tuatha Dé Danann arriving in Ireland, and the great voyage tales fill the narrative. Rolleston aimed at story first, where Charles Squire, his contemporary, aimed at system.

Less scholarly than Squire and more narrative, the book gives the stories as stories, in readable English dress, with the Irish material especially full. Rolleston, an Irish writer involved in his country's cultural revival, wrote to make a heritage available. For many readers this remains the Celtic myths' friendliest single-volume telling.
turgot-oeuvres-daire-vol1-1844:
Eugène Daire edited the works of Turgot for a great series of French economists, and the first volume appeared in 1844. Turgot, who died in 1781, had been Louis the Sixteenth's finance minister and the Enlightenment's best hope in power. Daire's edition gathered writings that had been scattered or buried since the Revolution.

Volume 1 holds the young Turgot: his Sorbonne discourses on the progress of the human mind, his encyclopaedia articles, and early pieces on trade and money. Readers watch the statesman-philosopher in his formative years, forming the ideas he would later try to enact. His praise of free trade and his sketch of history as progress both appear here. The volume lets the mind that would reform France be studied before power came, and before power broke it.
turgot-oeuvres-daire-vol2-1844:
Daire's edition of Turgot's works closed with a second volume in 1844. The first volume had shown the young thinker; this one gives Turgot the minister. By the 1770s Turgot ran first a province, then the finances of France itself, the great test of Enlightenment ideas in office.

The volume prints his edicts, his official letters, and his plans to free the grain trade, end forced labor on roads, and cut court waste. Each reform met fierce resistance from the privileged orders it threatened. In 1776 the king dismissed him, and the attempt to save the monarchy by reform collapsed with his fall. Daire's edition preserves the record of that campaign in Turgot's own words. It reads as the Enlightenment in power, and its tragic defeat, documented by the man who led it.
un-ga-res-44:
India brought a complaint to the young United Nations in 1946: the treatment of people of Indian origin in the Union of South Africa. The General Assembly took up the charge in Resolution 44, adopted on 8 December 1946. It was one of the first times the Assembly judged how a member state treated people inside its own borders.

The Assembly states that the treatment has harmed friendly ties between India and South Africa, and that ties will worsen without a fair settlement. It holds that the treatment must match the deals struck between the two states and the pledges of the UN Charter. Both states must report back at the next session.
un-ga-res-a-69-44:
Missiles that can carry mass-kill warheads are the target of Resolution A/69/44, from the General Assembly's sixty-ninth session. The spread of such ballistic missiles, it says, feeds growing strains on safety at home and abroad. The text recalls Assembly votes on the point since 2004 and the UN's duty, under the Charter, to guard peace.

Praise goes to the Hague Code of Conduct against Ballistic Missile Proliferation, adopted at The Hague on 25 November 2002. The code asks states to show restraint and to share word of their missile plans in advance. Such open steps, the Assembly holds, build trust and help curb the spread of the missiles themselves.
un-ga-res-united-nations-general-assembl: General Assembly Resolution 44 was adopted on 8 December 1946, at the fifty-second plenary meeting. It took up India's complaint about the treatment of Indians in the Union of South Africa. The Assembly stated that this treatment had harmed friendly ties between the two member states. It would harm them more without a fair settlement. The treatment should match the two governments' agreements and the Charter. Holding that, the Assembly asked both to report back at the next session on steps taken.

Resolution 69/44 of the General Assembly supports the Hague Code of Conduct against Ballistic Missile Proliferation, adopted at The Hague in 2002. The Assembly welcomes the fact that 137 states have subscribed to the voluntary code. The code builds transparency through pre-launch notifications and annual declarations on missile and space policies. It calls on states that have not subscribed to do so. This applies especially to those with ballistic missile or space launch capabilities. It urges subscribers to widen participation and improve how it is carried out.
un-sc-res-1244: Among the formal acts of the United Nations Security Council sits Resolution 1244, which the catalog dates to 1999. The Council is the UN body charged with world peace and security, and it speaks formally through texts like this one. For students of the UN, the record offers the Council's language itself rather than a summary written later.
un-sc-res-1344:
UNMEE, the border mission for Ethiopia and Eritrea, was renewed in March 2001. On 15 March 2001 the Security Council extended it until 15 September 2001. Troop and observer levels stayed as set in 2000. The Council restated both states' sovereignty and borders. It also stressed their duties under humanitarian and refugee law. The December 2000 peace deal framed the whole text.

Both parties had to finish the steps left under their agreements. Rearranging forces to create the Temporary Security Zone mattered most. The Council stressed a hard link in the deal. The peacekeeping mission would end only when the border was fully drawn and marked. The parties also had to fund the boundary commission.
un-sc-res-144:
A quarrel between Cuba and the United States reached the Council in July 1960. Cuba's foreign minister addressed the members. On 19 July 1960 the Council decided to pause its own debate. It would wait for a report from the Organization of American States. Both countries belonged to that regional body. Its charter, like the United Nations Charter, favored peaceful settlement. The Council noted the deep concern the dispute had caused.

Regional states were invited to help find a peaceful solution. Meanwhile every other state had to avoid acts that raised tension. The step favored the regional route over a New York fight. Cuba objected, but the adjournment held. The dispute soon hardened into a lasting feature of the Cold War.
un-sc-res-1444: From the Council's official record comes the text numbered 1444, catalogued here at 2001. Behind each numbered text lies a meeting, a draft, and a vote, even when the final wording runs to a few lines. Read in sequence with its neighbours, it helps trace how Council practice grew across the postwar decades. No summary replaces it; the record itself is the content of the entry.
un-sc-res-1544: Resolution 1544 stands in the Council's numbered sequence as a formal act of the fifteen-member body. The version here is the official record as transcribed on English Wikisource. Readers get the complete decision text: the findings the members recorded first, then the operative paragraphs through which the Council exercises its power over peace and security questions.
un-sc-res-1644:
The Hariri murder inquiry was extended on 15 December 2005. The investigation commission's report, S/2005/775, laid out its findings on the 14 February 2005 Beirut bombing. It had killed former prime minister Rafiq Hariri and 22 others. Lebanon's prime minister wrote on 5 December asking for six more months. The Council praised the commission's professional work under hard conditions.

The Council welcomed the report. As the commission advised and Lebanon asked, it extended the commission's mandate for a further six months. Syria's duty to cooperate fully and without conditions was underlined once more. The commission would report on the inquiry's progress every three months, or sooner if events required. The Council noted Lebanon's wish that those finally charged be tried by a court of an international character. The commission could also give Lebanon technical help on its inquiries into the other attacks since October 2004.
un-sc-res-1744:
Resolution 1744 let the African Union send its own peace mission into Somalia, a country without a working central government since 1991. Somalia's weak interim government faced Islamist fighters and clan militias. The Council backed African troops as the force on the ground.

The text sets the mission's tasks: guard government sites and airports, protect aid convoys, and help train Somali security forces. It also calls on other states to fund and supply the effort. Readers get the founding terms of AMISOM, the African-led mission that became a central actor in Somalia's long war.
un-sc-res-1844:
On 20 November 2008, Resolution 1844 on Somalia was adopted. Violence and blocking of the peace process continued across the country. Piracy off the coast was rising fast. Piracy money could pay for weapons that broke the long-standing arms embargo.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council creates targeted sanctions for Somalia. People and groups named by the sanctions committee face travel bans and asset freezes. No one may supply them with weapons or military help. The targets are those who threaten the peace deal, attack the transitional bodies or the African Union mission, break the embargo, or block aid. Listed names get a public summary of the reasons, and a way to ask for removal.
un-sc-res-1944: Resolution 1944, adopted in 2010, is a Security Council act kept in this collection through a transcription of the record. The fifteen members' joint text is the whole content: what they found, what they decided, and what they set in motion. The entry preserves that joint text entire, in the order and wording of its adoption.
un-sc-res-244:
A sharp crisis shook Cyprus in the autumn of 1967, and the Secretary-General appealed directly to Greece, Turkey, and Cyprus. His appeals went out in November and December that year. He offered his good offices to all three governments, and each of them accepted. His report of 8 December said the peacekeeping force was still required. Resolution 244 was adopted unanimously on 22 December 1967.

The Council extended the force's stationing for three months, ending on 26 March 1968. The parties were invited to use the Secretary-General's good offices at once. Moderation was called for on all sides. Above all, the text asked for a fresh and determined effort toward a lasting settlement of the Cyprus problem. The crisis of that autumn had shown how fast the island could slide back toward war between Greece and Turkey.
un-sc-res-344: The formal record of the Security Council includes the text numbered 344, catalogued for 1973. The Charter gives the Council power to bind member states, which is why its resolutions are kept with such care. Here the primary source stands on its own, with the formal phrasing that lawyers and historians rely on. The catalog places it in the DECLASSIFIED group of official public records.
un-sc-res-44: Palestine's future went back to the General Assembly under Security Council Resolution 44, passed on 1 April 1948. The Council had the Palestine Commission's first two monthly reports and its special report on safety in the land. The five permanent members had met, as asked in March, and their talks had been reported. The Council now asks the Secretary-General to call a special session of the Assembly, under Article 20 of the Charter, to weigh the future rule of Palestine anew.
un-sc-res-444:
Lebanon's interim force faced obstruction in the south in early 1979. On 19 January 1979 the Security Council renewed UNIFIL for five months. The new term ran until 19 June 1979. The Secretary-General's report described grave problems on the ground. The Council deplored the lack of cooperation, above all from Israel. Israel, it said, was helping irregular armed groups in the south. Those groups blocked the force's deployment.

Lebanon's government earned praise for sending its army south. The Council urged it to do more, in step with UNIFIL. The aim was to restore Lebanese authority in the area. The Secretary-General and the force's soldiers also won warm thanks. The text mixes a routine renewal with open frustration.
un-sc-res-744:
Security Council Resolution 744, adopted on February 25, 1992, recommended San Marino for membership in the United Nations. The tiny republic, ringed by Italy, counts itself the oldest surviving republic in the world, with roots in the year 301. Size had long kept it outside the world body, but the end of the Cold War opened the door to Europe's small states.

The Assembly admitted San Marino on March 2, 1992. The council's text is brief and formal, like all admission votes of that season. For San Marino, the seat carried a point of pride: a state older than most kingdoms at last took the same formal place as the largest powers in the General Assembly hall.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci:
Security Council resolution 1244, adopted in 1999 under Chapter VII, sets the terms for ending the Kosovo crisis. The Federal Republic of Yugoslavia had agreed to the peace principles put forward in Belgrade on 2 June 1999. The Council demands an immediate, checkable end to violence and repression in Kosovo, and a rapid, phased withdrawal of all Yugoslav and Serb military, police and paramilitary forces.

The resolution sets up an international security presence in Kosovo, able to use all necessary means. It is to deter renewed fighting, disarm the Kosovo Liberation Army, and protect returning refugees. It establishes a United Nations interim administration. It is to run basic government, build democratic institutions for the interim, and hold elections, pending a final settlement. Both presences start for an initial twelve months. The Council reaffirms Yugoslavia's sovereignty and territorial integrity. It promises Kosovo substantial autonomy and real self-administration.

A shaky peace in the Horn of Africa needed more time in 2001. Ethiopia and Eritrea had signed their peace in Algiers the past June and December. A UN force, UNMEE, kept the two foes apart. Its term was set to lapse. Resolution 1344 passed with no dissent on 15 March 2001.

The force won six more months, to 15 September 2001. Both states had tasks to finish. Troops had to shift so a buffer zone could form. UN staff needed free roads and a direct air link between the two capitals. Mine maps had to change hands. The text ties the force's end to a drawn and marked border. Both sides had to fund the team doing that work.

Cuba and the United States faced off at the Council in July 1960. Havana's foreign chief spoke of threats from the north. The split had grown since Castro's rise. A rule from the Charter's book framed the clash. So did the pact of the Americas group, the OAS. Resolution 144 passed on 19 July 1960 by nine votes to none. Poland and the Soviet team held back.

The Council chose to wait. Its own probe was put on hold. Word from the OAS would come first. That body had the case in hand. Its states were asked to help find a calm fix. All other states had to shun acts that would heat the clash. The move showed a young UN at ease with turf: some fights were left, for a time, to the region's own house.

Another year is granted to the International Security Assistance Force in Afghanistan on 27 November 2002. The force, authorized in December 2001, helped the Afghan authorities keep security in Kabul. Command had passed from the United Kingdom to Turkey in June 2002, with a joint German-Dutch lead planned next.

The authorization is lengthened for one year beyond 20 December 2002. States in the force may use all necessary measures to carry out its mandate. More contributions of troops, equipment, and money are called for, including to the force's trust fund. Its leadership is to report every three months through the Secretary-General on how the work is going.

Israel's military operation in Rafah, in the Gaza Strip, draws a response on 19 May 2004. Palestinian civilians had been killed in the area, and Israeli forces had demolished many homes in the Rafah refugee camp. Grave concern is voiced at the worsening situation in the territory occupied since 1967.

Israel is called on to respect its duties under international humanitarian law, and in particular not to demolish homes in breach of that law. An end to violence is demanded, and both sides are called on to carry out their duties under the Road Map peace plan at once. The vote was 14 in favour and none against, with the United States abstaining.

Resolution 1644, adopted on 15 December 2005, follows the inquiry into the Beirut bombing that killed former Lebanese prime minister Rafiq Hariri and 22 others on 14 February 2005. An International Independent Investigation Commission was helping Lebanon find who did it. Lebanon asked for six more months of that help, and the commission backed the request.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council extends the commission's mandate until 15 June 2006 and demands that Syria cooperate fully and without delay. It notes with concern that Syria had not yet given full help. It also asks the Secretary-General to study what kind of international tribunal could try those charged, and lets the commission help Lebanon probe other attacks there since October 2004.

An African Union mission in Somalia, AMISOM, is authorized on 20 February 2007. Somalia's transitional federal institutions needed support to build national governance and hold an inclusive political process. The African Union, the Arab League, and the regional authority had all backed reconciliation, and the Union had offered to deploy.

African Union member states are authorized to establish the mission for six months. Its tasks include supporting dialogue and reconciliation, protecting the transitional institutions, and helping create conditions for aid delivery. The 1992 arms embargo is lifted for supplies and training meant solely for the mission and for building Somalia's security sector. Union members are urged to contribute troops and resources.

Somalia gains targeted sanctions in Resolution 1844, adopted on 20 November 2008. The 1992 arms embargo stood alone. The Council had warned it would act against those blocking a peaceful political process, threatening the Transitional Federal Institutions or AMISOM by force, or breaking the embargo. Piracy off the coast, it noted, might be financing embargo violations.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council imposes three measures on individuals and entities the Sanctions Committee designates: a travel ban, an asset freeze, and a targeted arms embargo. The embargo covers weapons and military assistance. Designation covers those threatening peace or the Djibouti Agreement, violating the arms embargo, or obstructing humanitarian aid. Basic-expense and other exemptions apply. The Committee must publish narrative summaries of reasons for each listing. It must notify states so listed persons are informed and handle delisting requests, including petitions through the Focal Point set up by Resolution 1730 (2006).

Haiti was preparing to vote nine months after the earthquake that struck in January 2010. Resolution 1944, adopted on 14 October 2010, concerns MINUSTAH, the United Nations mission in the country. Presidential and legislative elections were set for 28 November. Camps of displaced people still faced gang violence and health risks.

The Council extended MINUSTAH's mandate until 15 October 2011. Its strength stayed at up to 8,940 troops and 4,391 police. The mission had to support the elections and help rebuild the Haitian National Police. It also had to help the courts and speed up the resettlement of displaced families. Once a new government took power, a fresh review of security in Haiti would follow.

Weeks after a flare-up that nearly brought Greece and Turkey to war, the Council acted on Cyprus again. On 22 December 1967, it adopted Resolution 244 without dissent. The Secretary-General had appealed to all three governments that autumn. He had also offered his good offices, and each capital had replied.

His report said the island still needed the peace force. Cyprus agreed to the force staying on. The text restates the founding decision, Resolution 186. It then extends the posting for three months. The move kept troops in place while talks cooled tempers in Athens, Ankara, and Nicosia. It marks the Council mopping up after the November crisis.

A peace conference on the Middle East was about to open in Geneva in December 1973. It would meet under United Nations auspices. Resolution 338 had ordered talks on carrying out Resolution 242, the land-for-peace plan of 1967. Resolution 344 was adopted on 15 December 1973, just before the conference began.

The Council expressed the hope that the Geneva conference would move quickly. Its goal was a just and durable peace in the Middle East. The Council said it trusted the Secretary-General to play a full and effective part at the conference. He would chair its proceedings if the parties wished. He was asked to keep the Council informed of the talks. He also had to supply all the help and facilities the conference needed.

The Palestine partition plan had stalled amid growing violence by the spring of 1948. Under Resolution 42, the Council's permanent members had consulted and reported back. The Palestine Commission's progress reports were also before the Council. Resolution 44 was adopted on 1 April 1948. It passed the question upward. The Council asked the Secretary-General to call a special session of the General Assembly, under Article 20 of the Charter. The special session would consider the future government of Palestine further. That single step is the whole content of the resolution.

Some notes place this text in Cyprus. Its true home is south Lebanon. The force there, UNIFIL, was ten months old and blocked at every turn. Its second term had run out with tasks undone. The chief's report of 12 January 1979 laid out the mess. Resolution 444 passed on 19 January 1979 by twelve votes to none.

UNIFIL won five more months, to 19 June 1979. The Council blamed poor help from the sides, Israel most of all. Israel was charged with aiding armed bands in the south. Praise went to the force's troops and chiefs. Lebanon was cheered for sending its army south. It had to draw up a staged plan to retake full rule there. The Council vowed to meet in three months for a fresh look.

The world's oldest republic waited longest for its UN seat. On 25 February 1992, the Council adopted Resolution 744 without a vote. San Marino, a tiny enclave inside Italy, had applied to join the United Nations. Most states of its size had joined decades before.

Having weighed the bid, the Council urges the Assembly to admit San Marino. The Assembly acted the next month. The microstate's late arrival fit a wider shift of the era. Even the smallest sovereign states were taking seats and votes. The UN edged closer to truly full membership. San Marino brought with it a claim to seventeen centuries of self-rule.
ynglinga-saga-laing-1844: The Ynglinga Saga, the first part of Snorri's Heimskringla, in Samuel Laing's 1844 translation. It traces Norway's kings from mythic beginnings. This edition preserves that Norse historical saga. Its pages add to the record of the past.
zoist-vol-02-1844:
Volume two of The Zoist covers April 1844 to January 1845. Elliotson's journal presses on with its twin subjects, cerebral physiology and mesmerism. Case reports arrive from doctors across Britain who tried the mesmeric sleep. Operations without pain hold pride of place in the reports.

Somnambulists and their strange sight supply the journal's wonders. Critics in the medical press trade blows with Elliotson's circle in print. The journal binds those fights beside the clinical record. Across thirteen volumes the set forms the English movement's full archive. Volume two shows the fight at full heat. Surgeons, patients, and skeptics all speak here. The record stays primary and direct.
